01 / READ THIS FIRST

The constitutional design, not just a list of Articles

Parliament and State Legislatures are representative institutions with law-making, financial, deliberative and accountability functions. Their authority is extensive, but it is derived from—and limited by—the Constitution. The central thread of this DU topic is the reconciliation of representative government, executive accountability, legislative autonomy and constitutional supremacy.

What this guide covers—and what it does not pretend to cover

  • All 89 Articles in the assigned ranges: Articles 79–122 and 168–212. Paired Union/State notes explain the operative clauses, distinctions and connections. A searchable constitutional-text appendix supplies the complete extracted text of these Articles.
  • All ten prescribed cases, syllabus numbers 21–30: facts, procedural setting, issues, competing submissions, holdings, reasoning, principles, limitations and examination applications.
  • All five directly relevant PYQ sub-questions verified in the uploaded papers: three from the centenary-chance paper and two from December 2024, each with a developed model answer. Six closely related questions are answered separately.
  • No invented exam history: additional practice problems are expressly labelled practice. “All PYQs” here means all relevant questions discoverable in the supplied papers, not every DU examination ever held.

Read the topic through four recurring questions

  1. Who constitutes the institution? Houses, nominated/elected members, presiding officers, terms and sessions.
  2. Who may enter or remain? Positive qualifications, constitutional and statutory disqualifications, adjudicating forums, vacancy and ministerial eligibility.
  3. How is an authoritative decision made? Ordinary Bills, Money Bills, financial business, voting, assent and the effect of dissolution.
  4. How far is autonomy protected? Speech and vote immunity, contempt and expulsion, judicial review and constitutional rights.

Essential distinctions before beginning

Do not confuseThe legally important difference
Parliament / a HouseArticle 79 includes the President and both Houses; the President is not a member of either House. Article 168 similarly includes the Governor.
Non-member / disqualified personA qualified non-member can temporarily be a Minister. A disqualified person cannot use the six-month window to defeat eligibility requirements.
Disqualification / expulsionDisqualification rests on a constitutional/statutory ground and its designated mechanism. Expulsion is a distinct disciplinary privilege; it does not itself create a general future electoral disqualification.
Appeal / suspension of sentence / stay of convictionThey have different effects. Mere appeal or bail does not neutralise conviction-based disqualification. An express stay of conviction is legally different.
Irregularity / illegalityArticles 122 and 212 protect proceedings against challenges based only on procedural irregularity, not substantive illegality or unconstitutionality.
“Six months” in different provisionsMinisterial non-membership, the session gap, ordinary-Bill deadlock, election scheduling and bye-election deadlines do not share one legal rule.

Edition and nomenclature cautions

The 2022 DU booklet calls LB-301 Constitutional Law-I; the uploaded December 2024 paper prints Constitutional Law II. Both titles are preserved rather than silently “corrected.” The scanned centenary paper prints no examination year; a handwritten date is not treated as official dating. The upload named constitution.pdf contains five pages of handwritten constitutionalism/federalism notes, not the Constitution’s bare text.

Legal supplements are individually dated. Preparation on 30 September 2026 does not imply that every development through that date, or every institution’s changing membership, has been exhaustively audited. The authoritative statutory edition used for the Article text is the Government of India’s 1 May 2024 edition.

02 / INSTITUTIONAL ARCHITECTURE

Composition, representation and duration

Indian bicameralism is not uniform. At the Union level, both Houses are constitutionally essential and ordinary legislation normally needs both. At the State level, the Council is optional, can be created or abolished through Article 169, and generally exercises a suspensive rather than an equal veto.

Articles 79 and 168 · What constitutes the legislature?

Article 79: Parliament consists of the President, the Council of States and the House of the People. This is a constitutional description of the law-making institution; it does not make the President an MP or give the President an ordinary vote in either House. Bicameralism at the Union is compulsory within the present constitutional structure.

Article 168: every State has a legislature consisting of the Governor and either one House or two Houses. In a bicameral State the Houses are called the Legislative Council and Legislative Assembly; in a unicameral State the sole House is the Legislative Assembly. The Governor is not an MLA/MLC merely because the Governor forms part of the institution.

Functional difference: the political executive is accountable to Lok Sabha/Assembly under Articles 75(3)/164(2), not to the President/Governor as an independently governing political superior. Legislative membership and executive responsibility overlap in a parliamentary system, but constitutional heads have their own defined functions.

Textual list versus an actually functioning Council

The official 2024 Article 168 text includes editorially bracketed references to Madhya Pradesh and Tamil Nadu whose associated creation provisions were not brought into operation as explained in that edition’s footnotes. Do not infer a functioning Council merely from an uncommenced textual amendment. The established Council framework familiar to this syllabus is Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh. A current institutional count should always be checked against commencement notifications and subsequent Article 169 legislation, not an unqualified textbook list.

Constitution, Arts. 79, 168; Article 168 footnotes in the official 1 May 2024 edition. See constitutional source [1].

Article 80 · Rajya Sabha: constitutional maximum, election and nomination

  1. Clause (1): twelve members nominated by the President plus not more than 238 representatives of States and Union territories: a constitutional ceiling of 250, not an assertion that 250 seats are filled at any particular time.
  2. Clause (2): allocation of territorial seats is governed by the Fourth Schedule. States do not enjoy the equal representation found in the US Senate. The Council is federal in representational purpose without a rule of numerical equality between States.
  3. Clause (3): nominated members must have special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art or social service. Nomination enriches deliberation with expertise; it does not dispense with constitutional qualifications.
  4. Clause (4): State representatives are elected by the elected members of the State Legislative Assembly using proportional representation by the single transferable vote. The entire State electorate does not directly elect them, and MLCs are not part of this constitutional electoral college.
  5. Clause (5): Parliament determines by law the manner in which Union-territory representatives are chosen.

Related statutory provisions

RPA 1951 Section 3 requires a person chosen as a State/UT representative to be an elector for a Parliamentary constituency in India. The uploaded Act records the 2003 substitution of “in India” for the previous State/territory formulation. Do not impose an obsolete same-State elector requirement. This particular section concerns territorial representatives; do not automatically treat its wording as a condition expressly written for Presidential nominees.

Section 154 ordinarily gives a Rajya Sabha member a six-year term. A member filling a casual vacancy ordinarily serves the unexpired term, not a fresh six years. Article 83 makes the chamber continuing; it does not itself state the individual six-year term.

Illustration: if a State has several Rajya Sabha seats becoming vacant together, preferential voting under STV can permit representation of more than one political formation. The number of seats allocated to the State still depends on the Fourth Schedule, not the number of first-preference votes cast.

Constitution, Art. 80 and Fourth Schedule; uploaded RPA, s. 3 (PDF p. 10), s. 154 (PDF pp. 61–62). Article 84 qualifications are discussed below.

Article 81 · Lok Sabha: territorial and population-based representation

Clause (1): not more than 530 members chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies in the States, and not more than 20 to represent Union territories, chosen in the manner Parliament provides by law. The elected-seat constitutional ceiling is therefore 550. This is not the same thing as the number of currently allotted or occupied seats.

Clause (2)(a): the ratio between the seats allotted to a State and its population should, so far as practicable, be the same for all States. The proviso excludes States whose population does not exceed six million from this inter-State allocation requirement. Clause (2)(b): within a State, the population-to-seat ratio should, so far as practicable, be uniform across constituencies.

Clause (3): population normally refers to the last preceding census with published relevant figures, but the constitutional freeze retains the 1971 basis for inter-State allocation and the 2001 basis for intra-State constituency division until the relevant figures for the first census taken after 2026 are published. The date 2026 does not by itself automatically redraw constituencies or enlarge Lok Sabha.

Why “552” is an unsafe present-law answer

The older figure added up to two Anglo-Indian nominees under Article 331. Article 334(b)’s seventy-year period for Anglo-Indian representation by nomination ended in January 2020. The 104th Amendment extended SC/ST reservation but did not similarly extend Anglo-Indian nomination. Historical wording of Article 331 must be read with Article 334 rather than treated as a presently operative extra two seats.

Constitution, Arts. 81, 331, 334; official edition incorporating the 104th Amendment. The special election qualifications in RPA s. 4 are treated in the membership chapter.

Article 82 · Readjustment after a census

Upon completion of each census, Parliament may determine by law the authority and manner for readjusting (i) allocation of Lok Sabha seats to States and (ii) division of each State into territorial constituencies. The first proviso protects representation in the existing House until its dissolution. The second proviso allows the President to specify the effective date and permits elections using existing constituencies until readjustment takes effect. The third proviso preserves the specified 1971/2001 bases pending the first post-2026 census’s published figures.

Related legislation: the Representation of the People Act, 1950 provides the representational/electoral-roll framework; the Delimitation Act, 2002 is an important statutory implementation of boundary readjustment. The RPA 1951 principally governs qualifications, election conduct and election disputes. These Acts have different jobs.

Examination point: equal representation is an aspiration qualified by “so far as practicable,” census freezes, small-State protection and reservation. Delimitation changes constituency geography; an increase in the total membership requires compliance with the applicable constitutional ceiling and statutory allocation scheme.

Constitution, Arts. 81–82; related-statute connection is supplementary to the DU case extracts.

Article 169 · Creation or abolition of a State Legislative Council

  1. Initiating resolution: the Legislative Assembly must pass a resolution supporting creation or abolition by (a) a majority of its total membership and (b) a majority of not less than two-thirds of members present and voting.
  2. Parliamentary law: following the qualifying resolution, Parliament may provide by law for abolition of an existing Council or creation in a State without one. The Assembly resolution is not itself the creation/abolition instrument and does not legally compel Parliament to act.
  3. Consequential provisions: the Parliamentary law may contain necessary amendments to the Constitution and supplemental, incidental and consequential provisions.
  4. Clause (3): this law is not deemed a constitutional amendment for Article 368 purposes. Parliament does not need the Article 368 special majority merely because the Article 169 law makes the authorised consequential constitutional adjustments.

Worked majority: an Assembly has 200 members; 150 are present and 135 vote. Two-thirds of those voting is 90, but a majority of total membership requires at least 101. Consequently 100 affirmative votes fail, even though they exceed two-thirds of 135.

Rationale: the Constitution leaves States a locally initiated choice of a revising chamber while maintaining Parliament’s role in altering the institutional framework. It is not a State-government executive decision, nor a matter the Council can veto under the Article 169 route.

Constitution, Art. 169. Compare the distinct “effective majority” for removal of presiding officers in Arts. 94, 179 and 183.

Article 170 · Legislative Assemblies

Clause (1): the general range is not more than 500 and not less than 60 directly elected members from territorial constituencies. Special constitutional arrangements qualify the minimum: for example, Article 371F(a) provides a minimum of 30 for Sikkim, Article 371I a minimum of 30 for Goa, and Article 371G(c) a minimum of 40 for Mizoram. These are special minima, not necessarily the actual present membership of each Assembly.

Clause (2) and its explanation: constituency division should, as far as practicable, secure a uniform population-to-seat ratio within the State. Published census population ordinarily governs; the specified 2001 reference continues pending the first post-2026 census’s relevant figures.

Clause (3): after each census, Assembly membership and territorial constituencies are readjusted by the authority and manner Parliament determines by law. Existing representation is protected until dissolution; the President specifies the effective date; the constitutional freeze distinguishes the total-seat 1971 basis from the territorial-division 2001 basis.

Link to representation: Article 332 provides SC/ST reservation in State Assemblies. Article 333’s historical Anglo-Indian nomination must be read with the expiry rule in Article 334(b), just as Article 331 must at the Union level.

Constitution, Arts. 170, 332–334, 371F, 371G, 371I; official 2024 edition.

Article 171 · Legislative Councils: five channels of membership

Clause (1): total Council membership must not exceed one-third of total Assembly membership, subject to a minimum of forty. The forty-member minimum is a specific proviso; do not apply the fraction mechanically without reading it. Clause (2) makes the following composition applicable until Parliament otherwise provides by law.

Article 171(3)Approximate shareSelection channel and elements
(a)One-thirdElectorates composed of members of municipalities, district boards and other local authorities specified by Parliamentary law.
(b)One-twelfthElectorates of State residents who have been graduates for at least three years, or possess qualifications Parliament treats as equivalent.
(c)One-twelfthElectorates of State residents who have, for at least three years in the preceding six years, taught in educational institutions within the State not lower in standard than a secondary school, as Parliamentary law prescribes.
(d)One-thirdElected by members of the State Legislative Assembly, from persons who are not Assembly members.
(e)Remainder, conventionally one-sixthNominated by the Governor according to clause (5).

Clause (4): elections under (a), (b), (c) and (d) use proportional representation by single transferable vote; Parliamentary law regulates the territorial constituencies for the first three categories. Clause (5): nominees have special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art, the co-operative movement or social service.

Important differences from Rajya Sabha: a Council represents differentiated functional electorates within a State; Rajya Sabha territorially represents States/UTs. Article 171 expressly includes the co-operative movement, whereas Article 80’s nomination list does not. The graduate/teacher qualification is a qualification of the electorate for that category; it must not be carelessly converted into a universal requirement that every MLC hold a degree or be a teacher.

RPA connection: Section 6 requires an elected Council candidate to be an elector for an Assembly constituency in that State; a Governor-nominated Council candidate must be ordinarily resident in the State. Article 173 still supplies citizenship, oath and age qualifications. Section 156 supplies the ordinary six-year term and treatment of casual vacancies.

Constitution, Art. 171; uploaded RPA, s. 6 (PDF p. 12), s. 156 (PDF pp. 62–63).

Articles 83 and 172 · Duration of institutions and terms of members

InstitutionConstitutional ruleWhat follows
Rajya Sabha / State CouncilNot subject to dissolution; as nearly as possible one-third retire every second year according to Parliamentary law.The chamber continues even while individual seats turn over. Ordinary member term: six years under RPA ss. 154/156.
Lok Sabha / State AssemblyFive years from the date appointed for its first meeting, unless sooner dissolved; expiry itself operates as dissolution.Do not count the five years from declaration of election results or from every member’s individual oath date.
Emergency extensionWhile a Proclamation of Emergency operates, Parliament may by law extend the popular House’s duration for no more than one year at a time, and not beyond six months after the Emergency ceases.Extension is by Parliamentary law, not by the President/Governor merely issuing an order. The proviso does not make every kind of emergency proclamation interchangeable.

Case connection: the Gujarat Reference distinguishes the life of an existing Assembly under Article 172 from the frequency of its sessions under Article 174. Once dissolved, the outgoing Assembly has no “next session.” U.N.R. Rao, discussed in the DU material, separately explains why dissolution does not eliminate the mandatory Union Council of Ministers.

Constitution, Arts. 83, 172; DU Gujarat Reference pp. 132–137; DU U.N.R. Rao pp. 66–68.

Related constitutional representation provisions

Articles 330 and 332: provide reserved seats for Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes in Lok Sabha/Assemblies, with specified territorial arrangements. The general constitutional reservation period in Article 334(a), extended by the 104th Amendment, runs to eighty years from commencement of the Constitution. Articles 325–326: prevent specified discriminatory exclusions from electoral rolls and provide adult suffrage for Lok Sabha/Assembly elections, subject to lawful disqualifications. Voter age eighteen is not the age for becoming an MP/MLA.

POST-2022 ENACTMENT · NOT DU TEXT

106th Amendment, 2023: women’s reservation framework

The enacted framework inserts Articles 330A, 332A and 334A, and amends Article 239AA for Delhi. It provides as nearly as possible one-third reservation for women in Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and the NCT Delhi Assembly, including one-third of the SC/ST-reserved direct-election seats within the relevant scheme. It does not establish an equivalent reservation in Rajya Sabha or Legislative Councils.

Article 334A links implementation to a delimitation exercise after publication of the relevant figures of the first census taken after the Amendment’s commencement. It states a fifteen-year period from the specified commencement, contains a Parliamentary continuation provision, provides rotation after subsequent delimitation as Parliament determines by law, and protects existing representation until dissolution. Enactment, statutory commencement, census publication, delimitation and operational reservation are separate steps. No particular implementation year is assumed here.

Official 2024 Constitution, Arts. 239AA, 330A, 332A, 334A; 106th Amendment Act, ss. 1–6: [2]. The official 2024 edition marks commencement notification status in its footnotes; check later Gazette notifications for a current commencement assertion.

Comparative evaluation for an examination answer

Bicameralism can improve scrutiny, continuity and plural representation, but it can also delay policy and create party-political conflict. The constitutional response differs by level: an ordinarily equal Union second chamber helps express federalism, while the optional State Council has restricted legislative and financial powers. Hence it is inaccurate to describe a State Council simply as a smaller Rajya Sabha. Establish the constitutional purpose, composition and voting powers before evaluating democratic legitimacy.

03 / MAKING THE INSTITUTION WORK

Presiding officers, secretariats and sessions

A legislature needs institutional continuity and internal order. The Constitution separately regulates the holder of an office, the person presiding at a particular sitting, the House’s duration, and the duration of a session. Many examination errors result from treating these as one thing.

Articles 89 and 182 · Chairmanship of the upper chambers

Rajya Sabha: the Vice-President is the ex officio Chairman. Rajya Sabha chooses a member of the Council as Deputy Chairman as soon as may be, and chooses a replacement whenever that office becomes vacant. The Chairman is not a Rajya Sabha member; the Deputy Chairman is.

State Council: under Article 182, the Council chooses two of its own members as Chairman and Deputy Chairman, and fills vacancies in either office. Unlike the Rajya Sabha Chairman, the State Council Chairman does not hold office by virtue of a separate Vice-Presidential election.

Why the difference matters: it affects removal, ordinary voting rights when not presiding, and the constitutional source of tenure. Article 90 does not provide for removal of the Vice-President; Article 67(b) does.

Constitution, Arts. 89, 182; related Art. 67(b).

Articles 90 and 183 · Vacation, resignation and removal

Article 90 applies to the Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman: the office is vacated on cessation of Council membership; resignation is by signed writing addressed to the Chairman; removal is by a Council resolution passed by a majority of all the then members, with at least fourteen days’ notice of the intention to move it.

Article 183 applies to both Chairman and Deputy Chairman of a State Council: office ends with Council membership; each resigns by writing to the other; either may be removed by a resolution supported by a majority of all the then members after the same fourteen-day notice requirement.

Related Vice-Presidential rule: Article 67(b) requires a Rajya Sabha resolution passed by a majority of all its then members and agreed to by Lok Sabha, with at least fourteen days’ notice. It is not removal by the Rajya Sabha Chairman’s internal deputy-office provision.

Effective-majority illustration: a chamber has a sanctioned membership of 100 but five vacancies. “All the then members” refers to the 95 existing members; 48 affirmative votes are required. It is not two-thirds of those voting and not necessarily a majority of the sanctioned 100.

Constitution, Arts. 90, 183, 67(b).

Articles 91 and 184 · Vacancy of office versus absence from a sitting

  1. Article 91(1): while the Rajya Sabha Chairman’s office is vacant, or while the Vice-President acts as President/discharges Presidential functions, the Deputy Chairman performs the Chairman’s duties. If the Deputy Chairmanship is also vacant, the President appoints a Council member for that purpose.
  2. Article 91(2): at a sitting where the Chairman is absent, the Deputy Chairman presides; if also absent, the House’s rules determine the person; failing that, the House determines another person.
  3. Article 184: in a State Council, the corresponding vacancy chain is Chairman → Deputy Chairman → Council member appointed by the Governor. For absence at a sitting, the rules and ultimately the Council determine the substitute.

Key distinction: a temporary absence calls for an acting presiding officer; a vacant constitutional office calls for performance of its duties according to the vacancy mechanism. The President/Governor is not given a general power to replace an inconvenient presiding officer whenever political controversy arises.

Constitution, Arts. 91, 184.

Articles 92 and 185 · No presiding over one’s own removal

Article 92(1): the Chairman must not preside while a resolution to remove the Vice-President is under consideration; the Deputy Chairman must not preside while a resolution to remove the Deputy Chairman is under consideration. The ordinary substitute-presiding mechanism applies as if the relevant officer were absent.

Article 92(2): during consideration of the Vice-President’s removal, the Chairman may speak and otherwise participate but is not entitled to vote on the resolution or any other matter during those proceedings. The Chairman is not a Council member, and this clause does not create a first-instance vote.

Article 185: the State Council Chairman/Deputy Chairman similarly cannot preside over their own removal. The Chairman has a right to speak and participate and, because the Chairman is a Council member, may vote in the first instance but not exercise a casting vote during these proceedings. Do not import the Rajya Sabha Chairman’s complete no-vote rule here.

Institutional principle: these provisions prevent a person from controlling the conduct of proceedings concerning that person’s tenure. They are not identical to the separate questions about a Speaker’s adjudication under the Tenth Schedule.

Constitution, Arts. 92, 185, 100 and 189.

Articles 93 and 178 · Election of Speaker and Deputy Speaker

Lok Sabha and every State Assembly must, as soon as may be, choose two of their members as Speaker and Deputy Speaker and fill a vacancy in either office. Article 93 supplies the Union rule; Article 178 the State rule. The phrase “as soon as may be” creates a constitutional obligation but does not specify a numerical period of days in the Article itself.

Functions within the broader scheme: presiding over debate, maintaining order, administering procedural rules, certifying Money Bills, assessing the voluntariness and genuineness of resignation, and deciding defection disputes under the Tenth Schedule. Each function has its own legal source and review standard; the title “Speaker” is not a general source of unreviewable power.

Pro tem role: a temporary officer commonly facilitates oaths and election of the regular Speaker. Seniority is a parliamentary convention, not wording expressly inserted into Articles 93 or 178. Anil Kumar Jha deals with the risk of manipulation through a comparatively junior pro tem appointee and gives interim floor-test safeguards.

Constitution, Arts. 93, 178; supplement: Anil Kumar Jha, judicial order ¶¶4–6.

Articles 94 and 179 · Speaker/Deputy Speaker tenure

  • Cessation of House membership: ordinarily vacates the office.
  • Resignation: Speaker writes to Deputy Speaker; Deputy Speaker writes to Speaker.
  • Removal: resolution of the popular House passed by a majority of all its then members, after at least fourteen days’ notice of intention to move it.
  • Continuity exception: on dissolution, the Speaker does not vacate office until immediately before the first meeting of the new Lok Sabha/Assembly. This explicit protection is for the Speaker, not a general continuation of every dissolved-House member or of the entire institution.

Connection to Gujarat: the Union argued that continuation of the Speaker meant the “House” survived independently of the dissolved Assembly. The advisory opinion rejected that institutional fiction: continuity of a specified office does not create a live Assembly capable of having a next session.

Constitution, Arts. 94, 179; DU Gujarat Reference, pp. 132–134, especially ¶¶40–48 and the submission recorded in ¶56.

Articles 95 and 180 · Acting Speaker arrangements

Office vacant: the Deputy Speaker performs duties; if both offices are vacant, a House member appointed by the President (Lok Sabha) or Governor (Assembly) performs them. Absent from a sitting: the Deputy Speaker acts; if also absent, the rules determine the substitute; if no such person is present, the House itself determines another person.

This is the constitutional foundation for temporary arrangements, not authority to choose an outsider to preside. The relevant person must be a member when the Article expressly requires one. House rules, panels of chairpersons and pro tem practice operate within this constitutional framework.

Constitution, Arts. 95, 180. Compare Arts. 91 and 184 for upper chambers.

Articles 96 and 181 · Speaker’s participation during removal

The Speaker/Deputy Speaker cannot preside while the officer’s own removal resolution is under consideration; the substitute mechanism applies. The Speaker may speak and participate, and may vote in the first instance only, but not exercise a casting vote, on the removal resolution or another matter during these proceedings. Article 96 governs Lok Sabha; Article 181 governs the Assembly.

Voting consequence: ordinary proceedings give the presiding officer only a casting vote on a tie. Removal proceedings reverse the Speaker’s special position: the Speaker is not presiding and has the permitted first-instance vote, without a tie-breaking vote. A tied removal vote will not thereby obtain the constitutionally required effective majority.

Constitution, Arts. 96, 181, read with 94/179 and 100/189.

Articles 97 and 186 · Salaries of presiding officers

Parliament determines by law the salaries and allowances of the Rajya Sabha Chairman/Deputy Chairman and Lok Sabha Speaker/Deputy Speaker; until then, the Second Schedule applies. State legislatures similarly determine the remuneration of Assembly Speakers/Deputy Speakers and Council Chairmen/Deputy Chairmen under Article 186.

Related law: the Salaries and Allowances of Officers of Parliament Act, 1953 gives statutory form to the Union arrangements. Separate laws govern MPs and Ministers; the different Acts should not be confused. Charged-expenditure provisions in Articles 112(3) and 202(3) help protect the institutional independence of specified offices by removing their listed remuneration from an ordinary demand-for-grant vote.

Constitution, Arts. 97, 186 and Second Schedule; related statute identified as supplementary.

Articles 98 and 187 · Separate legislative secretariats

Clause (1): each House has a separate secretarial staff, without preventing common posts for both Houses. Clause (2): Parliament/State legislature may regulate recruitment and service conditions by law. Clause (3): pending such a law, the President/Governor may make rules after consultation with the relevant Speaker/Chairman, and the rules operate subject to a later law.

Purpose: administrative support for parliamentary proceedings should not simply be an executive department answerable to the very Ministers whom the legislature scrutinises. At the same time, separate secretariats do not mean that common staffing arrangements are constitutionally forbidden.

Operational distinction: secretariat administration is not automatically a protected speech, vote or internal proceeding. Determine the legal character of the act before invoking Article 122/212 immunity.

Constitution, Arts. 98, 187.

04 / SITTINGS & RESPONSIBLE GOVERNMENT

Sessions, participation and dissolution

Articles 85 and 174 · Summoning, prorogation and dissolution

Clause (1): the President/Governor summons each House to meet at such time and place as the constitutional head thinks fit; no six months may intervene between its last sitting in one session and the date appointed for its first sitting in the next session. This is a mandatory rule about the frequency of sessions of an existing House.

Clause (2): the President/Governor may prorogue either House and dissolve Lok Sabha/the Assembly. Rajya Sabha and a Legislative Council are not dissolved. The head’s formal power must be understood within Articles 74 or 163 and the doctrine of responsible government, not as a routine personal political veto.

State discretion: the DU’s Nabam Rebia note states that a Governor cannot use independent discretion to summon, prorogue or dissolve an Assembly while the Chief Minister commands its confidence. Doubt about majority can call for a constitutionally justified floor test. The Governor cannot simply take over the Assembly’s agenda or use the office to settle an internal party dispute.

The Gujarat rule

Article 174 is not a general six-month deadline between the outgoing Assembly’s last sitting and the incoming Assembly’s first sitting. A dissolved Assembly has no “next session.” Article 174 and Article 324 operate in different fields. Elections must nevertheless be organised promptly; the DU extract records the opinion that elections after premature dissolution should ordinarily be held within six months from dissolution under the overall constitutional/statutory scheme. See the full case analysis.

Constitution, Arts. 85, 174; DU Gujarat Reference pp. 127–138; DU Nabam Rebia note pp. 402–403 (extracted pages 413–414).

Articles 86 and 175 · General addresses and messages

The President may address either House or both Houses assembled together and require members’ attendance; a Governor may address a sole House or both Houses assembled together. Either constitutional head may send messages concerning a pending Bill or otherwise. The House receiving the message must, with all convenient despatch, consider the matter required to be considered.

Distinguish the powers: an address communicates with members; a message places a matter for consideration. Neither is an ordinary vote, nor a device to give a non-member the power to pass legislation alone. In a bicameral State, a general address to both assembled Houses is not an Article 108-style joint sitting empowered to settle a legislative deadlock.

Constitution, Arts. 86, 175.

Articles 87 and 176 · Mandatory special addresses

At the commencement of (i) the first session after each general election to Lok Sabha/the Assembly and (ii) the first session of each year, the President/Governor addresses the appropriate House(s) and informs the legislature of the causes of its summons. Rules must allocate time for discussion of matters referred to in the address.

Political significance: the address communicates the government’s programme in the constitutional head’s name; the ensuing discussion and motion of thanks permit criticism and accountability. The Constitution requires the address at the designated occasions, not at the beginning of every session.

Textual support for Gujarat: Article 176 expressly uses “after each general election”; Article 174’s “next session” does not. The Court uses this distinction to reject the conflation of reconstitution with resumption of a session.

Constitution, Arts. 87, 176; DU Gujarat Reference ¶40, p. 132.

Articles 88 and 177 · Ministers and law officers in the legislature

Every Minister and the Attorney-General has the right to speak and otherwise take part in either House of Parliament, a joint sitting, and a Parliamentary committee of which the person is named a member. State Ministers and the Advocate-General have analogous rights in the State House(s) and a committee to which they are named. The Article itself gives no right to vote.

A Minister who is already a member retains voting rights by virtue of that membership in that member’s own House. A non-member Minister cannot vote anywhere merely because of ministerial office. A Rajya Sabha Minister can participate in Lok Sabha, but does not acquire a Lok Sabha vote from Article 88.

Connection to S.P. Anand: participation without an immediate membership vote permits the temporary appointment of an otherwise eligible non-member while keeping the executive answerable to the popular House. Article 75(5)/164(4), not Article 88/177 alone, supplies the time restriction.

Constitution, Arts. 88, 177; DU S.P. Anand ¶5, p. 70; ¶¶14–16, pp. 73–74.

The non-member Minister rule: a four-stage test

Nuance: appointment power lies in Article 75(1)/164(1); Article 75(5)/164(4) is a cessation/restriction provision in the scheme. The person need not immediately be a member of Lok Sabha/the Assembly specifically: membership of either constitutionally relevant House suffices for the non-membership rule. Governmental accountability nevertheless remains to Lok Sabha/the Assembly.

Related 91st Amendment rules: Article 75(1A) caps the Union Council of Ministers, including the PM, at fifteen per cent of Lok Sabha membership. Article 164(1A) caps a State Council of Ministers, including the CM, at fifteen per cent of Assembly membership, subject to a minimum of twelve. Articles 75(1B) and 164(1B) bar specified defectors from ministerial appointment for the constitutionally stated period; Article 361B similarly addresses remunerative political posts. The six-month rule cannot circumvent these separate prohibitions.

DU S.P. Anand pp. 69–74; DU B.R. Kapur ¶¶19–30, pp. 107–111; supplementary constitutional connections: Arts. 75(1A)–(1B), 164(1A)–(1B), 361B.

05 / ENTRY, CONTINUANCE & EXIT

Qualifications and disqualifications of members

A positive qualification determines whether a person can enter the legislature. A disqualification can prevent election or require an existing member to leave. Identification of the ground is only the first step: the time it arose, the relevant forum and the legal consequence must also be established.

Articles 84 and 173 · Positive qualifications

ElementParliament · Article 84State Legislature · Article 173
Citizenship and candidature oathCitizen of India; makes and subscribes the Third Schedule oath/affirmation before a person authorised by the Election Commission.Same citizenship and prescribed oath/affirmation requirement.
Minimum ageRajya Sabha: 30. Lok Sabha: 25.Council: 30. Assembly: 25.
Additional qualificationsSuch other qualifications as Parliament prescribes by law.Such other qualifications as Parliament prescribes by law—not a general power of each State to add electoral qualifications at will.

Oath content: true faith and allegiance to the Constitution as by law established and upholding the sovereignty and integrity of India. The candidature oath under Article 84/173 must be distinguished from the pre-seat oath under Article 99/188 and from a Minister’s oaths of office and secrecy under Article 75(4)/164(3).

16th Amendment connection: S.P. Anand explains why the allegiance oath introduced at the candidature stage does not eliminate the six-month non-member Minister arrangement. Taking a legislative qualification seriously is not equivalent to requiring immediate membership as a condition for every ministerial appointment.

Constitution, Arts. 84, 173, Third Schedule; DU S.P. Anand ¶4, pp. 69–70.

RPA 1951 Sections 3–6: the qualification matrix

SectionOperative qualification and special elements
3 · State/UT representative in Rajya SabhaElector for a Parliamentary constituency anywhere in India. The uploaded text records the 2003 removal of the same-State/UT elector restriction.
4 · Lok SabhaOrdinary seat: elector for any Parliamentary constituency. Reserved SC seats: membership of a Scheduled Caste of that or another State plus Parliamentary elector status. ST reservations have additional territorial exclusions/special rules for Assam autonomous districts and Lakshadweep. The Sikkim seat requires an elector for Sikkim’s Parliamentary constituency.
5 · State AssemblyOrdinary seat: elector for an Assembly constituency in that State. SC/ST reserved seats ordinarily require membership of the relevant State’s SC/ST group and State Assembly elector status. Special rules apply to Assam autonomous-district ST seats.
5A · Sikkim AssemblySpecial qualifications for Bhutia-Lepcha, SC, Sangha and other seats. The Sangha seat requires an elector of the Sangha constituency; the other stated categories combine community qualification and the appropriate State Assembly electorate.
6 · State CouncilElection: elector for an Assembly constituency in the State. Governor nomination: ordinarily resident in that State. This is distinct from the special graduate/teacher electorate requirements in Article 171.

Reserved versus general seats: RPA Section 55 allows an SC/ST member to contest a non-reserved seat if otherwise qualified. Reservation is not a prohibition on broader candidature. The Act’s territorial details matter: do not write “a candidate can contest every reserved seat anywhere” as a universal rule.

Uploaded RPA, ss. 3–6 and 5A (PDF pp. 10–12); s. 55. Exact application to a particular reserved constituency requires the relevant statutory category and reservation notification.

Articles 99 and 188 · Oath before taking a seat

Every member must, before taking a seat, make and subscribe the prescribed Third Schedule oath/affirmation before the President/Governor or an authorised person. The obligation is not satisfied merely by taking a Minister’s office-and-secrecy oaths; the different oaths serve different legal purposes.

Three-stage distinction: nomination and candidature qualification → election/naming in the notification → oath before sitting as a legislator. Elections can constitute a House before every member has taken the sitting oath; this helps explain why “constituting” a legislature is not the same as “summoning” its first session.

Constitution, Arts. 99, 188; DU Gujarat Reference ¶40, p. 132. Penalty for sitting/voting before the oath: Arts. 104/193.

Articles 100 and 189 · Voting, validity despite vacancies, and quorum

  1. Default voting rule: save as otherwise provided, decisions are by a majority of members present and voting. Abstentions are not affirmative/negative votes in that denominator. The presiding officer does not vote initially, but has and exercises a casting vote on an equality.
  2. Vacancies: a House can act despite vacancies. Proceedings are not invalid merely because it is subsequently discovered that an unentitled person sat, voted or participated. This institutional saving does not legalise that person’s conduct or remove the Article 104/193 penalty.
  3. Parliamentary quorum: until Parliament otherwise provides by law, one-tenth of the total membership of the House.
  4. State quorum: until State law otherwise provides, ten members or one-tenth of total membership, whichever is greater.
  5. Absence of quorum: the presiding officer must adjourn or suspend the meeting until quorum exists.

Worked examples: in a hypothetical 60-member Assembly, the default quorum is 10, not 6. In a 200-member Assembly it is 20. If 100 members vote on an ordinary motion and 20 others abstain, an ordinary majority is 51 of the 100 votes, subject to the presiding officer rules—not 61 of the 120 present.

Special-majority caution: Article 169’s dual majority, presiding-officer removal’s effective majority, and Article 368’s constituent majority are express departures from the default. Always identify the motion before choosing the denominator.

Constitution, Arts. 100, 189; special exceptions in Arts. 94/179, 169, 368.

Articles 102 and 191 · Constitutional grounds of disqualification

The opening words apply to “being chosen as, and for being” a member. The same constitutional disqualification standards govern election and continued membership. Clause (1) supplies five grounds; clause (2) separately incorporates the Tenth Schedule.

GroundElements which must be provedImportant limitation
(a) Office of profitAn office; profit attached; held under the Union or relevant State government; no applicable legislative exemption.For MPs, exemption is by Parliamentary law. For State members, it is by State legislative law under Article 191(1)(a). Ministerial office alone does not disqualify under the constitutional explanation.
(b) Unsoundness of mindUnsound mind and a declaration by a competent court.A political allegation, a medical rumour or unusual behaviour is not the constitutional court declaration.
(c) Undischarged insolvencyLegal status as an undischarged insolvent.Ordinary debt or financial difficulty is not synonymous with that legal status.
(d) Citizenship/allegianceNot an Indian citizen; voluntarily acquired foreign citizenship; or acknowledgment of allegiance/adherence to a foreign State.Citizenship qualification and prohibited foreign allegiance are distinct stated routes.
(e) Parliamentary lawDisqualified by or under a law made by Parliament.RPA ss. 8–10A are central examples. This is not an independent State power to create arbitrary additional disqualifications.
Clause (2)Disqualification under the Tenth Schedule.Separate grounds and adjudicative machinery; do not route every defection case through the President/Governor–ECI mechanism.

Lily Thomas principle: Parliament’s specific power to create disqualifications cannot be used to maintain an incumbent-only exception inconsistent with these opening words and the vacancy provisions. The office-of-profit exemption under clause (1)(a), however, is an expressly authorised and analytically different legislative power.

Constitution, Arts. 102, 191; DU Lily Thomas pp. 117–125, especially ¶¶26–33.

Office of profit: analyse all four limbs, not only payment

Purpose: preserve legislative independence from executive patronage and conflicting obligations. The Constitution adopts parliamentary government, so it expressly excludes ministerial office alone from the disqualification. This is a tailored exception, not a doctrine that every government-linked position held by a politician is harmless.

Related enactment: the Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act, 1959 identifies exempted offices and conditions. Section 2’s compensatory-allowance concept and Section 3’s exemptions make the nature of remuneration legally important. The 2006 Amendment added exemptions and retrospective validation, analysed in Consumer Education. State exemption Acts must be considered when the alleged disqualification concerns an MLA/MLC. A State exemption relevant to State membership is not automatically the Parliamentary exemption needed for an MP.

Real case: Jaya Bachchan’s appointment carried an honorarium and facilities, although she said she did not use them. Waiving a receivable benefit did not transform the office into a non-profit office. Hypothetical: a statutory committee reimburses only verified train fares and actual hotel costs; that must be distinguished from a fixed monthly allowance capable of yielding a personal gain.

DU Consumer Education summary, p. 126; full Jaya Bachchan judgment ¶¶6–13, [1]. General multi-factor governmental nexus is supplementary doctrinal explanation; this judgment principally settles the profit/receivability limb.

RPA Section 8 · Three distinct conviction routes

RouteTriggerDuration in the uploaded statute
8(1)Conviction for a specifically listed offence. Do not assume a two-year sentence is necessary for this subsection.Fine only: six years from conviction. Imprisonment: from conviction and a further six years after release.
8(2)Contravention of a law preventing hoarding/profiteering, a law concerning food/drug adulteration, or the Dowry Prohibition Act, plus imprisonment of at least six months.From conviction and a further six years after release.
8(3)Any offence other than those in (1)/(2), with imprisonment of at least two years.From conviction and a further six years after release.
Former 8(4)Incumbent-only postponement for three months and then during a timely appeal/revision.Invalidated in Lily Thomas, 2013. Not an operative saving merely because its historical text appears in the uploaded bare Act.
Complete category map of Section 8(1) in the uploaded statutory edition
  1. IPC provisions listed in clause (a): promotion of enmity/prejudicial acts (153A); electoral bribery (171E); electoral undue influence/personation (171F); specified rape provisions (376 and 376A–D as reproduced); cruelty by husband/relatives (498A); specified statements promoting enmity/ill-will (505(2)/(3)).
  2. Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955: preaching/practising untouchability and enforcing the associated disabilities.
  3. Customs Act, 1962, s. 11: prohibited import/export as described in the uploaded provision.
  4. Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, ss. 10–12: unlawful-association membership, dealing with its funds and contraventions concerning notified places.
  5. Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973.
  6. Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985.
  7. TADA 1987, ss. 3–4: terrorist/disruptive activities.
  8. Religious Institutions (Prevention of Misuse) Act, 1988, s. 7.
  9. RPA offences: s. 125 election-related enmity; s. 135 removal of ballot papers; s. 135A booth capturing; s. 136(2)(a) fraudulent defacement/destruction of nomination papers.
  10. Places of Worship (Special Provisions) Act, 1991, s. 6.
  11. Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971, ss. 2–3.
  12. Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act, 1987.
  13. Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.
  14. Prevention of Terrorism Act, 2002.

The list reproduces the categories of the uploaded edition, not an assertion that every listed legacy Act remains in force or that every IPC number is the correct present-day charge after the criminal-law transition. Repeal, savings, date of offence and later amendments must be checked. The continuing examination lesson is the distinction between the listed-offence route and the residual two-year route.

Section 8 explanations: “hoarding/profiteering law” includes legally operative orders, rules and notifications governing production, prices, acquisition/storage/transport/disposal/use of essential commodities and withholding goods from sale. The uploaded definition cross-references the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, Essential Commodities Act, 1955 and the then food-adulteration legislation. These cross-references matter for the class of offence; they are not separate constitutional qualifications.

Uploaded RPA, s. 8, PDF pp. 12–14; DU Lily Thomas pp. 118–120.

What does—and does not—stop a conviction disqualification?

A pending prosecution alone: ordinarily not a conviction trigger under Section 8. Conviction with the applicable sentence: triggers the appropriate rule. Filing an appeal: no general automatic protection after Lily Thomas. Bail/suspension of execution of sentence: does not eliminate the conviction or the sentence imposed; B.R. Kapur. Express stay of conviction: disqualification will not operate while the stay is effective; Lok Prahari v. ECI. Acquittal on appeal: different from a temporary stay; its legal effects must be assessed in the particular election/seat setting.

Sentence date nuance: Kapur notes that if conviction and sentence occur on different dates, the cumulative Section 8(3) trigger is established when the qualifying sentence is imposed. Do not say that a disqualification requiring a sentence exists before any qualifying sentence has been awarded.

Temporal nuance: Lok Prahari concerns the non-operation of disqualification on an effective stay; it does not erase the conviction as if there had been an appellate acquittal, nor mechanically resolve all consequences where a bye-election has already intervened.

Criminal-procedure connection

The DU cases discuss CrPC Section 389, which permits suspension of execution of sentence/order pending appeal. Its modern counterpart is BNSS Section 430. BNSS Section 531’s repeal-and-savings framework means the governing procedure for an older pending matter must be checked; do not retrospectively rename the provision cited in a 2001/2018 judgment. A stay of conviction requires a specific judicial order and exceptional justification, not merely the ordinary bail order.

DU Kapur ¶¶32–40, pp. 111–112; DU Lok Prahari, p. 126. BNSS statutory connection verified in the original Gazette text, Ministry of Home Affairs PDF: ss. 430 and 531, PDF pp. 132 and 156–157, [1].

Sections 8A–11 · Additional disqualifications and relief

SectionElementsPeriod / authority / limitation
8A · Corrupt practicesA finding of corrupt practice by an order under s. 99; statutory submission to President.President determines whether to disqualify and for how long, acting according to ECI opinion. Maximum six years from when the s. 99 order takes effect. Distinguished from a criminal conviction under s. 8.
9 · DismissalHeld office under Union/State government and dismissed for corruption or disloyalty.Five years from dismissal. ECI certificate is conclusive proof; an adverse certificate requires opportunity to be heard.
9A · Government contractA subsisting contract entered in the person’s trade/business with the appropriate government for supply of goods or execution of its works.For so long as it subsists. If the person fully performed, mere non-performance by government does not keep it subsisting for this purpose. Not every unrelated private contract attracts this provision.
10 · Government company officeManaging agent, manager or secretary of a company/corporation other than a co-operative society, in which the appropriate government holds at least 25% of capital.While holding that specified position. Do not replace the stated threshold with 51%, or treat every shareholder/employee as a listed officer.
10A · Election-expense defaultFailure to lodge accounts in the required time/manner and no good reason or justification.ECI’s published order; three years from the order. Read with ss. 77–78 and applicable election-expense rules.
11 · Removal/reductionECI may act for recorded reasons.May remove a Chapter disqualification or reduce its period, except s. 8A. The authority is statutory, not a pardon that expunges a conviction or overrides a constitutional disqualification at will.

Section 7: “appropriate Government” is Central for Parliamentary disqualification, State for State-legislature disqualification. Its Chapter-specific definition of “disqualified” must be read in context; it does not delete the Constitution’s own office-of-profit, citizenship or Tenth Schedule grounds.

Voting is separate: Sections 11A–11B deal with specified voting disqualifications/removal. A person’s right to vote, right to stand for election, right to sit in a House and right to hold a ministry are connected but not identical legal statuses.

Uploaded RPA, ss. 7–11B, PDF pp. 12–16; s. 77–78. See also the office-of-profit statutory exemption, which is constitutionally authorised by Art. 102(1)(a), not by RPA s. 11.

Articles 103 and 192 · Who decides a subsequent disqualification?

If a question arises whether a sitting member has become subject to a clause (1) disqualification, it is referred to the President for an MP, or Governor for an MLA/MLC. Before deciding, the constitutional head must obtain the Election Commission’s opinion and act according to it. The stated finality does not confer power to ignore the Commission or exclude constitutional judicial review altogether.

Pre-election versus subsequently incurred: the “has become subject” formulation is important. A qualification/disqualification existing at election is ordinarily addressed by Returning Officer scrutiny and an election petition. The constitutional reference mechanism addresses a subsequent disqualification. Consumer Education explains the distinction; Articles 103/192 should not be treated as universal substitutes for time-bound election petitions.

Evidence and inquiry: RPA Sections 146–146C supply ECI inquiry powers and procedural protections for disqualification inquiries. ECI’s statutory machinery explains why a Governor is not expected personally to conduct the equivalent of a civil trial, yet the Kapur appointment cannot be saved by pretending that a plainly disqualified non-member has a constitutional right to office.

Constitution, Arts. 103, 192; uploaded RPA ss. 146–146C; DU Consumer Education, p. 126, with full-judgment supplement ¶¶20–37.

Articles 101 and 190 · Vacation of seats

  1. Both Houses of the same legislature: a person cannot simultaneously be a member of both. Parliament/State law provides which seat is vacated on dual election.
  2. Parliament and a State legislature: Article 101(2) makes the Parliamentary seat vacant after the period prescribed in Presidential rules unless the State seat is first resigned. Article 190(2) separately prohibits membership of legislatures of two or more States; after the prescribed period, all those seats become vacant unless all but one were first resigned.
  3. Disqualification: becoming subject to a disqualification mentioned in Article 102(1)/(2) or 191(1)/(2) produces the stated vacancy consequence, read with the applicable ground and adjudication scheme.
  4. Resignation: signed writing addressed to the Chairman/Speaker plus acceptance. If the presiding officer is satisfied from information or inquiry that resignation is not voluntary or genuine, it must not be accepted.
  5. Absence: if a member is absent without permission from all meetings for sixty days, the House may declare the seat vacant. It is a House power, not an automatic expiry at midnight. Periods of prorogation and adjournment for more than four consecutive days are excluded from the computation.

Related law: the Prohibition of Simultaneous Membership Rules, 1950 implement the constitutional reference to a prescribed period; RPA Sections 68–70 address specified dual/multiple election situations, including different Houses and more than one seat. Do not confuse the time to choose a seat with RPA Section 33(7)’s restriction on how many constituencies may be contested.

Timing caution from the prescribed cases: Consumer Education speaks of declaration/adjudication in a disputed office-of-profit case. Lily Thomas later rules that Parliament cannot defer a conviction disqualification for incumbents. The former is not authority for a universal proposition that every convicted legislator remains fully entitled until a fresh Presidential order. See the reconciliation note.

Constitution, Arts. 101, 190; uploaded RPA ss. 33(7), 68–70; DU Lily Thomas ¶33, p. 124; DU Consumer Education, p. 126.

Articles 104 and 193 · Penalty for unauthorised sitting or voting

A person who sits or votes (i) before complying with the oath requirement, (ii) knowing that the person is not qualified or is disqualified, or (iii) knowing that Parliamentary law prohibits the person from doing so, is liable to ₹500 for each day of sitting or voting, recoverable as a debt due to the Union/State. The sum is the constitutional amount, not an inflation-adjusted figure supplied by this guide.

Institution/person distinction: Article 100(2)/189(2) saves the House’s proceedings against later discovery of an unentitled participant. It does not remove the participant’s personal liability under Article 104/193.

Constitution, Arts. 104, 193.

Articles 106 and 195 · Members’ salaries and allowances

Parliament/State legislature determines members’ salaries and allowances by law. Pending such provision, the constitutional transitional arrangements apply. The Union statutory connection is the Salary, Allowances and Pension of Members of Parliament Act, 1954; States have their corresponding legislative laws.

Conceptual connection: constitutionally authorised legislative remuneration is not the same thing as an executive office-of-profit benefit. Do not infer that every paid legislator is thereby disqualified. An additional executive-controlled office has to be analysed independently under Articles 102/191.

Constitution, Arts. 106, 195; related remuneration enactment is supplementary.

Tenth Schedule · Anti-defection in its proper place

The 52nd Amendment introduced the Tenth Schedule; the 91st Amendment removed the former split exception and strengthened related ministerial restrictions. Article 102(2)/191(2) incorporates the Schedule. It is distinct from the criminal conviction and office-of-profit regimes.

ParagraphSubstance and examination elements
1 · InterpretationDefines “House,” “legislature party” and “original political party.” The party which set up the elected member is central to the deeming rules; a nominated member’s initial affiliation is separately dealt with.
2(1)(a) · Party memberVoluntarily gives up membership of the political party. Formal written resignation is not the only possible evidence; conduct can matter.
2(1)(b) · Voting/abstentionVotes or abstains contrary to a direction from the party or authorised person/authority, without prior permission; no condonation within fifteen days. Identify the valid direction, the conduct, prior permission and timely condonation.
2(2) · IndependentAn independently elected member is disqualified on joining a political party after election.
2(3) · Nominated memberJoining a political party after six months from taking the seat attracts disqualification; the first six months operate differently.
Former 3 · SplitOmitted by the 91st Amendment. A one-third split is not a current defence.
4 · MergerQualifying merger and the statutory deeming condition involving not less than two-thirds of legislature-party members. Members accepting merger, and those electing to function as a separate group in the prescribed situation, receive the stated protection. Do not turn “two-thirds” into a free-standing licence to ignore the other merger elements.
5 · Presiding officersSpecified exemption for a member elected to a listed presiding office who gives up party membership for that election and remains unaffiliated while holding it, with the stated protection for rejoining after leaving office.
6 · DecisionSpeaker/Chairman decides; where the question concerns the presiding officer’s own disqualification, a House-elected member decides. Finality and deemed-proceedings language do not eliminate constitutional review.
7 · Court barInvalidated in Kihoto Hollohan because the change to Supreme Court/High Court jurisdiction required State ratification. The rest of the Schedule survives.
8 · RulesSpeaker/Chairman may frame implementation rules; prescribed laying/House approval and modification mechanism applies. House-specific 1985 defection rules regulate references, petitions and procedural steps.

Review standard: the Speaker acts as an adjudicatory tribunal for paragraph 6, not as a sovereign chamber immune from all legal control. The DU Raja Ram Pal extract quotes Kihoto to explain that finality cannot eliminate review for jurisdictional error and recognised constitutional defects. Courts do not normally conduct a fresh political merits vote in place of the Speaker.

Practical caution: resignation does not necessarily erase the legal consequences of earlier defection; a party dispute does not automatically justify a Governor-ordered floor test. The relevant Speaker adjudication, executive majority and legitimate legislative proceedings are distinct questions. This is a constitutional framework note, not a purported complete survey of every post-2022 defection decision.

Constitution, Tenth Schedule and Arts. 75(1B), 164(1B), 361B; DU Raja Ram Pal ¶¶371–375, pp. 153–154, quoting Kihoto Hollohan. Detailed Schedule explanation is a statutory/constitutional supplement to the assigned ten cases.

06 / LEGISLATIVE PROCEDURE

From proposal to law

Do not use one legislative route for every Bill. The applicable House of introduction, role of the second chamber, recommendation requirement, deadlock mechanism and assent procedure depend on the Bill’s constitutional category.

Articles 107 and 196 · Introduction, passage and lapse of ordinary Bills

  1. House of introduction: subject to the special Money/financial-Bill rules, an ordinary Bill can originate in either House. Article 196 permits the same in a bicameral State; a unicameral State necessarily has only the Assembly route.
  2. Agreement: Parliamentary passage ordinarily requires both Houses to agree, either without amendment or with amendments agreed by both. At State level this is subject to Articles 197 and 198, which limit Council power.
  3. Prorogation: a Bill pending in the legislature does not lapse merely because a session is prorogued.
  4. Continuing upper House: a Bill pending in Rajya Sabha/Council which has not been passed by Lok Sabha/Assembly does not lapse on dissolution of the popular House.
  5. Popular-House involvement: a Bill pending in Lok Sabha/Assembly, or passed by it and pending in the upper House, lapses on its dissolution, subject to the Parliamentary joint-sitting exception in Article 108.

Why this pattern? the dissolved popular House’s unfinished legislative will cannot automatically bind its successor. A Bill whose only pending parliamentary stage is in the continuing upper House and which was never passed by the dissolved House has no equivalent attribution to that dissolved popular House.

Assent-stage distinction: a Bill which has completed the legislative passage stage and awaits constitutional assent is not simply a Bill still “pending in” the House. The lapse provisions must be applied to their wording and stage, not to every unfinished executive formality indiscriminately.

Constitution, Arts. 107, 196; DU Gujarat Reference’s general dissolution explanation, pp. 133–134, must be read with these express exceptions. The assent-stage distinction is also discussed through Purushothaman Nambudiri in the 2025 supplemental reference.

The three readings: procedure supplied by House rules

First reading

Introduction and publication, subject to the governing rule and any required recommendation. A private member’s Bill is one introduced by a member who is not a Minister; it is not a different constitutional category merely for that reason.

Second reading

General consideration; possible referral to a select/joint/standing committee or circulation, as the relevant rules and House decision provide; detailed clause-by-clause consideration and amendments.

Third reading

Final consideration of passage of the Bill in its resulting form. The other House then undertakes its required process; agreement or the lawful deadlock route precedes assent.

These are procedural-rule concepts, not three numbered clauses of Article 107. Committee examination is valuable but do not assume every Bill is constitutionally invalid merely because no committee examined it: the source and mandatory character of any claimed requirement must first be established.

Supplementary rules source: Lok Sabha Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business, Chapter X (Bills), [1]; DU Consumer Education summary and full judgment ¶39 for the distinction between a procedural practice and constitutional invalidity.

Article 108 · Parliamentary deadlock and joint sitting

Three triggers after one House has passed and sent a Bill to the other: (a) rejection; (b) final disagreement over amendments; or (c) more than six months elapsing from reception by the second House without passage. The President may notify an intention to convene a joint sitting by message if the Houses are sitting or public notification otherwise, unless the Bill has already lapsed through Lok Sabha dissolution.

Clause (2) calculation: periods when the second House is prorogued or adjourned for more than four consecutive days are excluded from the six-month computation. It is not a crude calendar count from the Bill’s introduction.

After notification: neither House proceeds further with the Bill individually; the President may summon the joint sitting. If a majority of total members of both Houses present and voting passes the Bill, with constitutionally permitted amendments, it is deemed passed by both Houses.

Amendment restrictions: where the Bill was not passed by the second House with amendments and returned, only amendments necessitated by the passage delay are allowed. Where the second House did pass amendments and return it, amendments necessitated by delay and those relevant to the areas of inter-House disagreement are permitted. The presiding person’s decision on admissibility under clause (4) is final in the stated procedural scheme.

Clause (5) preservation: if the President notified the intention before Lok Sabha dissolution, the joint sitting can still occur notwithstanding that later dissolution.

Limits to remember

  • No joint sitting for a Money Bill: express Article 108 proviso.
  • No joint sitting to force a constitutional amendment: Article 368 requires passage by each House using its own special majority; Article 108 cannot substitute a combined simple majority.
  • No analogous State joint-sitting mechanism: Article 197 uses Assembly repassage and deemed passage instead.
  • Ordinary financial Bills are not automatically excluded: decide whether the Bill is a true Article 110 Money Bill or a financial Bill requiring ordinary bicameral passage.

Chair: Article 118(4) and joint-sitting rules govern presiding arrangements. The usual Speaker’s chairing role does not give the Speaker a power to convene a joint sitting personally.

Constitution, Arts. 108, 118(3)–(4), 368. Rules on joint sittings supplement the constitutional framework.

Article 197 · State Council’s suspensive veto

If an Assembly-passed non-Money Bill goes to the Council and the Council rejects it, lets more than three months elapse without passage, or passes amendments unacceptable to the Assembly, the Assembly may pass it again in the same or a later session, with or without Council-suggested amendments, according to its rules.

On the second transmission, if the Council again rejects it, lets more than one month elapse without passage, or passes unacceptable amendments, the Bill is deemed passed by both Houses in the form last passed by the Assembly, with Council amendments the Assembly agrees to.

Consequences: the Council cannot permanently veto an Assembly-passed ordinary Bill. The familiar “three months + one month” describes the two constitutional waiting periods, not a compulsory total four-month delay for every Bill: rejection or disagreement can activate the mechanism earlier, and time the Assembly itself spends reconsidering is a separate matter.

Council-originated Bill: an ordinary Bill may begin in the Council, but the Assembly is not similarly compelled to accept it; an Assembly rejection cannot be overridden by the Council. Article 197’s protection is for a Bill passed by the Assembly, not a symmetrical right of each House to compel the other.

Clause (3): this Article does not apply to Money Bills; Article 198 supplies their special route.

Constitution, Art. 197, read with Arts. 196 and 198.

Articles 110 and 199 · What makes a Money Bill?

The critical word is “only”. The Bill must contain only provisions dealing with all or any of the enumerated matters, including matters incidental to them. Merely having a tax clause or costing public money does not turn any large Bill into a Money Bill.

ClauseUnion subject · Article 110(1)State adaptation · Article 199(1)
(a)Imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of a tax.Corresponding tax matters.
(b)Government of India borrowing/guarantees, and law concerning its financial obligations.State borrowing/guarantees and financial obligations.
(c)Custody of Consolidated Fund/Contingency Fund of India; payments into/withdrawals from them.State’s corresponding funds.
(d)Appropriation from Consolidated Fund of India.Appropriation from State Consolidated Fund.
(e)Declaring expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund, or increasing such expenditure.State charged expenditure.
(f)Receipt of money on account of Consolidated Fund/Public Account, custody or issue; audit of Union/State accounts.State Consolidated Fund/Public Account receipts, custody or issue and audit of State accounts.
(g)Any matter incidental to (a)–(f).Same incidental-matter connection.

Clause (2) negatives: a Bill is not a Money Bill by reason only that it imposes fines/other pecuniary penalties, demands/payments of licence or service fees, or imposes/alters local-authority taxation for local purposes. These express negatives prevent over-expansion of the category.

Clause (3): the Speaker of Lok Sabha/Assembly determines a question whether a Bill is a Money Bill, and the Article calls that decision final. Clause (4): the Speaker’s certificate is endorsed when sending it to the upper House and when presenting it for assent.

Review caution: constitutional “finality” is not the same as an absolute licence to disregard the definition. The prescribed Raja Ram Pal framework warns against treating a finality clause or Article 122/212 as protection for substantive unconstitutionality. This guide does not assert that every certification dispute has the same scope of review or that the separate post-2007 Money Bill jurisprudence has been fully surveyed.

Illustrations: a Bill confined to imposing an income tax and machinery truly incidental to it can satisfy Article 110. A broad criminal-law Bill containing fines is not a Money Bill merely for that reason. A public-service Bill creating expenditure is not necessarily a Money Bill; consider Article 117(3).

Constitution, Arts. 110, 199; DU Raja Ram Pal ¶¶359–397, pp. 152–154, on irregularity versus substantive illegality. The connection to certification is analytical, not a claim that that case decided an Article 110 dispute.

Articles 109 and 198 · Passage of Money Bills

  1. May not be introduced in Rajya Sabha/the Council. Introduction occurs in Lok Sabha/Assembly and requires the relevant recommendation under Article 117(1)/207(1).
  2. After popular-House passage, the Bill goes to the upper House for recommendations, not equal legislative consent.
  3. The upper House must return it within fourteen days from receipt with recommendations.
  4. The popular House may accept all, some or none. If accepted, the Bill is deemed passed by both Houses with those accepted amendments; if none is accepted, it is deemed passed in the original popular-House version.
  5. If not returned within fourteen days, it is deemed passed by both in the popular-House version at the expiry of that period.

Two errors to avoid: (i) the upper House does not have fourteen days to veto; it has fourteen days to recommend; (ii) a Money Bill deadlock does not require a joint sitting. The dominant role of the popular House is constitutional, but only for a Bill actually falling within the Money Bill definition.

Constitution, Arts. 109, 198, with Arts. 110/199 and 117/207.

Article 111 · Presidential assent to Parliamentary Bills

After Parliamentary passage, the Bill is presented to the President, who declares assent or withholding. The President may, as soon as possible, return a non-Money Bill with a message requesting reconsideration of the Bill or specified provisions and recommending amendments. If Parliament reconsiders and passes it again, with or without amendment, the President shall not withhold assent.

Money Bills: the return-for-reconsideration proviso does not apply. Constitutional amendments: Article 368(2), not merely the ordinary Article 111 route, mandates Presidential assent once the applicable constituent procedure has been completed.

Case-based real example: in Consumer Education, the 2006 office-of-profit Amendment Bill was passed in May, returned by the President on 30 May for reconsideration, repassed without amendment, and received assent on 18 August 2006. This is a concrete illustration of the non-Money Bill reconsideration mechanism, not of the President enacting a law without Parliament.

Constitution, Art. 111 and related Art. 368(2); Consumer Education full-judgment supplement ¶7, full text. DU p. 126 supplies the case’s basic statutory setting, not that detailed chronology.

Article 200 · Governor’s assent: text and distinct functions

After the relevant State legislative passage, the Bill goes to the Governor. The Article provides assent, withholding and reservation for the President’s consideration. The first proviso allows return of a non-Money Bill, as soon as possible, with a reconsideration message and recommended amendments. On legislative repassage, with or without amendment, the Governor “shall not withhold assent therefrom.” The second proviso requires reservation—not assent—if, in the Governor’s opinion, the Bill so derogates from High Court powers as to endanger the High Court’s constitutionally designed position.

Do not mechanically equate Article 200 with Article 111: the Governor has an express reservation function within a federal scheme; the President considering a State Bill acts through Article 201. The limits of the Governor’s options, advice obligations and judicial review have also been considered in later decisions. The updated position is separately identified below.

Related reservation/assent provisions: Article 254(2) for specified repugnant State laws in the Concurrent field; Article 31A’s Presidential-assent proviso for the relevant State law; Article 288(2) concerning specified State taxation affecting water/electricity; Article 304(b)’s previous sanction for its Bill/amendment is a different stage and requirement. Recommendation, reservation, assent and previous sanction are not interchangeable terms.

Constitution, Arts. 200, 254(2), 31A, 288(2), 304(b); see the dated 2025 supplement before stating the current judicial doctrine.

Article 201 · A reserved State Bill before the President

The President declares assent or withholding. For a non-Money Bill the President may direct the Governor to return it to the House(s) with the Article 200-type message. The House(s) must reconsider it within six months from receipt of that message. If repassed, with or without amendment, the Bill is presented to the President again for consideration.

Crucial asymmetry: unlike the first proviso to Article 200 and the Article 111 reconsideration rule, Article 201 does not say that the President must assent after repassage. The six-month period is a reconsideration period for the State legislature, not a general deadline requiring the President to dispose of every reserved Bill in six months.

Constitution, Art. 201. Subsequent judicial treatment is in the supplement below.

POST-DU UPDATE · SUPREME COURT, 20 NOVEMBER 2025

Special Reference No. 1 of 2025 · 2025 INSC 1333

This advisory opinion must be kept distinct from the 2022 DU baseline and the earlier 2025 State of Tamil Nadu decision. Its conclusions reject importing general court-fixed assent deadlines and “deemed assent” into Articles 200/201.

  1. Three Governor options: assent; reserve for the President; or, for a non-Money Bill, withhold and return with comments. The first proviso restricts the substantive withholding option; it does not create a fourth free-standing option of indefinite withholding simpliciter.
