  2. Advice/discretion: the opinion recognises discretion in choosing Article 200 options, rather than binding ministerial advice for that function. This is a specific function, not a general enlargement of gubernatorial authority in appointments, sessions or floor tests.
  3. After repassage: the text bars withholding again; the opinion’s discussion recognises assent or reservation. Do not assume that a textual “shall not withhold” necessarily erases the distinct reservation option.
  4. Merits versus inaction: the Article 200/201 choices are not subject to a pre-enactment merits review of the Bill in the stated scheme. Glaring, prolonged, unexplained and indefinite gubernatorial inaction can attract a limited mandamus to exercise the constitutional function within a reasonable time, without directing which substantive option to choose.
  5. No automatic judicial timeline or substituted assent: courts cannot create general timelines where the Constitution does not, nor exercise Article 142 to deem a Bill assented to in place of the proper constitutional authority.
  6. Article 361: personal immunity is distinct from the limited institutional review of inaction; it cannot be used to negate that limited review.
  7. Presidential reference: the President need not seek an Article 143 opinion each time a State Bill is reserved. Advisory jurisdiction itself is not ordinary pre-enactment judicial adjudication.

Exam use: explain the bare text first, then identify the dated post-DU opinion if a current-law answer is required. Do not attribute these 2025 conclusions to Raja Ram Pal or to the 2022 teaching extract.

Official opinion, ¶¶98–105, 153–165, especially ¶¶¶98–102 (after repassage) and 165.1–165.14 (conclusions): [1].

Lapse and continuation: rapid scenario table

EventResult
Session ends by prorogationPending Bill does not lapse merely for that reason.
Lok Sabha dissolves; Bill pending only in Rajya Sabha, not passed by Lok SabhaDoes not lapse under Article 107(4).
Lok Sabha dissolves; Bill pending in it or passed by it and pending in Rajya SabhaNormally lapses under Article 107(5).
Joint-sitting intention notified, then Lok Sabha dissolvesArticle 108(5) allows the notified joint sitting to continue.
Assembly dissolves; Council-only Bill not passed by AssemblyDoes not lapse under Article 196(4).
Assembly dissolves; Bill pending in Assembly or passed by it and pending in CouncilLapses under Article 196(5); no State Article 108 substitute.
07 / CONTROL OF THE PUBLIC PURSE

Financial procedure: authorisation, not merely announcement

A budget statement estimates receipts and expenditure; a demand for grant seeks the popular House’s approval; an Appropriation Act authorises withdrawals; taxation requires its own lawful authority. These are different legal steps, even when considered within one budget process.

Articles 112 and 202 · Annual financial statement

For every financial year the President/Governor causes a statement of estimated receipts and expenditure to be laid before both Parliamentary Houses or the State House(s). The Articles use annual financial statement; “Budget” is the conventional description.

Separate presentation: estimates must distinguish (i) expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund and (ii) other expenditure proposed from that Fund. They must also distinguish revenue-account expenditure from other expenditure.

Charged items at the Union level

  • President’s emoluments/allowances and expenditure relating to the office.
  • Rajya Sabha Chairman/Deputy Chairman and Lok Sabha Speaker/Deputy Speaker salaries/allowances.
  • Union debt charges: interest, sinking-fund and redemption charges and other listed borrowing/debt-service costs.
  • Specified judicial remuneration: Supreme Court salaries, allowances and pensions; the stated legacy Federal Court pensions and relevant High Court pensions.
  • Comptroller and Auditor-General’s salary, allowances and pension—expressly charged under Article 112(3)(e), distinct from CAG office administration in Article 148(6).
  • Sums required to satisfy a judgment, decree or award of a court or arbitral tribunal.
  • Any other expenditure declared charged by the Constitution or by Parliamentary law—for example, the separate constitutional provision concerning CAG expenditure in Article 148(6).

Charged items at State level

Governor’s emoluments/allowances and office expenditure; salaries/allowances of Assembly Speaker/Deputy Speaker and Council Chairman/Deputy Chairman; State debt charges; High Court judges’ salaries/allowances; judgment/decree/award payments; and expenditure otherwise constitutionally or statutorily declared charged.

Subtle distinction: the Article 202 judicial item concerns High Court salaries and allowances; Article 112 contains the specified High Court pension provision. Do not simply transplant the Union list word-for-word into a State answer.

Why charging matters: it protects specified constitutional obligations from ordinary grant-voting pressure. It does not eliminate the legislature’s ability to discuss them or the need for a lawful appropriation.

Constitution, Arts. 112, 202, with Art. 148(6). The complete Article text is in the reference appendix.

Articles 113 and 203 · Demands for grants

Charged expenditure: not submitted to the vote of Lok Sabha/Assembly, but can be discussed in either competent chamber. Other expenditure: submitted as demands for grants to the popular House, which may assent, refuse, or assent with a reduction. Recommendation: no demand may be made except on the President’s/Governor’s recommendation.

Upper-House role: Rajya Sabha/a State Council discusses the financial statement but does not vote demands for grants. Popular-House financial predominance therefore exists independently of the later Money Bill transmission procedure.

Related rules: policy, economy and token cut motions are procedural tools for reducing a grant and highlighting objections. They are not independent constitutional powers to increase a grant beyond the demand. The “guillotine” for completing outstanding demands is a House-rule scheduling device; assess any legal complaint by distinguishing rules of procedure from mandatory constitutional voting requirements.

Illustration: the Assembly may reduce a ₹100-crore demand to ₹90 crore. It cannot use the Article 203 reduction power to increase that demand to ₹120 crore. Charged judicial salary expenditure may be criticised in debate but is not defeated by an ordinary grant vote.

Constitution, Arts. 113, 203; supplementary Lok Sabha Rules, financial-business chapter, [1].

Articles 114 and 204 · Appropriation

As soon as may be after grants are made, an Appropriation Bill authorises the money required from the Consolidated Fund for (a) the grants made by Lok Sabha/Assembly and (b) charged expenditure, not exceeding the amount shown in the earlier financial statement.

Amendment restriction: no amendment may vary the amount or destination of a grant already made or vary charged expenditure. The presiding person determines inadmissibility under this clause. This protects the result of the grant stage from being reopened through appropriation amendments.

Withdrawal rule: subject to the supplementary and exceptional authorisations in the following Articles, no money is withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund except under appropriation made by law according to the Article. A budget speech or a cabinet announcement is not a legal substitute.

Related funds: Article 266 distinguishes the Consolidated Fund from the Public Account. Article 267 permits a Contingency Fund for advances pending legislative authorisation. A contingency advance does not permanently avoid the later appropriation process.

Constitution, Arts. 114, 204, 266–267; Appropriation Bills also fall within the Money Bill subject in Arts. 110(1)(d)/199(1)(d).

Articles 115 and 205 · Supplementary, additional and excess grants

SituationWhat the Article requiresIllustrative example
Amount proves insufficient for a current-year serviceAnother statement of estimated expenditure; the normal grant and appropriation provisions apply.Existing public-health scheme needs more funding because actual costs exceed the original allocation.
New service not contemplated in the annual statementStatement and authorisation for supplementary/additional expenditure.A new disaster-rehabilitation programme is created mid-year.
Money already spent beyond a grantAn excess demand is presented to Lok Sabha/Assembly; Articles 112–114 or 202–204 apply with necessary adaptation.Actual spending on a service exceeded the amount legally granted.

Accountability: excess authorisation is not proof that unauthorised spending was acceptable in advance; it is the constitutional machinery for legislative regularisation and scrutiny of the excess. Audit and Public Accounts Committee review can expose the underlying default.

Constitution, Arts. 115, 205, read with 112–114/202–204. Committee/audit connection is supplementary constitutional practice.

Articles 116 and 206 · Vote on account, vote of credit and exceptional grant

  • Vote on account: a grant in advance for part of a financial year pending completion of the normal financial-statement, grant and appropriation procedures. It is temporary authorisation, not a new annual financial statement.
  • Vote of credit: for an unexpected demand whose magnitude or indefinite character prevents ordinary itemised budget description. It accommodates genuinely exceptional financial demands.
  • Exceptional grant: for a purpose that forms no part of the current service of any financial year.

Lok Sabha/Assembly makes the grant; Parliament/State legislature authorises withdrawal by law. The normal financial and appropriation Articles apply to these grants and authorising laws. Rajya Sabha/a Council does not thereby acquire a grant-voting power.

Interim Budget distinction: “interim budget” is political/administrative terminology; a vote on account is the express constitutional authorisation for temporary expenditure. One should not assume that every interim budget is legally identical to a vote on account.

Constitution, Arts. 116, 206.

Articles 117 and 207 · Financial Bills: recommendation and bicameralism

Clause (1): a Bill or amendment making provision for the enumerated financial matters in Article 110(1)(a)–(f), or Article 199(1)(a)–(f), needs Presidential/Gubernatorial recommendation for introduction/moving. Such a Bill cannot be introduced in the upper House. An amendment merely reducing or abolishing a tax does not require the recommendation under this clause.

Clause (2): fines, pecuniary penalties, licence/service fees and local-authority taxes for local purposes do not, by reason only of their presence, create the clause (1) financial matter.

Clause (3): a Bill which, if enacted, would involve expenditure from the Consolidated Fund must not be passed by a House unless the President/Governor has recommended its consideration to that House. This is a consideration/passage requirement, not an automatic prohibition on introduction in the upper House.

CategoryIntroductionRecommendation stageSecond chamber
Money BillPopular House onlyFinancial recommendation under cl. (1)Recommendations only; fourteen days; no Parliamentary joint sitting.
Financial Bill commonly called Category IPopular House only; financial (a)–(f) provisions plus other, non-incidental provisionsIntroduction/moving stage under cl. (1)Parliamentary ordinary bicameral consent; joint sitting possible where Art. 108 conditions hold. In a State, Council restrictions under Art. 197 apply.
Financial Bill commonly called Category IIEither House where bicameral; expenditure Bill not within cl. (1)Recommendation for consideration before passage under cl. (3)Ordinary route, not Money Bill recommendations-only treatment.

Terminology: “Category I/II” is a teaching classification, not the exact caption used by the Constitution. A Bill may be called a Finance Bill in political discussion; its legal category still depends on its contents and the Articles.

Related Article 255: specified defects concerning recommendation/previous sanction may be cured where the constitutionally relevant assent has been given under its terms. Do not generalise that provision into a licence to ignore all financial procedure or to cure lack of legislative competence. Identify the exact recommendation and assent involved.

Constitution, Arts. 117, 207, 255; read with the exhaustive-definition “only” rule in Arts. 110/199.

Related statutory and institutional layer

Article 265: no tax may be levied or collected except by authority of law. Articles 148–151: establish CAG auditing arrangements and legislative laying of reports. FRBM Act, 2003: supplies Union fiscal-responsibility and budget-management obligations; States may have corresponding fiscal-responsibility legislation. Committee scrutiny: Public Accounts, Estimates and Public Undertakings Committees have differentiated functions; not all exercise the power to pass grants.

These connections explain why parliamentary financial control is both ex ante (tax, grant and appropriation authority) and ex post (audit, accounts and responsibility). They supplement, rather than replace, the prescribed Article range.

Constitution, Arts. 265–267, 148–151; related Acts and committees are supplementary framework notes.

08 / PROCEDURE GENERALLY

Rule-making, language and judicial-conduct restrictions

Articles 118 and 208 · Rules of procedure

House rules: each House may make rules regulating procedure and conduct of business, subject to the Constitution. Pending such rules the stated pre-Constitution rules/standing orders apply, with the permitted adaptations.

Union joint sittings: the President, after consultation with the presiding officers of both Houses, may make joint-sitting rules under Article 118(3). Article 118(4) provides for the Speaker or the person determined by those rules to preside.

State communication procedure: the Governor, after consultation with Assembly Speaker and Council Chairman where a Council exists, may make rules about communications between the two Houses under Article 208(3). This is not a power to create a State legislative joint sitting to override the Council; Article 197 remains the deadlock rule.

Operational examples: Questions, motions, committee references, legislative stages, amendments, privilege notices and suspensions are regulated by House rules. The existence of a rule is not proof it was complied with, but departure from every rule is not automatically substantive constitutional illegality.

Constitution, Arts. 118, 208; DU Raja Ram Pal ¶431(q)–(s), pp. 155–156. Supplementary rules: [1].

Articles 119 and 209 · Law securing timely financial business

Parliament/State legislature may, for timely completion of financial business, regulate by law procedure and conduct of business concerning financial matters and appropriation from the relevant Consolidated Fund. If that law conflicts with House rules made under Article 118/208 or the stated transitional rules, the law prevails.

Hierarchy: Constitution → valid Article 119/209 procedural law → House rules within their sphere. A statutory overriding power in financial procedure does not authorise a law contrary to the Constitution itself.

Constitution, Arts. 119, 209.

Articles 120 and 210 · Language in legislative business

Parliament: subject to Article 348, business is in Hindi or English. The Chairman/Speaker may allow a member who cannot adequately express themselves in either to address the House in their mother tongue. The Article contains a fifteen-year transitional English provision qualified by Parliamentary law.

State legislature: business is in the State’s official language(s), Hindi or English, subject to Article 348. Mother-tongue permission is similarly available. Article 210(2) contains the fifteen-year default and special transitional twenty-five-year periods for Himachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya and Tripura, and forty-year periods for Arunachal Pradesh, Goa and Mizoram, unless the legislature otherwise provides by law.

Related legislation: the Official Languages Act, 1963 addresses continuing use of English for specified Union purposes and Parliamentary business. State continuation must be examined under the appropriate State law rather than assumed from the Union Act alone. Article 348 separately concerns authoritative legislative/legal texts and court language.

Constitution, Arts. 120, 210, 348; Official Languages Act, 1963, s. 3 is the supplementary Union connection.

Articles 121 and 211 · Protecting judicial independence

Article 121: Parliament may not discuss the conduct of a Supreme Court/High Court judge in discharge of judicial duties except upon a motion presenting an address to the President praying for removal in the constitutionally prescribed manner.

Article 211: prohibits such discussion in a State legislature. It has no corresponding State removal-motion exception: the State legislature is not the constitutional body which presents the Parliamentary judicial-removal address.

Scope: the wording concerns a judge’s conduct in the discharge of duties; it is not a ban on all discussion of legal policy, institutional reform or the implications of a judgment. Conversely, an indirect attack on a judge’s judicial conduct cannot escape merely by changing the label of the motion.

Related removal law: Articles 124(4)–(5) and 217(1)(b), and the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 and its rules, govern the prescribed removal process. Article 121’s exception does not allow an ordinary State confidence motion to become an impeachment proceeding.

Keshav Singh connection: Article 211, judicial tenure protection and Articles 226/32 helped defeat the proposition that the Assembly could punish High Court judges simply for entertaining a lawful habeas corpus petition.

Constitution, Arts. 121, 211, 124(4)–(5), 217; DU Raja Ram Pal discussion of Keshav Singh, pp. 144–145 and 151–153; full advisory-opinion supplement.

09 / AUTONOMY WITH CONSTITUTIONAL LIMITS

Legislative privileges and the courts

A privilege exists to enable the legislature to perform its constitutional functions, not to create a superior class of citizens. The core DU progression is Keshav Singh → constitutional judicial control; Raja Ram Pal → expulsion power recognised, but its exercise remains reviewable within defined limits.

Articles 105 and 194 · Four clauses, four legal functions

ClauseContentInterpretive point
(1)Freedom of speech in Parliament/State legislature, subject to the Constitution and procedural rules/standing orders.Institutional speech freedom is not identical to ordinary Article 19(1)(a) freedom. The House can regulate decorum and constitutionally prohibited discussion.
(2), first limbNo member is liable to proceedings in any court in respect of anything said or any vote given in the House or its committee.Protection attaches to the speech/vote in the constitutional legislative setting. A speech at a public rally is not protected merely because the speaker is an MP.
(2), second limbNo person is liable in court for publication by or under the authority of a House of a report, paper, votes or proceedings.Authorised publication is distinct from a private media republication. The protection is not confined to members.
(3)Other powers, privileges and immunities may be defined by Parliamentary/State law; until so defined the specified pre-44th-Amendment privileges continue.The historical House of Commons reference explains their origin, but does not transplant British sovereignty or every historically incompatible Commons power.
(4)These provisions also apply to constitutionally entitled non-members who may speak/participate, such as Ministers and the Attorney-General/Advocate-General.Participation rights can support corresponding speech protection without creating a general House vote or converting the participant into a member.

The 44th Amendment: change of formulation, not removal of privilege

Originally the residual clause expressly referred to privileges of the House of Commons at commencement of the Constitution. The 44th Amendment replaced that formulation with the privileges of the Indian House and its members/committees immediately before the coming into force of the relevant amending section—Section 15 for Article 105, Section 26 for Article 194. Raja Ram Pal treats the removal of the British reference as cosmetic for the interpretive question before it, not a destruction of the inherited powers.

Codification: there is no comprehensive Union code cataloguing all privileges in the DU case’s setting. Particular enactments can regulate defined aspects, and House rules regulate procedure. A rulebook is not automatically the same thing as a law comprehensively defining the substantive residual privilege.

DU Raja Ram Pal ¶¶9–11, 43, 62–65, pp. 141–146; Constitution, Arts. 105, 194.

Individual and collective privileges

Individual protections

  • Legislative speech and vote immunity.
  • Corresponding protection for constitutionally entitled participants.
  • Specified civil-arrest protection connected to attendance, not immunity from criminal law.
  • Protection against interference, threats or obstruction which prevents members from performing legislative functions.

House/committee powers

  • Regulate proceedings and maintain order.
  • Exclude strangers where appropriate.
  • Control authorised publication and protected/confidential proceedings.
  • Require witnesses and documents in its lawful committee sphere.
  • Punish breach of privilege or contempt.
  • Discipline members, including expulsion in the circumstances recognised by Raja Ram Pal.

Functional connection: obstruction of a committee’s lawful inquiry is a different matter from disagreement with a member’s politics. A privilege claim must identify the protected function and the actual interference. Parliamentary dignity cannot become a formula for suppressing all public criticism.

Civil arrest: CPC Section 135A protects specified legislative members from arrest/detention under civil process during attendance at a House/committee or joint meeting and during the forty days before and after the relevant meeting/sitting/session within the provision’s terms. It is not a bar on arrest for a criminal offence or a general immunity from preventive detention. The distinction is procedural and functional, not a declaration that members are above ordinary law.

Related law: the Parliamentary Proceedings (Protection of Publication) Act, 1956 concerns protection of the specified reporting/publication; it is not a wholesale codification of every parliamentary privilege.

Supplementary Rajya Sabha Secretariat Parliamentary Privileges (June 2022), pp. 5–7 and 18–19: [4]; Constitution and CPC s. 135A. DU Raja Ram Pal ¶¶64–70, pp. 145–146.

Publication: three different routes

PublicationLegal basisLimits
By/under House authorityArticles 105(2)/194(2)Constitutional authorised-publication protection; identify actual authority.
Substantially true newspaper report of House proceedingsArticle 361A, plus the relevant statutory protectionProtection against the specified civil/criminal court proceedings unless publication is proved malicious; does not apply to a secret sitting.
Broadcast report covered by Article 361A(2)Extension of the substantially true reporting protection to the specified broadcast formSame constitutional conditions; not a universal exemption for every online allegation.

Searchlight context in the DU extract: M.S.M. Sharma concerned publication of expunged parts of Assembly proceedings. The Court’s treatment of Article 19(1)(a) and residual privilege cannot be restated as a modern, unconditional rule that any substantially true report is punishable. Article 361A and the precise nature of the published material must now be included.

Constitution, Art. 361A; Parliamentary Proceedings (Protection of Publication) Act, 1956; DU Raja Ram Pal discussion of Sharma, ¶¶51–54 and 332–339, pp. 143 and 150–152.

Connected rules and protections, in practical detail

Rule/protectionOperative detailWhy it is distinct
Lok Sabha 222–224Speaker consent; written notice to Secretary-General by 10.00 hours on the proposed day, with the underlying document if based on one. Later notices are treated as received next sitting day. Rule 224 requires a specific recent matter needing House intervention; not more than one at the same sitting.These are admissibility/notice controls, not an adjudication that the accused is guilty.
Lok Sabha 225Short relevant statement while seeking House leave. If leave is opposed, at least 25 members must rise in support. The Speaker has the rule’s urgency discretion.Presiding-officer consent and leave of the House are not the same procedural step.
Lok Sabha 226–228The House may decide or refer to the Privileges Committee; Speaker may independently refer; Speaker may issue procedural directions.A committee investigates/recommends; its report must not be treated as identical to every final House sanction.
Lok Sabha 229–231Immediate intimation of arrest/detention/conviction and release, with reasons/place in the prescribed form; announcement in House or Bulletin, subject to the rule’s proviso.Information rights coexist with lawful criminal arrest; they are not criminal immunity.
Lok Sabha 232–233Speaker permission for arrest or civil/criminal service of process within House precincts.Protection of the premises/process differs from complete exemption from ordinary legal liability.
Rajya Sabha 187–203Chairman consent, notice, admissibility, leave and reference framework. The official committee-rules extract states a ten-member Privileges Committee and quorum of five, with inquiry/evidence/report provisions.Apply that House’s rules; do not substitute Lok Sabha notice timings automatically.
Custodial contempt punishmentThe Secretariat guide describes legislative contempt imprisonment as limited by the duration of the session, ending with prorogation in this privilege context.It is not a sentence after an ordinary criminal trial; detention legality remains reviewable under Keshav Singh.
CPC 135ASpecified protection against arrest/detention under civil process for House/committee/joint-meeting attendance and the stated forty-day periods; re-arrest after protected release is subject to the provision.Neither preventive-detention nor criminal-offence immunity follows.

Ethics complaints are not automatically privilege notices

The 2019 Lok Sabha rulebook’s Rules 233A–233B separately regulate ethics complaints: a written complaint, identity and substantiating evidence; a non-member’s complaint is forwarded/countersigned by a member and supported by the stipulated affidavit. Complaints must be in good faith, respectful and in Hindi/English or accompanied by a signed translation. Merely unsubstantiated media reports are insufficient. The committee does not take up a matter it treats as sub judice. Speaker may refer unethical conduct independently.

These provisions were added in 2015: do not pretend they governed the 2005 proceedings in Raja Ram Pal. Ethical misconduct, a specific privilege breach, criminal liability and sitting disorder have different procedural routes even when the same conduct may engage more than one.

Official Lok Sabha Rules,16th edition 2019, printed pp.85–89/PDF pp.118–122; Rajya Sabha Rules 187–203, [1]; Rajya Sabha Secretariat 2022 privilege guide, pp.11–12 and 18–19. These are edition-specific supplements, not a claim that every later procedural amendment has been surveyed.

Breach of privilege and contempt: overlapping, not identical

Breach of privilege is infringement of a particular recognised privilege. Contempt of the House includes conduct obstructing or impeding the House, members or committees in their functions, or conduct having a relevant tendency to do so. A contempt need not always be pleaded as infringement of one narrowly enumerated individual privilege.

Potential situations: obstructing a member from attendance; intimidating a witness; deliberately misleading a competent committee; unauthorised disclosure of protected committee material; misconduct with a direct legislative connection such as taking money to raise questions. The constitutional and factual nexus must be established; an insult uttered in public is not automatically enough in every case.

Procedure under the rules, not punishment by allegation

The Lok Sabha privilege framework begins with Speaker consent (Rule 222), written notice (Rule 223), admissibility considerations (Rule 224) and the mode of raising the question (Rule 225). The House can consider it or refer it to the Committee of Privileges (Rule 226); the Speaker has the stated reference power under Rule 227. The committee’s inquiry/report and the House’s decision supply the relevant procedural setting. Rajya Sabha uses its own rules, including the privilege provisions in Rules 187–203 ([1]); State legislatures have their own Article 208 rules.

The procedure is not identical to a criminal trial. Nevertheless, a reasonable opportunity to answer the allegations is material, and gross denial of natural justice may take the matter outside a mere procedural-irregularity complaint. The House—not a private broadcaster—ultimately exercises its constitutional disciplinary authority.

Official Lok Sabha Rules, Chapter XX: [1]; official Rajya Sabha privilege guide [3]; DU Raja Ram Pal ¶¶447–454, pp. 157–158.

Discipline: warning, withdrawal, suspension, contempt and expulsion

The DU Raja Ram Pal extract records disciplinary measures including admonition, reprimand, withdrawal, suspension, imprisonment for contempt and expulsion. Each should be distinguished by legal source, purpose and consequence. Suspension normally excludes participation for the specified period without terminating membership; expulsion ends membership. Neither label automatically establishes a criminal conviction.

Lok Sabha rules connection: Rules 373, 374 and 374A address withdrawal and the specified suspension mechanisms for disorder. They should not be confused with the residual constitutional expulsion power or with RPA disqualification. Rule-specific time limits and conditions must be applied to the exact measure imposed.

Expulsion is not an extra RPA criminal disqualification: the majority in Raja Ram Pal recognises expulsion within Article 105(3)’s power to protect the House’s integrity. Expulsion does not, merely as expulsion, disqualify a person from standing again. If a separate statutory disqualification exists, it operates independently.

Concurrent legal spheres: institutional discipline and criminal prosecution can proceed in distinct spheres. A House may act on conduct undermining its integrity without waiting for a criminal conviction, but cannot thereby grant criminal immunity or conduct every ordinary criminal trial itself.

DU Raja Ram Pal ¶4, p. 139; ¶¶162–168, pp. 148–149; ¶¶292–295, p. 149; rules source [1].

Articles 122 and 212 · Protection from procedural challenges

Clause (1): the validity of legislative proceedings must not be questioned on the ground of an alleged irregularity of procedure. Clause (2): an officer/member vested with authority under the Constitution to regulate procedure, conduct business or maintain order is not subject to court jurisdiction in respect of exercise of those powers within the constitutional protection.

What the shield does not mean: Parliament is not sovereign in the British sense; it is not the sole final judge of the existence and scope of every privilege it claims. Constitutional courts may examine substantive illegality, jurisdictional excess and constitutional violation. The Court distinguishes the House’s ordinary internal procedural control from an asserted authority to override the Constitution.

Grounds and restraint must both be included: the Court respects the legislature as a co-ordinate organ, presumes regularity unless rebutted, and does not decide the necessity/expediency of discipline or reweigh the evidence as an appellate chamber. It can nevertheless intervene for gross illegality, violation of constitutional mandate or the recognised serious defects described in Raja Ram Pal.

DU Raja Ram Pal ¶¶359–397, pp. 152–154; ¶431(a)–(u), pp. 154–156. Constitution, Arts. 122, 212.

Privileges and fundamental rights: avoid both absolutisms

The DU account of M.S.M. Sharma treats the specific constitutional privilege as controlling the particular Article 19(1)(a) complaint. Keshav Singh clarifies that this is not a blanket doctrine that every fundamental right must yield. Article 21 remains relevant, and the constitutional writ jurisdiction cannot be defeated by an unexplained general warrant. Raja Ram Pal rejects the broad argument that privilege cannot ever be tested against constitutional provisions and fundamental rights; it particularly identifies complaints under Articles 20 and 21.

The proper method is harmonious construction: protect the specific speech/vote immunity where applicable, but do not extend residual privilege beyond the Constitution. Saying “fundamental rights always override every privilege” is as inaccurate as saying “privilege overrides every fundamental right.” Identify the clause, protected act, claimed right and nature of the interference.

DU Raja Ram Pal ¶¶332–339, pp. 150–152; ¶431(h)–(j), p. 155; full Keshav Singh supplement, especially ¶¶33–43 and the final answers in ¶143.

POST-DU UPDATE · 4 MARCH 2024

Sita Soren v. Union of India · 2024 INSC 161

A unanimous seven-judge Bench overruled the bribery-immunity aspect of the majority decision in P.V. Narasimha Rao. A legislator cannot claim Article 105(2)/194(2) immunity from prosecution for accepting a bribe connected with a speech or vote.

  • Two-fold test for an individual privilege claim: it must be tethered to the collective functioning of the House and necessary to the discharge of the essential duties of the legislator.
  • Bribery is distinct: accepting illegal gratification is not essential to making a free speech or vote. The offence is complete independently of whether the promised vote is cast, cast in a different direction or not cast at all.
  • Separate jurisdictions: House discipline and a criminal court’s prosecution have distinct scope, purpose and consequences.
  • Scope of legislative protection: relevant electoral functions such as Rajya Sabha elections cannot be excluded merely because they are not law-making at a sitting. That protection of the vote does not immunise a separate bribery transaction.
  • No guilt finding implied by immunity rejection: denying constitutional immunity is not a substitute for the prosecution proving the offence under the applicable criminal law.

Connection to the DU core: Raja Ram Pal protects legislative integrity through discipline subject to review. Sita Soren prevents the same constitutional privilege from being inverted into a shield for the corruption which damages that integrity.

Official judgment, ¶¶175–189, especially ¶188.1–188.12: [2]. This update is not part of the uploaded 2022 casebook.

Why constitutionalism matters here

The uploaded constitutionalism readings describe government limited by law and institutional checks. This topic supplies concrete examples: a Governor cannot install a disqualified majority-party leader; Parliament cannot invent an unconstitutional incumbent saving; a House can maintain integrity but not retaliate against a court for exercising lawful jurisdiction. These illustrate limited government, not a judicial claim to run all legislative business.

Conceptual context: uploaded Stanford Constitutionalism, introductory and separation-of-powers sections; Whittington, Constitutionalism, pp. 1–2. The operative Indian rules in this guide remain anchored in the constitutional text and prescribed DU cases, not these general philosophical readings.

10 / PRESCRIBED CASE FILES · PART I

Eligibility, conviction and ministerial office

These four cases form a sequence, but decide different questions: non-membership, present disqualification, legislative power to postpone disqualification, and the effect of a judicial stay of conviction.

21
DU EXTRACT · pp. 69–74

S.P. Anand v. H.D. Deve Gowda

(1996) 6 SCC 734 · A.M. Ahmadi CJI and Sujata V. Manohar J

Holding in one line: an otherwise eligible person who is not a member of either House may be appointed Prime Minister, subject to the six-consecutive-month rule and confidence of Lok Sabha.

Full case analysis · facts, issues, arguments and ratio

1. Material facts and procedural posture

H.D. Deve Gowda was appointed Prime Minister in 1996 although he was not then a member of either House of Parliament. S.P. Anand filed an Article 32 challenge, contending that the President had committed a serious constitutional error in administering the oath to a non-member. The appointment was alleged to violate Articles 14, 21 and 75 and to be void from the outset.

The DU extract situates the issue against earlier Har Sharan Verma litigation concerning non-legislator Chief Ministers/Ministers and against Delhi and Calcutta High Court challenges to the same Prime Minister’s appointment. Those prior cases are legal context, not separate facts about Deve Gowda’s own membership.

2. Issues

  1. Does the permission for a non-member “Minister” under Article 75(5) include the Prime Minister?
  2. Does the Prime Minister’s special constitutional/political status require immediate Parliamentary membership even if ordinary Ministers need not be members?
  3. Is the temporary arrangement incompatible with democratic legitimacy and collective responsibility?
  4. Can a British convention requiring membership be imported to displace the express Indian constitutional scheme?

3. Petitioner’s submissions

  • Representative legitimacy: a person not elected as an MP should not hold the highest political executive office; responsibility in peace and war made the supposed risk especially serious.
  • Prime Minister distinct from Minister: even if Article 75(5) permits temporary non-member Ministers, it should not extend to the Prime Minister because that office has a special status and no separate textual exemption.
  • British convention: the Prime Minister is conventionally a member of one House, preferably the House of Commons. The petitioner relied on Halsbury’s statement of that practice.
  • Reconsider earlier cases: earlier non-member decisions were described as old and unsuitable to changed circumstances.
  • Constitutional challenge: Articles 14 and 21 were invoked along with Article 75, although the main interpretive controversy concerned the ministerial scheme.

4. Respondent/Attorney-General position in the DU extract

The Attorney-General relied on the existing line of decisions accepting non-member Ministers and Chief Ministers. The extract records and answers that position through the comparison of Articles 74–75 with Articles 163–164 and the earlier cases. It does not reproduce a separate complete written reply; the following is an analytical summary of the supported position, not an invented transcript:

  • Article 75(5) deliberately accommodates a non-member for six months, and “Minister” includes the Prime Minister.
  • Articles 75(3) and 88 maintain Parliamentary accountability and participation during the interim.
  • The State analogues and consistent precedents support the same construction for a Prime Minister.
  • English practice cannot override the written Indian constitutional design.

5. Reasoning: how the Court reached the result

Text and structure: Article 75 is captioned “Other provisions as to Ministers.” There is no separate membership rule excluding the PM from the non-membership clause. The Constitution recognises the PM’s leadership but uses the same office oath and collective-responsibility structure for the Council. The special status of the head does not establish a different eligibility rule which the text does not contain.

Democratic accountability: direct election of the PM by the entire electorate is not the constitutional method. The President appoints the person able to command Lok Sabha confidence; the Council remains collectively answerable to that House. A non-member PM does not therefore govern free of Parliamentary scrutiny.

Comparative Articles: the Court places Union and State ministerial provisions alongside each other. Article 164(4) had already been interpreted to allow appointment of someone not a State legislator at all, not only continuance of a sitting Minister who subsequently lost a seat. The corresponding Article 75(5) serves the same temporary-accommodation purpose.

Constituent Assembly intention: the rejected proposal that only already elected members could be appointed Ministers supports the temporary appointment construction. The six-month condition is a real limit, not a permanent exception to representative government.

Conventions: a convention fills a constitutional silence; it cannot contradict an express permissive scheme. The claimed British convention was not the controlling Indian practice.

6. Decision and operative order

The petition was dismissed. The interim stay affecting proceedings pending elsewhere was vacated; those proceedings were to be disposed of in accordance with this ruling. The appointment was not unconstitutional merely because the PM was a non-member at appointment.

7. Ratio and principle

Article 75(5), read with Articles 74–75 and the parallel State provisions, covers the Prime Minister. An otherwise eligible non-member may be appointed temporarily; continued office beyond six consecutive months requires membership of either House. Collective responsibility to Lok Sabha supplies the democratic accountability during that period.

8. Limits and what the case does not decide

  • It does not authorise appointment of a person presently disqualified under Articles 102/191; B.R. Kapur addresses that different problem.
  • It does not allow repeated fresh six-month terms which defeat representative accountability.
  • It does not give a non-member a legislative vote through Article 88.
  • It does not require the PM to be a Lok Sabha member rather than a Rajya Sabha member once Parliamentary membership is obtained.

Use in an answer: begin with Articles 75(1), (3), (5) and 88; state inclusion of PM within “Minister”; explain accountability; then distinguish present disqualification and repeated appointment. Suitable for centenary Q 5(b) and the comparative part of December 2024 Q 5(b).

DU pp. 69–74: facts and prior cases ¶¶2–8; petitioner ¶¶9, 15; structure/history ¶¶11–16; dismissal ¶19. Paragraph numbers absent from the selected extract are not reconstructed as DU quotations.

22
DU EXTRACT · pp. 106–116

B.R. Kapur v. State of Tamil Nadu

(2001) 7 SCC 231 · Five-judge Bench; DU extract of S.P. Bharucha J’s opinion

Holding in one line: the six-month non-member Minister rule does not permit appointment of a person presently disqualified from legislative membership; majority support and suspension of sentence execution do not cure it.

Full case analysis · facts, issues, arguments and ratio

1. Facts that matter legally

Jayalalithaa had been Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu from 1991 to 1996. The DU factual introduction records convictions in two criminal cases relating to offences during that tenure, with imprisonment of three years and two years respectively and fines. The fines were paid. Criminal appeals were pending. The High Court suspended execution of the imprisonment sentences and granted bail, but applications to stay the operation of the conviction judgments were rejected.

For the 2001 Assembly election she filed nominations in four constituencies. The DU material records that three were rejected on Section 8(3) disqualification and the fourth because candidature exceeded the permissible two seats. She did not challenge those rejection orders. AIADMK won 132 of 234 seats and chose her as leader. She was sworn in as CM on 14 May 2001 although not an Assembly/Council member. The appointment was challenged through the proceedings considered by the Supreme Court.

2. Issues

  1. Can Article 164(1), read with 164(4), permit a six-month CM/Minister who is constitutionally/statutorily ineligible to become a legislator?
  2. Does suspension of execution of sentence remove the Section 8(3) disqualification?
  3. Must disqualification await a final appellate conviction, or does the trial-court conviction and qualifying sentence operate presently?
  4. Can the political mandate or the Governor’s appointment insulate the appointee from quo warranto?
  5. How should the Court protect otherwise lawful governmental acts already performed by the invalid appointee?

3. Petitioner’s arguments recorded in the DU introduction

  • Article 164(4) accommodates a competent but non-member person; it is not a route for an ineligible person.
  • The duty to obtain membership within six months necessarily presupposes ability to contest and acquire membership at the appointment stage.
  • Articles 163, 164, 173 and 191 must be read together with the RPA, not in isolated literal fragments.
  • The non-member appointment is an exception to representative ministerial government and must preserve the standards expected of legislators.
  • Collective responsibility under Article 164(2) supports accountability rather than an eligibility-free executive class.

4. Respondents’ arguments, recorded and addressed in the extract

  • Article 164(4) has no express qualification list: it should allow a short-term Minister for six months even if currently unable to contest.
  • Suspension argument: since imprisonment was suspended, the disqualification should also be regarded as suspended; the sentence was said to be the decisive element in Section 8(3).
  • Finality/presumption argument: disqualification should await final appellate affirmation; the accused should continue to receive the presumption of innocence during appeal.
  • Former Section 8(4) analogy: the incumbent-saving principle should be extended/read down to protect non-legislators, or disqualification should be postponed generally.
  • People’s will: the successful party’s election and choice of leader constituted a democratic mandate which the Governor should follow. Interference would enter the “political thicket.”
  • Governor’s institutional limits: the Governor had no detailed trial-like machinery to determine every possible qualification dispute, and the appointment should not be undone through quo warranto.
  • Possible future acquittal: her appeal might succeed before the remaining six-month window expired, so the Court should refrain from immediate removal.

5. Step-by-step judicial answer

Harmonious reading of Article 164: clauses (1), (2) and (4) are read as one scheme. The Governor appoints; the Council is answerable to the Assembly; the exceptional non-member must acquire membership within six months. That person must consequently satisfy Article 173 and not be disqualified under Article 191 when appointed. A different eligibility standard for non-member Ministers would be unreasonable and anomalous.

Purpose of the window: political exigency or the need for expertise may justify temporarily bringing in a qualified outsider. It does not justify six months of government by a person unable to enter the legislature. The Court rejects the construction of deliberately “short-term” Ministers free of legislative eligibility standards.

Criminal-law effect: suspension of execution of sentence and bail leave the conviction and imposed qualifying sentence intact. The High Court order did not stay the conviction. Section 8(3) therefore continued to operate. If sentence is imposed after conviction, the cumulative trigger is met when the requisite sentence is imposed.

No indefinite innocence saving: the conviction operates until set aside. Eventual acquittal and current legal disqualification are not the same inquiry. The Court rejects converting the incumbent-only historical Section 8(4) into a general saving by “reading up” its language.

Constitution over political mandate: a majority cannot require a constitutional head to appoint an underage, foreign-citizen, insolvent or otherwise disqualified CM. The absurd consequences of that submission expose its flaw. The will expressed through a majority prevails only consistently with the Constitution.

Judicial duty: the controversy is constitutional interpretation even if politically consequential. Quo warranto examines the legal authority of the appointee to hold public office. A constitutional head’s appointment cannot confer a higher right than the Constitution allows.

6. Decision, relief and protection of prior acts

The appointment was quashed and set aside; Jayalalithaa could not continue as CM under the invalid appointment. The Court would not wait for a possible appellate acquittal or the approaching end of the six-month period. It protected acts otherwise legal and valid performed by her, the Council and the State government during the interval from appointment to the judgment, against invalidity based only on the defective appointment.

That qualification matters: the ruling did not validate an independently unlawful act. It preserved continuity and third-party reliance without legitimising the ineligible appointment.

7. Ratio and evolved principles

  • Eligible outsider ≠ disqualified person: Article 164’s temporary non-member accommodation requires legislative qualifications and freedom from disqualifications.
  • Sentence execution ≠ conviction: bail or suspension of execution does not remove the conviction disqualification.
  • Constitutional supremacy: electoral majority is not authority to disregard constitutional eligibility.
  • Quo warranto: constitutional public-office appointments can be invalidated for lack of qualification notwithstanding their political setting.
  • Continuity: otherwise lawful governmental acts need not collapse merely because the office-holder’s appointment was invalid.

8. Embedded precedent: S.R. Chaudhuri

The DU extract describes Tej Parkash Singh’s repeated appointment as Minister within the same legislative term after failing to become a member within the first six months. That case rejects restarting the grace period through resignation and reappointment. Kapur uses the representative-government rationale to interpret the non-member exception narrowly enough to preserve accountability.

9. Limits and current-law reading

The case concerns the actual Section 8(3) rule and conviction position then before the Court. The RPA’s listed-offence route later includes Prevention of Corruption Act convictions in Section 8(1)(m); do not generalise that every corruption conviction requires two years to disqualify today. The former Section 8(4) discussion is historical; Lily Thomas later invalidated it. An express stay of conviction is different from the unsuccessful stay applications and sentence-execution order in this case.

Use in an answer: Articles 164(1), (2), (4) → 173/191 → RPA ground → sentence versus conviction → constitutional mandate → quo warranto → carefully limited protection of prior acts.

DU pp. 106–116: introduction and submissions; ¶19 (Chaudhuri); ¶¶21–30 (eligibility); ¶¶32–40, 45 (conviction); ¶¶46–53 (mandate and review); ¶¶54–60 (relief).

23
DU EXTRACT · pp. 117–125

Lily Thomas v. Union of India

(2013) 7 SCC 653 · A.K. Patnaik and S.J. Mukhopadhaya JJ

Holding in one line: Parliament lacked constitutional power to enact the incumbent-only postponement in RPA Section 8(4); the Court did not need to decide the separate Article 14 challenge.

Full case analysis · facts, issues, arguments and ratio

1. Background and challenged law

Two Article 32 public-interest petitions—WP(C) 490/2005 and 231/2005—challenged Section 8(4). Sections 8(1)–(3) laid down conviction-based disqualifications, but 8(4) postponed their operation for a person who was an MP or State legislator at conviction: three months initially, and thereafter until disposal of a timely appeal or revision. A newly contesting candidate had no equivalent saving.

The dispute was not an election petition against one particular returned candidate and not a fresh criminal appeal. It was a challenge to Parliament’s ability to create this protective statutory distinction.

2. Issues

  1. Does the constitutional power under Articles 102(1)(e)/191(1)(e) allow different operation of disqualification for new candidates and sitting members?
  2. Can a general residuary legislative power under Articles 246/248 and Entry 97 support the saving if the specific power cannot?
  3. Can Parliament postpone the vacancy consequence in Articles 101(3)(a)/190(3)(a)?
  4. Is Section 8(4) also discriminatory under Article 14?
  5. Should existing members who already relied on the saving and had pending timely appeals/revisions be affected by the declaration?

3. Petitioners’ arguments

Fali S. Nariman and S.N. Shukla argued that “being chosen as, and for being” requires the same disqualification standard for candidature and continuance. Saka Venkata Rao had described the same set of disqualifications for both. Parliament was empowered to create disqualifications, not to suspend them only for incumbents against the Constitution’s vacancy mandate.

  • A qualifying trial conviction operates until set aside; a pending appeal alone is no basis for continuing membership.
  • B.R. Kapur and K. Prabhakaran support the present operation of conviction and sentence.
  • The appropriate protection in a suitable case is an appellate order staying the conviction under CrPC Section 389, not a blanket incumbent saving.
  • The incumbent/candidate difference lacks a legitimate justification and separately violates Article 14.

4. Union/respondent arguments recorded in the extract

  • The provision changes only when the same disqualification takes effect, not the underlying grounds.
  • Continuity of the House justified Parliament prescribing postponed operation for existing members.
  • The vacancy arises only after the President/Governor has decided the constitutional question, which was said to support postponement.
  • Appellate courts cannot directly stay the statutory disqualification, so a legislative safeguard is needed.
  • The Constitution Bench’s discussion in K. Prabhakaran was relied on in support of the provision.
  • Alternatively, residuary Union legislative competence under Article 246(1), Article 248 and Entry 97 was said to supply power.

5. The reasoning, not just the headline

Specific power governs: Articles 102(1)(e) and 191(1)(e) are the specific constitutional grant for legislatively prescribed disqualifications. General Union–State distribution provisions and residuary power cannot enlarge that grant beyond its terms. The Court uses the written-constitution approach reflected in R. v. Burah: determine the affirmative power and its negative limits from the controlling instrument.

One constitutional standard: the language covers being chosen and being a member. Parliament cannot make an incumbent remain eligible where the identical disqualification prevents a non-member from being chosen. Describing the distinction as mere timing does not avoid the constitutional problem when the practical result is a different eligibility regime.

Vacancy provision: Articles 101(3)(a)/190(3)(a) prohibit Parliament from deferring the date of effective disqualification for sitting members in the manner Section 8(4) attempted. The provision exceeds the conferred legislative power.

Earlier authority: the Court notes that the specific lack-of-legislative-power issue had not been decided by the Constitution Bench in K. Prabhakaran. It does not purport to overrule a Constitution Bench on an issue that Bench had actually settled merely because this case has two judges.

Article 14: once the provision is invalid for lack of power, the discrimination challenge need not be decided. “Struck down because Article 14 was violated” is therefore an incomplete and inaccurate statement of the actual ratio.

6. Decision and temporal protection

Section 8(4) was declared ultra vires the Constitution; the writ petitions were allowed, without costs. The judgment protected sitting members who had already incurred a relevant conviction and had filed timely appeals/revisions which were pending and were consequently protected by the prior law. The Court invoked its capacity to mould the temporal operation of declared law and fairness to persons who had relied on it.

For convictions after pronouncement, the old saving no longer operates even if an appeal/revision is filed promptly. The protected earlier class must not be converted into a new three-month grace period for every future member.

7. Principle and connections

The legislature is a body with plenary power within constitutional limits, not power to alter the Constitution’s express conditions through an ordinary statute. Political cleanliness is the policy setting, but the ratio is the structure of disqualification power. The case links directly to Kapur’s present-conviction rule and to Lok Prahari’s recognition of a specific judicial stay of conviction.

8. Precise limits

  • No general disqualification merely on accusation or charge is created by this decision.
  • The ruling invalidates subsection (4), not the entire RPA or Sections 8(1)–(3).
  • The rule still requires the exact listed offence/sentence combination in the applicable subsection.
  • An express stay of conviction is not the same as the unconstitutional statutory blanket postponement.
  • The extract omits some intermediate paragraphs of the full judgment; missing text is not supplied as an alleged DU quotation.

Use in an answer: quote the operative constitutional phrase, identify the specific source of power, reject residuary enlargement, explain immediate operation and limited past protection, then distinguish stay of conviction.

DU pp. 117–125: ¶¶1–4 background; ¶¶5–13 petitioner submissions; ¶¶17–19 Union reply; ¶¶20–33 legislative-power reasoning; ¶36 Article 14 not decided; ¶¶37–39 temporal operation and disposition.

24
DU SUMMARY · p. 126

Lok Prahari (through General Secretary S.N. Shukla) v. Election Commission of India

(2018) 18 SCC 114 · Dipak Misra CJI, A.M. Khanwilkar and D.Y. Chandrachud JJ

Holding in one line: an effective appellate stay of conviction means that the Section 8 disqualification will not operate; it is not equivalent to mere suspension of the sentence.

Detailed analysis of the actual DU summary

1. Facts and procedural character

Lok Prahari sought a declaration concerning legislators convicted of offences attracting Section 8, whose convictions were stayed by appellate courts. The petition challenged the proposition that such a stay could prevent the constitutional vacancy consequences. This was a general legal challenge to the effect of stay orders, not a new factual trial of every legislator benefiting from one.

2. Issues

  1. Is there power to stay the operation of a conviction under Section 389 CrPC?
  2. If such a stay operates, does the conviction-based disqualification continue regardless?
  3. Do Articles 101(3)(a)/190(3)(a) make the seat irreversibly vacant notwithstanding a legally effective stay?

3. Petitioner’s argument as supplied by DU

The petitioner contended that the law did not provide for a stay of conviction which could wipe out the disqualification. Consequently, even an appellate stay of conviction for an offence attracting Section 8 should not neutralise disqualification, and the seat should be treated as vacant from the conviction date under the constitutional vacancy provisions.

4. ECI’s position—do not invent an opposing argument

The DU summary expressly states that the Election Commission supported the prayer in its counter-affidavit. Accordingly, the parties’ reported positions on the legal question were aligned. It would be false to write a conventional “ECI argued that every stay automatically restored membership” merely to produce two opposite sides. The summary does not separately set out any other respondent’s detailed submissions.

5. Decision and reasoning stated in the DU material

The Court rejected the proposed declaration as inconsistent with settled law in Lily Thomas and Ravikant S. Patil v. Sarvabhouma S. Bagali, (2007) 1 SCC 673. Upon a stay of conviction under Section 389, Section 8 disqualification will not operate. The continuing legal status of the conviction—not merely whether a person is physically in jail—determines this consequence.

6. Principle and doctrinal reconciliation

Kapur involved suspension of sentence execution without a conviction stay. Lily Thomas rejected legislative postponement solely for sitting members. Lok Prahari respects a court’s specific stay of the conviction itself. These are compatible propositions: no automatic appeal protection, but legal effect to an actual judicial conviction stay.

7. Limits

  • A stay does not amount to appellate acquittal and does not finally erase the conviction.
  • A stay of sentence, bail or mere filing of appeal is insufficient.
  • The case does not create an entitlement to receive a conviction stay merely because loss of a legislative seat is inconvenient.
  • The summary cannot establish every factual detail of an individual restoration case, or the treatment of an already completed bye-election. Those details are not fabricated.

Use in an answer: describe the order actually granted by the appellate court. If only the sentence execution is suspended, cite Kapur; if conviction is expressly stayed, use this case. Identify the temporal effect of the stay in the particular dispute.

DU p. 126, entire prescribed summary. The confined depth of the source is disclosed rather than padded with invented litigation facts. Modern procedural counterpart: BNSS s. 430, subject to the applicable savings.

One synthesis to remember

Anand permits an eligible non-member; Kapur excludes an ineligible non-member; Lily rejects an incumbent-only statutory exemption from present conviction consequences; Lok Prahari gives legal effect to a specific stay of conviction. These rulings answer four different questions.

11 / PRESCRIBED CASE FILES · PART II

Elections, floor tests and office of profit

25
DU EXTRACT · pp. 127–138

Special Reference No. 1 of 2002 (Re Gujarat Assembly Election Matter)

(2002) 8 SCC 237 · Five-judge Bench; DU extract of V.N. Khare J’s opinion for B.N. Kirpal CJI, Khare and Ashok Bhan JJ

Holding in one line: Article 174’s six-month gap regulates sessions of a live Assembly, not the interval between a dissolved Assembly and a newly elected successor; Article 324 governs election scheduling in its distinct field.

Full case analysis · facts, reference questions, positions and reasoning

1. Detailed factual and institutional setting

The Gujarat Assembly constituted in March 1998 had an ordinary term ending on 18 March 2003. Its last sitting was on 3 April 2002. On 19 July 2002 the Governor dissolved it on the Chief Minister’s advice. The Election Commission took steps for fresh elections but, in its order of 16 August 2002, proceeded on the legal assumption that Article 174(1) applied even to a dissolved Assembly.

On that assumption, the new Assembly would need to meet within six months from the outgoing Assembly’s last sitting—by 3 October 2002. The Commission assessed that elections could not be conducted before that date. The President made an Article 143(1) reference on 19 August 2002 to clarify the constitutional position and the possible role of Article 356.

Procedural caution: the reference addressed questions of public constitutional importance, not a judicial re-trial of all disputed ground conditions in Gujarat. The Court declined to adjudicate disputed facts from the Commission’s order in the advisory setting.

2. The three Presidential questions

  1. Is Article 174 subject to the Commission’s Article 324 decision about the election schedule?
  2. Can the Commission schedule elections on the premise that an Article 174 infraction can be remedied by Article 356?
  3. Must the Commission secure all requisite Union/State resources to fulfil Article 174’s mandate while ensuring free and fair elections?

The premise linking Article 174 to a dissolved Assembly had to be examined before answering the supposed conflict.

3. Competing positions in the DU extract

As an advisory reference there are not simply a plaintiff and defendant. The extract records the following institutional submissions/premises, which should be described as such:

  • Original ECI premise: the six-month Article 174 requirement was regarded as mandatory and applicable to the outgoing-to-incoming Assembly interval. The order also indicated Article 356 as a possible solution to a constitutional impasse.
  • Union’s continuing-House argument: “Assembly” was said to be dissolved but the “House” remained a continuing institutional entity. The Speaker’s continuance under Article 179 was relied on to argue that the six-month session rule still applied.
  • Concern over indefinite delay: counsel for a national party and a State warned that absence of any express deadline might allow the Commission never to hold an election, destroying democracy.
  • ECI clarification: in written submissions it said its election decision was taken without reliance on Article 356; the provision had only been mentioned as an answer to apprehended impasse.
  • Independent electoral field: the scheduling issue was to be analysed through Article 324 and the RPA, rather than by treating a dissolved Assembly as capable of further sessions.

4. Reasoning I: text and the “live Assembly” distinction

Article 174 speaks of “its last sitting in one session” and “its first sitting in the next session.” Those expressions refer to successive sessions of the same functional Assembly. A successor Assembly holds its own first session, not the outgoing body’s “next session.” The power to “summon” is directed to an existing House, whereas “constitution” of an Assembly follows the statutory election notification mechanism in RPA Section 73.

The contrast with Article 176’s express wording “after each general election” confirms the point. Continuation of the Speaker’s office cannot preserve the dissolved members’ representative capacity or create a House distinct from the Assembly for this purpose.

5. Reasoning II: history and Constituent Assembly debates

The DU extract traces the Government of India Acts of 1915, 1919 and 1935. Earlier arrangements had express executive responsibilities about calling a new chamber after dissolution. The constitutional design departed from those arrangements by establishing an autonomous Election Commission under Article 324. The session-frequency provisions were borrowed for their limited live-House purpose, not as an implied election deadline.

Debates on how frequently Parliament should meet concerned executive accountability and time for business. The original phrase requiring two meetings a year created the technical difficulty that a year-long single session might count as only one summons; its removal left the inter-session six-month safeguard. That history is incompatible with treating the provision as one governing elections to a different House.

6. Reasoning III: consequences and separate statutory scheme

If the Assembly dissolved in the fifth month after its last sitting, the proposed reading could require an entire general election within the remaining month. That was not the intended constitutional rule. RPA Sections 14 and 15 address general elections on expiry/dissolution and permit the formal pre-expiry election notification only within the stated six-month window. They do not make the outgoing Assembly’s last sitting the starting date for every fresh-election deadline.

Article 324 entrusts the Commission with superintendence, direction, control and conduct; Articles 327/328 permit election legislation within constitutional limits. The opinion distinguishes legislative regulation of election matters from the Commission’s constitutional scheduling responsibility. The legislature cannot confiscate the Commission’s constitutionally assigned function by ordinary law.

7. Answers and conclusions

  • Article 174 concerns an existing, live, functional Assembly.
  • The session-gap rule is mandatory for that body but gives no express/implied election deadline counted from the dissolved House’s last sitting.
  • Article 174 and Article 324 operate in different fields; neither is subordinated to the other in the supposed manner.
  • As there is no Article 174 infraction of the assumed kind, the Article 356 rescue premise is unnecessary; the Court does not determine a general licence to impose President’s Rule whenever elections are delayed.
  • The Commission must hold free and fair elections at the earliest; the Court’s conclusion records that under the overall constitutional/statutory scheme fresh elections should be held within six months of premature dissolution.
  • Ordinary public disorder should not be an excuse for postponing elections; the Union, State and other authorities must assist.

8. Ratio, important qualification and applications

The ratio is the field distinction and the live-House interpretation. The six-month expectation from dissolution should not be misstated as the rejected Article 174 deadline from the outgoing House’s last sitting. Absence of that Article 174 deadline equally does not mean unlimited ECI freedom to suspend democracy indefinitely.

The Court also distinguishes adjournment, prorogation and dissolution. Use the exact Article 107/196 lapse exceptions rather than repeating the extract’s broad description that all pending Bills lapse.

Use in an answer: identify whether the Assembly still exists; state the text; distinguish constitution from summons; explain ECI’s role and the RPA; reject automatic Article 356 “cure”; conclude with timely election obligations.

DU pp. 127–138: facts/reference; ¶¶10, 14–16, 19–37 history; ¶¶40–55 live-House analysis; ¶56 Union submission; ¶¶72–82 statute/ECI; ¶84 conclusions; ¶¶85–86 answers. Use the prescribed SCC citation rather than the extract’s inconsistent AIR heading.
