DU-PRESCRIBED · FULL ORDER SUPPLEMENT

Anil Kumar Jha v. Union of India

(2005) 3 SCC 150 · Order dated 9 March 2005 · R.C. Lahoti CJI, Y.K. Sabharwal and D.M. Dharmadhikari JJ

Holding in one line: the Court issued urgent interim directions for a peaceful, secure and video-recorded Jharkhand floor test confined to the elected members, without determining final guilt or replacing the legislative vote.

Detailed judicial-order analysis, with source limits

1. Why this is a supplement

The uploaded DU Topic 4 list prescribes this case but gives no standalone extract. The analysis below is based on the reported order itself, not a student-blog description. In particular, the reported disposition is interim directions and further listing, not a final judgment declaring the Governor’s appointment mala fide.

2. Facts and procedural setting

WP(C) 123/2005 was filed and urgently mentioned on 7 March 2005. It concerned contested post-election developments in Jharkhand. At the 9 March hearing, petitioner’s counsel reported developments after filing: the Governor had selected a comparatively junior MLA as pro tem Speaker despite the asserted convention of choosing the seniormost available member; a nomination under the then-operative Article 333 was reportedly imminent.

The petitioner said nomination could tilt the balance before the majority question was tested. A quo warranto challenge to the incumbent CM’s appointment was among the reliefs sought, and the contemplated nomination on that administration’s recommendation was questioned. A connected WP(C) 120/2005 was also before the Court for further listing.

3. Immediate issues

  1. Should urgent interim measures ensure that the competing claims are determined promptly on the Assembly floor?
  2. How can manipulation through procedural control or an imminent nomination be prevented before that test?
  3. What attendance, security and recording safeguards are appropriate without the Court casting the votes itself?

The order does not frame and finally decide a comprehensive list of substantive constitutional issues.

4. Petitioner’s contentions actually recorded

  • A seniority convention had been bypassed in appointing the pro tem Speaker.
  • The stage for the contemplated Anglo-Indian nomination was not ripe, and it could change the numerical balance.
  • The recommendation could be affected by the pending challenge to the CM’s authority.
  • A strong prima facie case justified immediate protection of the floor-test process.

5. Respondents’ position actually recorded

The order records hearing counsel for the respondents, but does not provide a detailed adversarial argument rejecting each petitioner claim. Counsel for Jharkhand, through the Chief Secretary and Director General of Police, assured compliance with the duty to allow members to attend freely and securely. That assurance must be recorded faithfully; opposing constitutional submissions not contained in the order should not be fabricated.

6. Seven substantive interim directions

  1. The Assembly session already convened for 10 March, when newly elected members were to take the oath, would continue on 11 March for a confidence test.
  2. The only agenda on 11 March would be the floor test between the competing political alliances to establish majority and the claim to Chief Ministership.
  3. Proceedings must be wholly peaceful; disturbance would be viewed seriously.
  4. The pro tem Speaker must announce the result faithfully and truthfully.
  5. The Court’s order itself constituted notice of the 11 March meeting; no separate notice was necessary.
  6. There was to be no Article 333 nomination until the specified date; the floor test was confined to the 81 elected members.
  7. The Chief Secretary and DGP were to secure free, safe attendance without interference or hindrance.

The Court declined to appoint an observer but required video recording and immediate transmission of the recording. Orders were to be promptly communicated, including by fax; the matters were listed for 14 March.

7. Reasoning and principle

The Court found a strong prima facie case on the sworn averments and relied on Jagdambika Pal for an expeditious floor-test remedy. Its intervention created conditions for the legislature to determine majority; it did not decide the vote count through predictions or appoint an alternative CM by judicial preference.

Principle illustrated: actual House confidence, established through a fair floor vote, is the appropriate basis for resolving contested majority claims. Ancillary protective directions can preserve the integrity of that constitutional process.

8. Limits, later context and critical evaluation

  • This order does not finally hold that every junior pro tem appointment is unconstitutional. The seniority convention is recorded as a petitioner submission.
  • It is not a final merits judgment proving gubernatorial mala fides or setting out a universal floor-test code.
  • The Article 333 direction is historically important but is not a presently available Anglo-Indian nomination route after Article 334(b)’s seventy-year expiry.
  • Its remedy is intrusive in scheduling and agenda, but functionally justified by returning the majority question to the House. Whether the measures were necessary/proportionate can be discussed as academic evaluation, not attributed as a dissent in this short order.

Use in an answer: write “interim floor-test safeguards,” not “Governor finally convicted of fraud.” Connect Articles 164, 174, 178/180, 188 and the historical 333 setting; preserve the elected-member majority process.

Full reported order, ¶¶1–10, especially ¶¶4–6: judicial-order text. DU 2022 Topic 4 list prescribes it; no standalone text is present in that upload.

27
DU-PRESCRIBED · FULL JUDGMENT SUPPLEMENT

Jaya Bachchan v. Union of India

(2006) 5 SCC 266 · 8 May 2006 · Y.K. Sabharwal CJI, C.K. Thakker and R.V. Raveendran JJ

Holding in one line: receivable pecuniary benefit makes an office one of profit; the holder’s wealth, non-use of facilities or voluntary decision not to draw the remuneration does not alter that character.

Full case analysis · appointment terms, contentions and principle

1. DU status and citation correction

This case is in the DU prescribed list, but not supplied as a standalone extract. The Consumer Education summary on p. 126 misprints a Jaya Bachchan citation as “(2005) 3 SCC 87.” The Topic 4 list and actual judgment use (2006) 5 SCC 266, which is followed here.

2. Facts and route to the Court

Jaya Bachchan was a Rajya Sabha member. The Uttar Pradesh government appointed her Chairperson of the Uttar Pradesh Film Development Council by an official memorandum on 14 July 2004, conferring Cabinet Minister rank and the associated remuneration/facilities under the government’s terms.

The Election Commission gave its Article 103(2) opinion on 2 March 2006 that the office was an office of profit under the State government and was not exempt under the Parliamentary exemption Act. By order dated 16 March 2006, the President decided that she stood disqualified from Rajya Sabha from 14 July 2004. She challenged both the Presidential order and ECI opinion through Article 32.

3. Financial terms which drove the dispute

  • Monthly honorarium of ₹5,000.
  • Daily allowance of ₹600 within the State and ₹750 outside it for the specified touring situation.
  • Entertainment expenditure of ₹10,000 per month.
  • A staff car with driver; telephones at office and residence.
  • Free accommodation and medical facilities for the holder and family under the stipulated terms, plus other facilities.

These are historical appointment terms from this case, not today’s general remuneration rates.

4. Issues

  1. Does an office capable of yielding financial benefit qualify even if no benefit was actually drawn?
  2. Does calling the appointment honorary/decorative negate the profit attached by the appointment terms?
  3. Do precedents involving genuine compensatory allowances or genuinely unpaid honorary appointments support her case?
  4. Does the appointment’s nomenclature, rather than its substantive financial terms, control whether it is an office of profit?

5. Petitioner’s submissions

She argued that the chairpersonship and rank were decorative and that she received no remuneration or monetary gain. She had not sought residence, used telephone/medical facilities or claimed travel reimbursement. Without a finding of actual payment, ECI could not classify the office as one of profit.

She relied on Umrao Singh v. Darbara Singh, Divya Prakash v. Kultar Chand Rana and Biharilal Dobray v. Roshan Lal Dobray to argue that an honorary appointment without remuneration should not disqualify.

6. Supporting position for the disqualification

The judgment sets out ECI’s reasoning and the undisputed appointment terms, but does not reproduce a separate complete Union submission section. The source-supported answer to her contention was that entitlement itself constituted a receivable pecuniary gain, the office was not a statutorily exempted office, and she was not protected merely by the honorific Cabinet-rank description. This is a summary of the disqualification position, not fabricated respondent dialogue.

7. Court’s reasoning

Capability, not receipt: an office of profit is an office capable of yielding profit or pecuniary gain. Salary, pay, emoluments, remuneration and non-compensatory allowance attached to the office are material. The question must be interpreted realistically, by substance rather than nomenclature.

Compensatory expenses differ: reimbursement of actual out-of-pocket expenditure is not automatically personal profit. A fixed honorarium and valuable attached facilities cannot be converted into mere reimbursements by declaring that the holder did not use them.

Precedents distinguished: Umrao Singh involved allowances intended to reimburse expenditure associated with duty. In Divya Prakash, the appointment was specifically honorary and the post as dealt with there did not carry the remuneration assumed in the petitioner’s comparison. The judgment also identifies obiter/error in the way the later precedent described Divya Prakash. None displaced the established receivability rule beginning with Ravanna Subanna.

Application: the honorarium, entertainment allowance, car/driver, telephones, accommodation and medical treatment were undeniable pecuniary benefits. Her affluence and unwillingness to claim them were irrelevant. The Court treated the potential entitlement as the decisive point.

8. Decision and ratio

The writ petition was dismissed and the disqualification upheld. The ratio is that an office entitling its holder to pecuniary gain other than genuine reimbursement is an office of profit even if the holder elects not to receive the gain.

9. Limits and extensions

  • The case does not replace the separate inquiry whether the office is under government.
  • Not every allowance is non-compensatory; examine its substance.
  • A statutory exemption, properly applicable to the office and legislature, may remove disqualification even though the office is otherwise of profit.
  • “Cabinet rank” does not mean the holder has constitutionally become an actual Minister protected by the explanation.
  • Consumer Education concerns the subsequent retrospective exemption legislation, not a reversal of this benefit-entitlement interpretation.

Use in an answer: identify office → government nexus → attached gain → genuine reimbursement exception → valid exemption → Article 103/192 or election forum. Do not stop at “she did not receive money.”

Full judgment ¶¶1–13, particularly ¶¶2–6 and 11–13: [1]. DU prescription and brief reference: Topic 4 list and p. 126.

28
DU SUMMARY · p. 126 DETAILS FROM FULL JUDGMENT

Consumer Education and Research Society v. Union of India & Ors.

(2009) 9 SCC 648 · 24 August 2009 · K.G. Balakrishnan CJI, R.V. Raveendran and J.M. Panchal JJ

Holding in one line: Parliament may retrospectively exempt offices of profit under Article 102(1)(a); the challenged 2006 Act was valid, and the relevant undeclared office-of-profit cases did not involve automatic reinstatement into already vacated seats.

Full case analysis · the short DU proposition and its essential limits

1. Primary DU proposition

The DU summary describes the post-Jaya Bachchan 2006 Amendment enlarging the exempted-office list, the retrospective-validity challenge, and the conclusion that Parliament could act before the Article 103 declaration in the disputed office-of-profit cases. The following chronology, detailed submissions and statutory limits are supplied from the judgment, explicitly as a supplement.

2. Facts, legislation and procedural history

Following Bachchan’s disqualification, concern arose that numerous MPs held other government-linked offices of profit. The Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Amendment Bill, 2006 was introduced and passed in Lok Sabha on 16 May and passed in Rajya Sabha the next day. Sent for assent on 25 May, it was returned by the President on 30 May. Both Houses repassed it without amendment; assent followed on 18 August 2006.

The Amendment Act added, among other offices, the National Advisory Council chairpersonship, inserted categories of specified statutory/non-statutory bodies, trusts and registered societies, and listed 55 bodies. The specified new categories/table were deemed inserted from 4 April 1959. Section 4(1) validated the stated exemptions notwithstanding judgments/orders; Section 4(2) expressly denied reinstatement or an equivalent claim to a person who had already vacated a seat under the relevant order/judgment.

Two Article 32 PILs challenged the Act. The case did not begin as an appeal against one particular election result.

3. Issues

  1. Does Article 102(1)(a) authorise retrospective exemption, or only future exemption?
  2. Did acceptance of the offices automatically vacate the MPs’ seats before the law, making the Act an unconstitutional re-entry without election?
  3. Was wholesale exemption of 55 offices without Joint Committee scrutiny colourable, contrary to a constitutional convention or violative of Article 14?
  4. How do Articles 101/103 distinguish pre-election and subsequent disqualification?

4. Petitioners’ contentions

Senior counsel Harish Salve and Ravinder Srivastava argued that the constitutional scheme immediately vacated seats of holders of disqualifying offices. Retrospective exemption could not re-induct persons who had ceased to be MPs without fresh elections. They addressed both offices held before election and offices accepted during membership.

  • The legislation was said to have been designed to protect particular incumbents rather than legitimate institutional compatibility.
  • Longstanding practice following the Bhargava Committee report required the Joint Committee’s examination of proposed exemptions; bypassing it for 55 offices breached a constitutional convention.
  • The exemptions lacked discernible rational criteria and offended Article 14.
  • The enactment was characterised as colourable legislation contrary to the constitutional disqualification structure.

5. Union’s submissions

Additional Solicitors General Gopal Subramaniam and Mohan Parasaran relied on Kanta Kathuria for retrospective exemption power. They argued that in a disputed subsequently incurred office-of-profit case vacancy follows the designated constitutional decision, not mere unadjudicated allegation. No relevant Presidential declaration had preceded the Amendment.

They also relied on Section 4(2): the law did not reinstate anyone who had already vacated under an order or judgment. Selection of exempt offices lay in Parliament’s domain; a Joint Committee practice was not a binding constitutional restriction extinguishing that law-making power.

6. Reasoning on retrospectivity

Kanta Kathuria established that the exemption power includes retrospective exercise. Article 102(1)(a) expressly permits Parliament to identify offices which do not disqualify; the power is not restricted to future holders. Retrospective removal of the legal ground is different from Parliament purporting to ignore a disqualification while leaving the ground fully operative.

7. Reasoning on timing, declaration and election-stage defects

The judgment distinguishes a disqualification existing when elected from one subsequently incurred. Pre-election defects are addressed by nomination scrutiny under RPA Section 36 and an election petition under Section 100; Articles 101/103’s “becomes subject” language concerns subsequent status.

In the disputed office-of-profit setting, adjudication/declaration by the President is necessary to crystallise the vacancy; the decision confirms a pre-existing disqualification rather than inventing it. The Court notes that the disqualification, when declared, operates from the date the office was accepted, while explaining why an unadjudicated dispute is not itself an automatic completed vacancy.

RPA Section 151A’s bye-election timetable was part of the practical reasoning: if an unknown/unresolved office-of-profit allegation automatically started an unascertainable vacancy period, timely filling could become impossible. Because the relevant members had not been declared disqualified before the retrospective exemption, they could continue; the law’s no-reinstatement clause remained important.

8. Equality, convention and colourability

Offices have different effects on member independence, time, loyalty and incompatibility. Parliament’s exemption choices cannot be invalidated merely because other allegedly similar offices were not also exempted, absent a supported constitutional defect. The actual claim before the Court did not establish the necessary incompatibility or arbitrary equivalence.

The Joint Committee practice was characterised as Parliamentary procedure, not a constitutional convention preventing valid legislative action. Failure to follow the practice did not denude Parliament of its express exemption power. A political motive allegation does not alone establish colourable exercise when the actual constitutional power exists and has been lawfully used.

9. Decision and principles

The Court upheld the Amendment Act and dismissed the petitions without costs. It reaffirmed retrospective exemption power, clarified the pre-election/subsequent distinction, upheld the challenged legislative selection against the presented Article 14 case, and rejected the supposed binding constitutional-convention condition.

10. Limits: do not overclaim

  • The law did not automatically reinstate Bachchan or another person whose seat had already been vacated under the specified order/judgment; Section 4(2) said the opposite.
  • The decision does not say all offices of profit must be exempted or that Parliament’s choices can never be constitutionally reviewed.
  • It does not make Joint Committee scrutiny worthless; it rejects the asserted legal invalidity consequence.
  • Its declaration language should not be mechanically extended to neutralise Lily Thomas’s later conviction ruling.
  • The cure operates by changing the legal status of the office retrospectively, not merely by granting personal grace to one incumbent.

Use in an answer: Article 102(1)(a) → retrospective exemption power → Article 103 disputed office-of-profit adjudication → no prior declaration in the relevant cases → Section 4(2) no reinstatement → equality/convention analysis.

DU p. 126. Full-judgment supplement ¶¶1–15 (setting and submissions), 16–20 (power and timing), 23–37 (vacancy/adjudication), 38–40 (equality/procedure/disposition): full judgment.

Deep reconciliation · Consumer Education and Lily Thomas

The 2009 case says a disputed subsequent office-of-profit vacancy requires the designated declaration; the 2013 case says Parliament cannot defer the conviction-disqualification date through an incumbent saving. They should not be flattened into one slogan.

  1. Different legal source: Consumer Education exercises Article 102(1)(a)’s express power to exempt an office; Lily limits the clause (1)(e) statutory disqualification power and the postponement of its consequences.
  2. Different trigger: whether an office is of profit and exempt can require an inquiry. A qualifying conviction and sentence are judicially established events, with their operative effect determined by Section 8 and any actual conviction stay.
  3. Adjudication versus grace: lawful resolution of a disputed fact is not the same as a blanket legislative waiting period after an established trigger.
  4. Chronology and textual tension: broad language about vacancy in the cases must be confined to their issues; do not claim the supplied sources contain a comprehensive express reconciliation of every possible conflict.

Exam conclusion: use Consumer Education for office-of-profit retrospectivity and its declaration setting; use Lily and Lok Prahari for conviction and stay. State the ground and procedural facts before announcing whether a seat is vacant.

12 / PRESCRIBED CASE FILES · PART III

Privilege under a written Constitution

Read these cases together. Keshav Singh rejects legislative detention immune from constitutional courts. Raja Ram Pal recognises a genuine expulsion power but subjects its exercise to limited constitutional review. Power and accountability coexist.

29
DU DISCUSSION IN RAJA · pp. 143–145 FULL REFERENCE OPINION

In re Keshav Singh

AIR 1965 SC 745 · Special Reference No. 1 of 1964 · Opinion delivered 30 September 1964 · Majority opinion of P.B. Gajendragadkar CJI; A.K. Sarkar J dissenting

Holding in one line: a legislature’s privilege to punish contempt does not make its detention orders conclusively immune from Article 226 habeas corpus; lawful resort to and exercise of that jurisdiction cannot itself be punished as legislative contempt.

Full majority analysis, five answers and dissent

1. Source discipline

The DU upload does not reproduce this as a standalone case. It contains a substantial synopsis in the prescribed Raja Ram Pal extract, particularly ¶¶56–57. The chronology, rival submissions, constitutional reasoning and Sarkar dissent below are from the full reference opinion. These are not represented as pages of a missing DU extract.

2. Facts: a conflict which escalated in days

Keshav Singh, a non-member from Gorakhpur, signed a pamphlet associated with allegations against a UP Assembly member. On 14 March 1964 the Assembly’s Speaker reprimanded him for contempt/breach of privilege. The House also ordered seven days’ imprisonment for his conduct when brought before it and an earlier disrespectful letter. He was detained in the District Jail at Lucknow under the Speaker’s warrant.

On 19 March, advocate B. Solomon filed a petition under Article 226 and Section 491 of the old CrPC, alleging unlawful imprisonment, want of authority, lack of hearing, mala fides and breach of natural justice. A Lucknow Bench of N.U. Beg and G.D. Sahgal JJ agreed to hear it at 3 p.m. The government advocate who had appeared at the earlier mention was absent at the appointed hearing. The Bench admitted the petition and granted conditional interim bail, pending determination of its legality.

On 21 March the Assembly resolved that Singh, his advocate and both judges had committed contempt through the litigation/bail order. It called for custody of the judges and advocate and further action against Singh. The judges moved the High Court. A Full Bench of 28 judges restrained implementation; Solomon’s later petition received similar protection. The Assembly then modified its stance, withdrawing the arrest warrants but requiring explanations. The President referred five questions under Article 143(1) on 26 March.

14 MarchReprimand and seven-day detention
19 MarchArticle 226 petition; interim bail
21 MarchHouse resolution against judges, counsel and detainee
23–25 MarchFull Bench protection; modified House demand for explanation
26 MarchPresidential reference

3. Five referred questions, in analytical form

  1. Could the Lucknow Bench entertain the detention challenge and grant interim bail?
  2. Did Singh, Solomon or the two judges thereby commit legislative contempt?
  3. Could the Assembly produce the judges/advocate in custody or require explanations for that alleged contempt?
  4. Could the Full Bench entertain the protective petitions and restrain implementation of the House resolution?
  5. More generally, is a judge who hears or grants relief against a legislative privilege/contempt order himself in contempt, and can the House proceed against him?

4. Assembly’s arguments: Seervai’s constitutional case

  • Exclusive jurisdiction: the House claimed to determine the existence, extent and exercise of its privileges for itself. Its appearance in the advisory reference did not concede submission to judicial authority.
  • British dualism: historical conflict between Parliament and courts left legislative privilege, particularly contempt, within the House’s exclusive domain.
  • General warrant conclusiveness: even where courts could examine a privilege’s existence or a speaking warrant’s stated reason, an unspeaking/general warrant of the Commons was treated as conclusive. Article 194(3) was said to import that immunity from scrutiny.
  • Consequential contempt: if the High Court could not go behind the detention warrant, presentation, acceptance and grant of bail against it were interference with legislative privilege.
  • Interim bail: the House separately denied jurisdiction to grant bail in such a habeas corpus challenge, especially before a return was filed.
  • Advisory status: there was no ordinary lis or binding inter-party judicial disposition; the House asserted that an advisory answer could not prevent its own determination.

5. Judges’/advocate’s constitutional position: Setalvad’s answer

  • Written Constitution: India cannot simply import an unresolved English antinomy. Article 194(3) must be read with Articles 32, 226 and 211.
  • Extent determined by courts: construing the constitutional source of privilege is a judicial task; the House cannot conclusively decide the scope of its own jurisdiction.
  • Historical convention not transplantable: English treatment of general warrants arose partly from Parliament’s superior-court-of-record history and convention/comity. An Indian Assembly was not such a court.
  • Habeas corpus remains: an imprisoned citizen can invoke Article 226, and the court can examine constitutional legality even when the warrant omits reasons.
  • Ancillary bail: effective Article 226 jurisdiction includes appropriate interim relief.
  • Judicial independence: lawful adjudication and professional presentation of a petition cannot be made an offence against the legislature merely because the House dislikes their effect.

The opposing side did not deny all Assembly power to punish genuine contempt outside the chamber. The dispute concerned alleged conclusive detention authority and punishment of lawful judicial process.

6. Majority reasoning: the core constitutional architecture

Constitutional, not Parliamentary supremacy: every organ derives authority from a written, supreme Constitution. Articles 194 and 226 are both parts of it. Their harmonious interpretation preserves genuine legislative functions and the judiciary’s assigned protection of legality and liberty.

The three privilege clauses: speech under 194(1), express court immunity under 194(2), and residual privileges under 194(3) are related but distinct. A claim under clause (3) is not self-proving and cannot silently extinguish express constitutional writ jurisdiction.

No superior-court-of-record fiction: the English conclusiveness of a general warrant was tied to a particular history. The Court does not treat an Indian legislative House as a court of justice entitled to make every detention lawful by issuing a non-speaking warrant. Reasons cannot be insulated merely by not stating them.

Article 226 breadth: a detainee’s challenge is within the High Court’s jurisdiction, which extends beyond fundamental-rights enforcement to other legal purposes. Constitutional detention review is not a forbidden appeal on ordinary Parliamentary procedure. Ancillary bail may be granted to make that jurisdiction effective.

Article 211 and judges: the State Legislature is constitutionally prohibited from discussing the conduct of Supreme Court/High Court judges in discharge of their duties. The majority treats this as a real constitutional restriction reflecting judicial independence, not an empty recommendation. It reinforces the incompatibility of demanding custody/explanation merely for lawful judicial adjudication.

Fundamental rights: the Court does not proclaim that every Part III right always defeats every privilege. It distinguishes the earlier Pandit Sharma speech/publication controversy and the Article 19 setting. Article 21 and judicial authority to test lawful deprivation of liberty remain highly material. The correct exam method is harmonious constitutional construction, not two competing absolute slogans.

Article 212: insulation from challenge on procedural irregularity does not make unconstitutional exercise of privilege immune. Whether the House possessed the claimed coercive jurisdiction is different from whether its internal procedure was ideally followed.

7. The majority’s actual five answers

QuestionAnswerMeaning
1YesThe Lucknow Bench was competent to hear the petition and grant interim bail.
2NoSingh, his advocate and the judges did not commit contempt by those lawful steps.
3NoThe Assembly could neither compel their production in custody nor call for explanations on this basis.
4YesThe Full Bench could entertain the petitions and issue restraining interim orders.
5No, with a defined scopeThe general answer was confined to the material context: a non-member’s alleged contempt outside the House and a lawful judicial challenge to the resulting action.

These are advisory answers. They are not a criminal acquittal after trial on every allegation about the original pamphlet or conduct.

8. Sarkar J’s dissent—why it matters

Sarkar J took a materially broader view of the imported Commons privilege. He regarded the conclusiveness of a general contempt warrant as part of the constitutionally conferred privilege, not merely a discardable convention. By harmonious construction, general liberty/writ provisions could not simply extinguish a specific privilege conferred by the Constitution itself. At the same time, he expressly accepted that courts determine the existence and extent of constitutional privilege; his position was not that the Assembly alone finally interprets Article 194(3).

Crucial nuance: the dissent did not mechanically answer every factual question opposite to the majority. The petition before the Lucknow Bench did not show detention under a general warrant, and the Speaker/jailor had not yet filed their return revealing it. Until apprised of that fact, the Bench retained competence to consider the petition. He therefore answered question 1 yes, while leaving the distinct legal propriety of bail in contempt proceedings undecided on this occasion.

QuestionSarkar J’s actual answer on the stated facts
1Yes: general habeas jurisdiction remained until the purported conclusive-warrant fact was established by return.
2No: the participants were not shown to know detention was under a general warrant; he found no wilfully illegal act amounting to contempt.
3Custody: no on these facts, including absence of a hearing and his conclusion of no contempt. Calling for explanations: yes, as an incident of ascertaining contempt—the important disagreement with the majority.
4Yes: the Full Bench could protect the judges/advocate against a finding of contempt which was not established on the stated facts.
5No on these facts; the question was too general for one answer across every possible circumstance.

He discussed the competing arguments about complete judicial immunity and Article 211 but declined to decide the abstract immunity question as unnecessary. He also urged both sides to exercise restraint; he believed the crisis could have been avoided through returns, proper factual information and institutional forbearance.

Contrast: the majority rejects imported general-warrant conclusiveness under India’s constitutional structure. Sarkar J accepts that privilege in principle, yet preserves preliminary jurisdiction before the warrant is established and largely agrees with factual protection here. Do not reduce this nuanced dissent to “no High Court jurisdiction at any stage.” The majority remains controlling.

9. Restraint and the doctrine’s limits

The majority urges restraint and avoidance of intemperate criticism by both constitutional organs. Judicial review does not confer authority to run House business, and privilege does not confer authority to imprison judges for lawful adjudication. It does not eliminate contempt punishment, nor establish absolute immunity for every unrelated act a judge, lawyer or litigant might commit.

Use in an answer: Article 194(3) claim → Article 226 habeas jurisdiction → historical warrant distinction → Articles 21/211/212 → five answers → mutual restraint. For the Supreme Court, explain Articles 32 and 143 and connect Raja Ram Pal.

DU Raja Ram Pal, pp. 143–145, ¶¶56–57. Full opinion supplement: ¶¶1–14 chronology/questions; 20–30 rival positions; 141–146 majority answers and restraint; 147 onward Sarkar dissent, especially ¶155, ¶¶209–221 answers and ¶227: full reference opinion.

30
DU EXTRACT · pp. 139–158 DISSENT FROM FULL OPINION

Raja Ram Pal v. Hon’ble Speaker, Lok Sabha

(2007) 3 SCC 184 · Majority: Y.K. Sabharwal CJI, K.G. Balakrishnan, D.K. Jain and C.K. Thakker JJ · R.V. Raveendran J dissenting

Holding in one line: expulsion for grave misconduct is a House privilege under Article 105(3), but the Constitution permits limited review for illegality and unconstitutionality, not appellate re-weighing of evidence or correction of mere procedural irregularity.

Full case analysis · both sides, judicial-review standards and dissent

1. Detailed facts and inquiry process

A television sting aired on 12 December 2005 purported to show ten Lok Sabha MPs and one Rajya Sabha MP accepting money for raising questions in Parliament. Allegations concerning the Members of Parliament Local Area Development Scheme were separately televised. Members disputed the allegations, accuracy, authenticity or inferences drawn from the recordings.

Lok Sabha appointed an inquiry committee. It concluded that the cash-for-questions conduct was unethical and unbecoming and impaired dignity and credibility; on 23 December 2005 the House accepted the recommendation and expelled the ten members. The Rajya Sabha Ethics Committee separately inquired into its member’s case and the House expelled him on the same date. Proceedings also addressed the separate MPLADS allegations. The Court was faced with Article 32 petitions challenging expulsion and connected transferred litigation.

Factual caution: the constitutional ruling on expulsion was not the Supreme Court conducting the original sting or acting as the criminal trial court. Parliament’s inquiries and the limited validity of their results were the matters before it.

2. Main issues

  1. Does Article 105(3) confer expulsion power, or is Parliament confined to specified vacancy/disqualification provisions and lesser punishment?
  2. Is expulsion simply a new statutory disqualification by another name?
  3. Does Article 122 or “exclusive cognisance” exclude every judicial challenge to internal privilege proceedings?
  4. What constitutional defects, if any, justify review?
  5. Did the actual inquiries/expulsions violate fundamental rights or natural justice sufficiently to be quashed?

3. Petitioners’ arguments: power and fairness

  • No expulsion power: Commons powers historically linked to sovereignty or its judicial functions cannot be imported wholesale into a written Indian Constitution.
  • Exhaustive membership scheme: Articles 101–103 and statutory/Tenth Schedule provisions control how an elected seat is lost. Article 105 should not add an unlisted route.
  • Democratic representation: expulsion removes the people’s chosen member; Parliament is not free to override the electorate.
  • Not necessary: suspension, contempt punishment or criminal prosecution were available, so expulsion was not inherent to effective functioning.
  • Unfair process: the inquiries were rushed; authenticity and completeness of video material were disputed; opportunity to contest the case, including cross-examination, was questioned.
  • Rights and legality: Article 122 protects only irregular procedure; serious constitutional and natural-justice defects remain reviewable.
  • Hardwari Lal: the contrary view on legislative expulsion supported their no-power argument.

4. Parliament/Union-supported position

  • Historical disciplinary privilege: Article 105(3) incorporated the Commons’ established expulsion power, not merely lesser punishments.
  • Institutional integrity: members selling questions compromise the deliberative institution itself; the House must protect its dignity and functioning.
  • Distinct concepts: expulsion is a disciplinary sanction removing current membership; disqualification is a status-based bar to candidature/membership.
  • Internal autonomy: the House is best placed to investigate misconduct connected with its own functions, and courts should not become an appeal over its procedure and evidence.
  • Fair opportunity: the proceedings gave notice of allegations and opportunities for explanation; Parliamentary inquiry need not imitate a criminal trial.
  • Article 122: intervention based on internal irregularity was constitutionally barred; strong institutional deference was warranted.

The summary separates arguments reflected in the DU reasoning from verbatim submissions. The extract is selective: it does not purport to reproduce every party’s complete written case.

5. Majority reasoning I: source and nature of expulsion

The power to expel was an established Commons privilege at the relevant constitutional adoption point, and its disciplinary basis was not dependent on importing British Parliamentary sovereignty. Articles 105(3)/194(3) bring genuine privileges into a different institutional setting: a written Constitution controlling all powers.

Expulsion protects the dignity and integrity of the House against grave misconduct. The majority rejects the contrary Hardwari Lal approach which treated disqualification/vacancy provisions as a complete exclusion of the disciplinary privilege.

The existence of lesser sanctions does not erase the historically recognised power. Whether the House chooses expulsion is not simply a judicial proportionality appeal; courts review within their constitutional limits.

6. Majority reasoning II: expulsion is not disqualification

Disqualification may attach at candidature or to continued membership and imposes the legal bar prescribed by the Constitution/statute. Expulsion is punishment for particular conduct terminating a present seat. It does not itself enact an additional continuing bar to candidature or prevent re-election under a fresh electoral mandate.

Vacancy/disqualification clauses must be read alongside, not as repealing, the privilege provision. This is the central answer to a claim that Article 105(3) cannot ever affect membership.

7. Majority reasoning III: courts determine constitutional boundaries

U.P. Assembly/Keshav Singh, Pandit Sharma and later constitutional decisions establish judicial authority to examine the existence and extent of claimed privilege. Parliament’s dignity does not make it supreme over the Constitution or convert it into the final judge of its own jurisdiction.

Article 122(1) protects proceedings against challenge on the ground of irregularity of procedure. It does not protect substantive illegality, jurisdictional excess or unconstitutionality merely because these occurred inside Parliamentary proceedings. The corresponding State rule is Article 212.

8. Paragraph 431: an usable judicial-review checklist

PropositionExam application
Presumption and respectBegin with the House as a co-ordinate constitutional institution; do not presume bad faith or treat every departure as fatal.
No appellate factual re-trialNo substitution of the court’s preferred conclusion merely because another factual inference is possible.
Procedure has autonomyMere violation of internal rules/ordinary procedural irregularity attracts Article 122 insulation.
Constitutional limits remainSubstantive illegality, unconstitutionality, want/excess of jurisdiction and fundamental-rights defects can be examined.
Natural justice is contextualAsk whether there was grave deprivation of fair opportunity, not whether every Evidence Act/criminal-trial formality was copied.
Mala fides require proofAllegations are not self-proving; the burden is heavy. Use relevant material rather than political rhetoric.
Material may be examined for validityCalling for the record to test a permitted constitutional ground is not the same as routine re-evaluation of evidence.
Constitutional necessity, not appealThe court intervenes when the threshold defect is demonstrated; it ordinarily respects the House’s expertise and autonomy.

This is a reorganised teaching checklist, not a purported verbatim reproduction of the alphabetised paragraph. Refer back to the DU paragraph for the precise formulations.

9. Application and outcome

The majority held that the expulsions followed the constitutionally permissible privilege power. The proceedings had afforded meaningful opportunities; the claimed defects did not establish a reviewable constitutional invalidity. Committee material, nature of the misconduct and institutional context did not justify substituting a judicial merits decision. The challenges were dismissed; the expulsions were upheld.

The Court was not saying the video evidence proved every conceivable criminal offence beyond reasonable doubt. It sustained the Parliamentary disciplinary decision within the applicable constitutional review standard.

10. Raveendran J’s dissent on the power

The DU extract supplies the majority, not the detailed dissent. The following is from the separate judicial opinion. Raveendran J accepted the gravity of accepting money for legislative work and acknowledged House discipline/contempt powers. He disagreed that Commons expulsion could be imported to override India’s specific representative-membership scheme.

For him, British expulsion reflected a history and sovereignty not shared by an Indian legislature; suspension, reprimand and lawful contempt punishment remained available. His central objection was structural: Articles 101 and 102 exhaustively regulate vacancy and disqualification, and a House resolution is not a Parliamentary law adding a disqualification under Article 102(1)(e). Loss of elected membership must follow the Constitution’s prescribed routes rather than an assumed additional power. He proposed lawful criminal prosecution, capable of being fast-tracked, temporary suspension if necessary, and statutory disqualification following a qualifying conviction. In his view, expulsion required suitable constitutional amendment or a valid enabling law; he would invalidate these expulsions and treat the petitioners as continuing members, subject to lawful cessation. These are the dissent’s conclusions, not the outcome adopted by the Court.

Thus his dissent addressed jurisdiction/power, not approval of cash-for-questions or a holding that the acts were ethical. The controlling majority’s answer is that a genuine disciplinary expulsion privilege exists independently of ordinary disqualification.

11. Principles and limits

  • Constitutional supremacy replaces both a theory of absolute Parliamentary sovereignty and a theory of judges supervising every House irregularity.
  • A disciplinary expulsion does not create a free-standing future electoral disqualification.
  • Article 122 is a limited non-interference rule, not a jurisdictional wall against all constitutional review.
  • Judicial review is available but exacting; the fact that Parliament has a power is separate from whether a particular exercise is constitutional.
  • The result does not hold that every accusation or minor misconduct must lead to expulsion.
  • Sita Soren later reinforces privilege’s functional character and denies immunity for bribery; it is not the expulsion decision here.

Use in an answer: state the textual privilege source → identify expulsion as distinct from disqualification → contrast British and Indian constitutional settings → explain Article 122’s narrow exclusion → apply ¶431’s standard → conclude with validity and appropriate limits.

DU pp. 139–158: ¶¶1–7 facts; 17–23 constitutional scheme; 53–62 earlier review cases; 65/70 privilege/history; 165–170 and 207 onward expulsion; 431 review; 454–456 outcome. Supplemental dissent: R.V. Raveendran J’s separate opinion.

KESHAV SINGH · DETENTION

“You cannot challenge us” rejected

House’s general warrant cannot oust Article 226. Courts, counsel and litigants do not commit contempt by lawfully using constitutional remedies.

RAJA RAM PAL · EXPULSION

“We have a power” does not mean “we are beyond review”

Expulsion power exists. Mere irregularity is protected; substantial illegality and unconstitutionality remain reviewable.

VERIFIED PYQDecember 2024 · Q 5(b) · 10 marks

When can a non-legislator be made Chief Minister or Minister?

“When can a non-legislator be made a Chief Minister or Minister under Article 164 of the Constitution of India? Support your answer with relevant legal provisions and judgments.”
Expanded model answer

Introduction: non-membership is not ineligibility

A non-legislator may be appointed CM or Minister temporarily, but only if otherwise constitutionally eligible to enter the State Legislature. The six-month period accommodates non-membership; it does not remove positive qualifications or disqualifications. Articles 164(1), (2) and (4) must be read with Articles 173 and 191.

The constitutional framework

Under Article 164(1), the Governor appoints the CM and appoints other Ministers on the CM’s advice. Article 164(2) makes the Council collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly. Article 164(4) says that a Minister who for any period of six consecutive months is not a member of the State Legislature ceases at the expiry of that period to be a Minister. This permits appointment of a non-member, rather than only preserving an incumbent Minister who loses a seat.

The exception applies to the CM as a member/head of the Council. If the State has two Houses, membership of either may satisfy it, although collective responsibility remains to the Assembly. In a unicameral State, the person must become an MLA. The Minister’s office oath under Article 164(3) is distinct from the legislative-membership oath under Article 188.

Eligible outsider: the permissive principle

In S.P. Anand v. H.D. Deve Gowda, the Supreme Court upheld appointment of a non-MP Prime Minister under the corresponding Article 75(5). The special status of the head of the Council does not exclude the PM/CM from “Minister.” Parliamentary/Assembly accountability continues through confidence and collective responsibility. Articles 88 and 177 permit ministerial participation, but do not give a non-member a legislative vote.

The Court’s earlier State precedents, discussed in Anand and Kapur, reject reading the clause as restricted to former legislators. Political necessity or useful expertise can explain the temporary appointment, but the constitutional conditions remain.

Ineligible outsider: B.R. Kapur

Jayalalithaa had convictions carrying the relevant imprisonment terms. Her criminal appeals were pending; execution of the sentences was suspended and bail granted, but the convictions were not stayed. After election rejection and her party’s victory, she was appointed CM despite not being a legislator.

The Court held that Articles 164(1), (2) and (4) form a scheme. A non-member appointee must possess Article 173’s qualifications and be free of Article 191/RPA disqualifications at appointment. Otherwise the duty to enter the legislature within six months would be emptied of its purpose, and a succession of ineligible temporary Ministers could govern without representative legitimacy. The appointment was quashed; otherwise lawful earlier governmental acts were protected from invalidity based only on the appointment defect.

Suspension of sentence execution is not a stay of conviction. A political majority or the Governor’s appointment cannot cure constitutional incapacity. The people’s will is exercised subject to the Constitution, not above it.

No serial restarting: S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab

The DU Kapur extract explains that a non-member Minister who failed to obtain membership in the first six months could not resign and be reappointed during the same legislative term simply to start another six-month allowance. Article 164(4) is an exception supporting representative government, not a revolving-door licence to avoid election.

Conviction update and practical application

In Lily Thomas, Section 8(4)’s incumbent-only appeal protection was invalidated; a future qualifying conviction cannot be bypassed simply by filing an appeal. Lok Prahari v. ECI recognises the different effect of an express conviction stay. Thus, identify the actual offence, sentence and order—not merely whether the prospective Minister is in prison.

If an otherwise qualified expert is appointed, can secure membership within six consecutive months and the government commands Assembly confidence, non-membership alone does not invalidate appointment. If the appointee is below the relevant minimum age, lacks citizenship/electoral qualification, or is presently disqualified, the window cannot rescue the appointment. Other prohibitions, such as Article 164(1B)’s anti-defection ministerial bar, must also be observed.

Conclusion

A non-legislator can be CM/Minister when the appointment satisfies Article 164, the person is otherwise eligible under Articles 173/191 and electoral law, membership is acquired within six consecutive months, and accountability to the Assembly is preserved. Qualified non-member, yes; presently disqualified appointee or repeated evasion, no.

VERIFIED PYQDecember 2024 · Q 8(b) · 10 marks

Does legislative privilege include expulsion of members?

“Does the powers and privileges of the Legislatures in India, include the power of expulsion of their members? Discuss with the help of relevant legal provisions and judgments.”
Expanded model answer

Introduction and textual basis

Yes. The controlling majority in Raja Ram Pal v. Hon’ble Speaker, Lok Sabha, (2007) 3 SCC 184, recognises expulsion as a disciplinary legislative privilege. But the House is subject to the Constitution; its exercise is not immune from all judicial review.

Article 105 deals with Parliament and Article 194 with State Legislatures. Clause (1) protects legislative speech subject to constitutional/procedural conditions; clause (2) immunises speech/votes and authorised publication from court proceedings; clause (3) deals with residual powers, privileges and immunities. Before statutory definition, the continuing privileges have the historically incorporated scope. The Forty-fourth Amendment replaced the direct British wording without turning the residual clause into unlimited sovereignty.

Raja Ram Pal: facts and majority holding

Televised sting material purported to show MPs accepting money to raise Parliamentary questions. After House inquiries, ten Lok Sabha MPs and one Rajya Sabha MP were expelled. They challenged both the House’s power and procedural fairness. The majority upheld the expulsions.

Expulsion was an established Commons disciplinary privilege within the constitutional incorporation. It protects a deliberative body against grave conduct destructive of integrity and public confidence. It is not excluded simply because lesser sanctions such as reprimand, imprisonment for contempt or suspension are possible.

Expulsion is different from disqualification

The petitioners argued that Articles 101–103 and the electoral/anti-defection framework exhaust the ways in which an elected seat can be lost. The Court rejected equating a disciplinary sanction with a status-based disqualification. Article 105(3) must be harmonised with, rather than erased by, the membership provisions.

Disqualification determines legal eligibility to be chosen or continue. Expulsion terminates the present membership for particular misconduct. It does not itself create a new continuing electoral bar or prevent the person from returning under a fresh election if otherwise eligible. Articles 190–192 and 194 supply the State analogues.

Judicial review: autonomy with constitutional boundaries

Article 122(1), and Article 212(1) for States, prohibit challenge based on mere irregularity of procedure. They do not exclude review for substantive illegality or unconstitutionality. Courts can determine whether the asserted privilege exists and whether its exercise violates constitutional limits.

Keshav Singh had already rejected the proposition that a House’s general warrant makes detention unreviewable or that lawful use of Article 226 can itself be punished as contempt. Raja Ram Pal carries that constitutional-supremacy approach into expulsion.

The reviewing court respects Parliament as a co-ordinate organ, presumes regularity and does not sit as an appeal to reweigh the sting evidence. The challenger must establish a reviewable defect—jurisdictional excess, substantive illegality, unconstitutionality, a grave fair-hearing defect or proved mala fides—not merely dissatisfaction with procedure or result.

Dissent and critical balance

Raveendran J’s separate dissent regarded the Indian membership scheme as controlling and denied an additional imported expulsion route, while accepting the gravity of the conduct and alternative discipline/prosecution. The majority is binding. The dissent nevertheless highlights a legitimate structural concern: a majoritarian House must not use a disciplinary power simply to silence an opponent.

The safeguards therefore lie in lawful grounds, contextual fair opportunity and limited constitutional review. Criminal liability is a distinct sphere. The 2024 Sita Soren ruling confirms that bribe-taking is not protected by speech/vote immunity, but it is not the source of the 2007 expulsion power.

Conclusion

Indian legislatures possess expulsion power under their residual privileges, according to Raja Ram Pal. The power is disciplinary and distinguishable from disqualification. It coexists with Articles 122/212’s protection of internal procedure and the courts’ duty to prevent substantive illegality or unconstitutionality.

10-mark route105(3)/194(3)cash-for-questionsexpulsion ≠ disqualification122/212 limitsmajority conclusion

VERIFIED PYQCentenary Chance · Q 1 · 20 marks

Supreme Court jurisdiction in relation to Parliamentary privileges

“Discuss the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in relation to Parliamentary Privileges with case laws.”
Full 20-mark study model

1. Introduction: neither absolute sovereignty nor routine judicial supervision

Parliamentary privilege secures independent and effective legislative functioning. It is not a personal licence to violate law, and Parliament is not sovereign above India’s written Constitution. The Supreme Court can determine the existence and extent of claimed privilege and examine unconstitutional exercise, while respecting express immunities and the internal-procedure bar in Article 122.

2. Constitutional sources and routes to the Court

Article 105(1) protects freedom of speech in Parliament subject to the Constitution and procedural rules; 105(2) gives members court immunity in respect of speech and votes and protects authorised publication; 105(3) supplies other privileges until defined by law. Article 194 is the State counterpart. These clauses must be distinguished: an expressly protected parliamentary vote is not the same as every act related to Parliamentary politics.

Article 32 allows the Supreme Court to enforce fundamental rights against unconstitutional action. Article 143(1) permits a Presidential advisory reference, as in Keshav Singh. Article 136 may provide an appellate route from a judicial decision in a legally appropriate proceeding; it is not a premise for an unrestricted direct factual appeal from every House resolution. High Courts have Article 226 jurisdiction, broader in subject-matter than Article 32.

Article 122(1) excludes attacks on validity based on irregularity of procedure. Clause (2) protects Parliamentary officers/members exercising constitutional powers to regulate procedure/conduct of business/maintain order from court jurisdiction in that functional respect. Article 212 is parallel. Neither can be casually expanded into universal exemption from constitutional review.

3. Early publication controversy: M.S.M. Sharma

The DU Raja Ram Pal extract discusses M.S.M. Sharma v. Sri Krishna Sinha (Pandit Sharma/Searchlight). A newspaper published proceedings including expunged portions and challenged legislative action. The decisions addressed the relation between legislative privilege and Article 19(1)(a), giving priority to the particular privilege in that setting and recognising the internal-procedure principle.

Do not turn that into “all privileges always defeat all rights.” The Court itself examined the existence and scope of the claimed privilege. The later cases distinguish procedural autonomy from constitutional illegality and analyse Article 21 and writ jurisdiction. An unauthorised publication also differs from authorised publication under 105(2) and a substantially true good-faith report under Article 361A; secret sittings, malice and expunged material require care.

4. In re Keshav Singh: writ jurisdiction cannot be erased by a general warrant

The UP Assembly imprisoned a non-member, who sought Article 226 relief through counsel. The High Court granted interim bail. The Assembly treated the petition, advocate’s appearance and judges’ order as further contempt, directing custody or explanations. Protective High Court orders followed; the President sought the Supreme Court’s opinion.

The Assembly claimed exclusive determination of its privileges and imported English conclusiveness of general warrants. The majority rejected that transplantation. The English rule was connected with historical superior-court-of-record status; an Indian Assembly is not such a court. Articles 194, 226 and 211 must be read within one supreme Constitution.

The High Court could hear the detention challenge and grant interim bail. Lawful resort to jurisdiction by the detainee/counsel and lawful judicial exercise did not constitute contempt. The House could not compel the judges/advocate to appear in custody or justify the order on that basis. The Full Bench could protect them. The general fifth answer was carefully confined to the relevant non-member/outside-House contempt setting.

The Supreme Court thereby recognised judicial competence to ascertain privilege’s constitutional limits while affirming genuine House contempt powers. Sarkar J’s dissent favoured the conclusiveness claim; the majority controls. Mutual restraint, not institutional humiliation, was urged.

5. Raja Ram Pal: genuine privilege and limited review coexist

After the cash-for-questions sting, House inquiries led to expulsions. The majority held expulsion a recognised Article 105(3) privilege, distinct from disqualification. An expelled person is not, by that sanction alone, subject to a future statutory candidature bar.

Equally, Parliament cannot conclusively certify its own jurisdiction beyond constitutional limits. Article 122 immunises mere procedural irregularity, not substantive illegality or unconstitutionality. Courts can examine the existence of power and review permitted legal defects without taking over the merits.

Paragraph 431 supplies the standard: respect and a presumption in favour of the co-ordinate institution; no re-evaluation of evidence as an ordinary appeal; no correction of every internal-rule departure; review for jurisdictional or substantial constitutional/legal defects; contextual natural justice; heavy burden for mala fides. The actual expulsions survived this review. Raveendran J dissented on the existence of the additional expulsion power, not on whether corruption was acceptable.

6. Current supplement: Sita Soren v. Union of India, 2024

The seven-judge Court overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao’s bribery-immunity holding. A bribe connected with speech or vote fails the functional necessity test. The privilege must connect with the House’s collective functioning and be essential to members’ duties; corruption does the opposite.

Bribery liability does not depend on the recipient ultimately casting the promised vote. Criminal prosecution and House discipline operate in distinct, potentially concurrent spheres. Immunity for a vote does not immunise a separate bribe. This dated supplement reinforces—not replaces—the prescribed Keshav and Raja framework.

7. Analytical application

First classify the act: speech, vote, authorised publication, ordinary reporting, contempt, expulsion or an external criminal act. Identify the relevant clause and the asserted privilege. Then identify the remedy route and constitutional ground. If a member is sued for what she said in the House, clause (2)’s express immunity is central. If a House imprisons an outsider and claims no court may inspect legality, Keshav applies. If the complaint is simply that an inquiry timetable breached an internal rule, Article 122 and Raja generally prevent a procedural appeal. If the order lacks constitutional power or gravely denies basic fairness, permitted review remains. If money was accepted for a vote, Sita Soren excludes bribery immunity.

8. Conclusion

The Supreme Court is guardian of constitutional boundaries, not supervisor of every Parliamentary debate. It recognises real privileges, respects express speech/vote immunities and internal procedure, and intervenes against demonstrated substantive illegality or unconstitutionality. M.S.M. Sharma, Keshav Singh, Raja Ram Pal and the dated Sita Soren supplement show a progression toward functional autonomy within constitutional supremacy.

20-mark routeprivilege clauses32/143/226122/212SharmaKeshavRajaapplication + conclusion

VERIFIED PYQCentenary Chance · Q 5(a) · part of a 20-mark question

Can a convicted and disqualified person be appointed Chief Minister?

“Can a person convicted for an offence and disqualified to be a member of the Legislature be appointed as a Chief Minister?”
Expanded problem-oriented model answer

Issue and short answer

No, so long as the person is presently disqualified. Non-membership can be accommodated for six months; disqualification cannot. The question stipulates both conviction and the resulting disqualification, so do not assume every minor conviction by itself necessarily disqualifies.

Constitutional and statutory rule

Article 164(1) authorises appointment, Article 164(2) requires Assembly accountability, and Article 164(4) permits only temporary non-membership. Article 173 sets qualifications; Article 191(1)(e) recognises disqualifications prescribed by Parliamentary law. RPA Sections 8(1)–(3) provide different listed-offence/sentence routes. The precise ground must be established.

The provisory ministerial window does not state that a person may be ineligible for legislative membership while remaining CM. Harmonious construction requires a prospective non-member Minister to be able to enter the legislature lawfully.

B.R. Kapur: directly controlling

Jayalalithaa’s convictions and qualifying sentences continued despite appeals, bail and suspension of execution. Her nominations were rejected; her party nevertheless won a majority and chose her leader. The Governor appointed her CM. The Supreme Court held the appointment unconstitutional and quashed it.

The Court rejected three main answers: first, that Article 164(4) silently permits an ineligible “short-term” Minister; second, that sentence-execution suspension suspends disqualification; third, that popular support removes constitutional constraints. A qualified outsider may be useful for six months, but an ineligible outsider would subvert the very duty to become a representative.

Constitutional supremacy limits the majority and the appointing authority. Quo warranto can test the appointee’s legal authority to hold the office. The Court protected otherwise lawful prior governmental acts from the defect in appointment alone; it did not retrospectively approve the appointment itself.

Appeal, bail and actual conviction stay

Appeal is a challenge, not automatic suspension of the conviction’s legal operation. Bail concerns custody. Suspension of sentence execution concerns carrying out punishment. An express stay of conviction concerns the conviction’s present legal effect.

Lily Thomas invalidated Section 8(4)’s incumbent-only statutory postponement. The candidate/office-holder cannot rely on a general three-month grace period or a pending appeal. Lok Prahari v. ECI states that an operative conviction stay prevents Section 8 disqualification from operating. Thus the exact judicial order may change the premise, but merely hoping for acquittal within six months does not.

Apply to the question

The hypothetical already says the person is disqualified. The appointment would therefore fail under Kapur, irrespective of a party’s majority or a promised future appeal success. The Governor must appoint a person capable of constitutionally holding office. If a later legally effective conviction stay or acquittal changes eligibility, assess a prospective appointment against that changed position and the actual terms; it does not establish that the earlier invalid appointment was lawful all along.

Nor can resignation/reappointment endlessly restart the window. S.R. Chaudhuri prevents that evasion. Other statutory grounds may independently survive even where one conviction ground is stayed.

Conclusion

A presently convicted and disqualified person cannot be CM through Article 164(4). The constitutional distinction is eligible non-member versus ineligible person, not popular versus unpopular leader. Appointment while the stipulated disqualification operates is vulnerable to quo warranto.

VERIFIED PYQCentenary Chance · Q 5(b) · part of a 20-mark question

Can a non-MP be appointed Prime Minister?

“Can a person who is not a member of the Parliament be appointed as the Prime Minister of India?”
Expanded model answer

Short answer

Yes, if otherwise eligible, for the constitutionally permitted period. Article 75(5) applies to the Prime Minister as well as other Ministers. Membership of either House must be acquired before six consecutive months of non-membership expire; Lok Sabha confidence and collective responsibility remain essential.

Read the correct provisions together

Article 74(1) establishes the Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at its head. Article 75(1) deals with appointments: the President appoints the PM, and other Ministers on the PM’s advice. Article 75(3) makes the Council collectively responsible to Lok Sabha. Under 75(5), a Minister who for any period of six consecutive months is not a member of either House ceases to be a Minister at expiry.

The text does not exclude the PM from “Minister.” Article 88 permits Ministers to speak and participate in either House and committees of which they are named members; it gives no membership vote merely by participation. Thus a non-member head can answer and participate during the interim without being counted as an MP.

S.P. Anand: facts and answer to the challenge

Deve Gowda was appointed PM without then belonging to either House. The petitioner challenged the appointment under Articles 14, 21 and 75, argued that PMship’s special responsibility required immediate membership, and relied on British convention.

The Court rejected those contentions. The ministerial provisions are a coherent scheme and the Prime Minister is included. Similar State non-member cases support that interpretation. The rejected Constituent Assembly proposal to restrict appointments to already elected members confirms the temporary-accommodation design. A British convention cannot displace an express Indian arrangement.

Democratic legitimacy and accountability

The Constitution does not provide direct popular election of the PM. Confidence is tested in Lok Sabha, and the Council is collectively responsible to it. Being an eligible non-member for a short period does not sever this accountability. In a hung House, the President’s choice must be directed toward a person able to command that confidence, not an unlimited personal preference.

Once membership is secured, the Constitution does not require that it be specifically Lok Sabha rather than Rajya Sabha. The governmental responsibility remains to the popular House even if the PM is a Rajya Sabha member.

Qualifications and three limits

First, the person must be otherwise eligible to become a member under Article 84 and electoral law and must not be disqualified under Article 102. The minimum age differs by House; eligibility for the lawful route actually pursued must be assessed. B.R. Kapur explains why the corresponding six-month State rule cannot accommodate a presently disqualified appointee.

Second, membership must be obtained within six consecutive months. The interval is not a permanent PMship outside Parliament. The rationale of S.R. Chaudhuri rejects manipulation by repeatedly resigning/reappointing to avoid representative accountability.

Third, ministerial participation under Article 88 does not allow a non-MP to cast a legislative vote or count toward quorum. The Council’s confidence depends on the elected House’s vote.

Conclusion

S.P. Anand supplies a clear yes to the question, qualified by eligibility, six-month membership and collective responsibility. The better constitutional statement is “an eligible non-MP may temporarily be PM,” not “any person can be PM for six months.”

Answer route74/75PM is a MinisterAnand88 participationeligibility + six months + confidence

Question: centenary paper p. 1. Primary DU Anand, pp. 69–74; Kapur, pp. 106–116. Office-head provision correctly identified as Article 74(1).
