VERIFIED · RELATEDDecember 2024 Q 8(a) · 10 marks

When can a Governor exercise discretionary power?

“As per the Constitution of India, when can a governor exercise discretionary power? Discuss with the help of relevant legal provisions and judgments.”
Developed model answer

General rule: the Governor is a constitutional head, not a parallel political government. Article 163(1) provides aid and advice except where the Constitution requires discretion. Samsher Singh v. State of Punjab, (1974) 2 SCC 831, establishes formal exercise ordinarily on ministerial advice, with limited constitutionally justified exceptions. Article 163 is not a general permission to substitute the Governor’s political preferences.

Classify the exceptions instead of listing unexplained powers

  1. Express/special constitutional discretion: the Constitution or special provisions may prescribe it—for example, Article 239(2), relevant parts of Article 371A and the Sixth Schedule provisions discussed in the DU M.P. Special Police extract. Apply the particular text rather than assuming identical discretion in every State.
  2. Necessary structural discretion: choosing a CM where majority is genuinely unsettled is constrained by ability to command Assembly confidence. Dismissal of a government which has actually lost confidence and refuses to resign, and a constitutionally compelled dissolution situation, are exceptional—not a power to pre-empt a government for partisan reasons.
  3. Disabling conflict/irrationality: in the rare sanction context recognised in M.P. Special Police Establishment v. State of M.P., the Council’s disabling decision can permit independent action.
  4. Specified Bill function: the Article 200 position must be explained with its actual text and the dated 2025 supplement, not folded into an unlimited Article 163 doctrine.

Floor confidence and legislative functioning

A disputed majority should ordinarily be established on the Assembly floor. Anil Kumar Jha illustrates judicial directions protecting a prompt, elected-member test. It does not finally adjudicate every gubernatorial allegation in that case. Summons, prorogation and dissolution under Article 174 are ordinarily part of responsible government; discretion is not established merely because the power is expressed in the Governor’s name.

Sanction exception

In M.P. Special Police, a Lokayukta report supplied substantial material against former Ministers. The Council refused sanction on the premise that no material existed; the Governor granted it. The Court upheld the Governor’s action because the refusal was ex facie irrational/non-consideration of relevant material. It did not presume every Council is biased whenever a Minister is accused. The norm of bona fide advice remains.

Dated assent update

The November 2025 five-judge Presidential Reference says that the Governor has constitutional discretion under Article 200 and is not bound by ministerial advice in exercising those Bill options. A non-Money Bill can be returned when withholding; repassage forecloses a repeated withholding/return course, but reservation remains possible under the opinion. No fixed judicial timelines or deemed assent are read in. Prolonged, unexplained indefinite inaction may attract a limited mandamus. This is an identified later development, not a proposition printed in the 2022 DU casebook.

Limits and conclusion

Discretion remains a constitutional function directed toward democratic government and legality. The Governor’s personal Article 361 protection and the confidentiality rule concerning advice do not make every institutional action constitutionally unreviewable. A sound answer identifies a specific express or necessarily implied basis, applies the facts and rejects an unlimited personal-power theory. The default is advice; exceptions require justification.

Primary DU Samsher Singh, pp. 75–88, and M.P. Special Police, pp. 89–98. Topic 4 Anil order and dated 2025 official assent opinion are supplements. Question verified in December paper p. 4.

VERIFIED · RELATEDDecember 2024 Q 6(b) · 10 marks

Theory of separation of power

Write a short note on “Theory of Separation of Power.”
Developed model answer

Meaning and Indian form

The theory separates legislative, executive and judicial functions to prevent concentration and arbitrary power. A rigid version requires separate personnel and exclusive functions. India instead adopts functional differentiation with constitutionally authorised overlap and checks. Parliamentary government deliberately links Ministers with legislative confidence; that overlap does not remove judicial independence or constitutional limits.

Ram Jawaya Kapur: the DU foundation

In Rai Sahib Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab, AIR 1955 SC 549, private textbook publishers challenged the State’s publication policy and argued that the executive could do no business without prior legislation. The Court rejected the narrow view that executive power consists only of implementing already enacted statutes.

Articles 73/162 chiefly distribute executive competence. A government can undertake lawful policy/administrative activity within its sphere without a statute for each step, but it cannot disregard an existing law, constitutional right or a field requiring legislative authority. Expenditure still needs the constitutionally prescribed budget/appropriation process. The Constitution does not follow absolute functional separation, but adequately differentiates the organs and subjects them to checks.

Apply this theory to Parliament and Legislatures

  • Representative executive: Articles 75(3)/164(2) establish collective responsibility; Ministers participate under 88/177. Legislative questions and confidence control the executive.
  • Financial checks: Articles 112–117/202–207 require budgeting, popular-House grant votes and appropriation; executive recommendation does not authorise expenditure without law.
  • Internal independence: privileges under 105/194 and procedure under 118/208 secure deliberative functioning. Articles 121/211 prevent legislative discussion of judges’ official conduct within their stated framework.
  • Judicial limits and remedies: Articles 122/212 bar a procedural appeal, but Keshav Singh and Raja Ram Pal preserve review for substantive constitutional illegality. Judges do not run every debate; Houses do not finally define their own unlimited jurisdiction.
  • Controlled temporary legislation: Articles 123/213 authorise ordinances subject to prompt legislative control; repromulgation cannot create a permanent executive legislature.

Illustrate the balance

An inquiry committee expelling a member exercises a quasi-judicial disciplinary function without becoming an ordinary court of criminal justice. A court invalidating an unconstitutional expulsion exercises constitutional review without acquiring the House’s daily disciplinary agenda. A Minister piloting an Appropriation Bill occupies a political role in both spheres without personally possessing unlimited spending power.

Conclusion

India’s separation is a structured balance of institutional functions, responsible government and checks, not watertight isolation. Overlap is lawful when constitutionally authorised; usurpation is not. Legislative autonomy and judicial review are complementary safeguards under a supreme Constitution.

DU Ram Jawaya, pp. 40–47; Raja, pp. 139–158; adjacent ordinance cases pp. 159–175. In the Ram Jawaya extract’s ¶7, “Article 172” in the executive-power discussion is a transcription/editorial error for Article 162, not the Assembly-duration provision.

VERIFIED · RELATEDDecember 2024 Q 5(a) · 10 marks

Does lapse of an ordinance automatically undo its legal effects?

“Where an ordinance has ceased to operate, would it result ipso jure in a revival of the state of affairs which existed before the ordinance was promulgated? Would the legal effects created by the ordinance stand obliterated as a matter of law upon the lapsing of an ordinance or passing of a resolution of disapproval?” Answer in light of the judgment printed as Krishna Kumar v. State of Bihar [(2017) 3 SCC 1].
Developed model answer

Frame the alternatives

The answer is neither automatic permanent survival nor automatic restoration of every pre-ordinance fact. Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar, (2017) 3 SCC 1, treats continuing effects as a question of constitutional construction, public interest and constitutional necessity, including whether consequences have become irreversible.

Facts and legislative accountability

Bihar used successive ordinances to take over 429 Sanskrit schools and regulate their staff. None was placed before the legislature; no regular replacement law was enacted. Employees claimed continuing governmental status and salary-related rights after the last ordinance lapsed. The seven-judge case reconsidered assumptions that ordinance-created effects automatically become enduring merely because an ordinance temporarily has the force of law.

Articles 123/213 create conditional, temporary legislative power. The ordinance must be laid before the legislature and ceases six weeks after reassembly, or earlier on the constitutionally specified disapproval. Same force and effect while valid does not establish a parallel, permanently rights-creating executive legislature.

The construction test

The Court asks what the particular legal consequences require. Public interest and constitutional necessity, including genuinely irreversible consequences, may justify preserving a consequence or moulding relief. Mere difficulty, inconvenience or expenditure in undoing a transaction is not automatically irreversibility. A new law can validly address matters within legislative power, but the executive cannot guarantee permanent effects by inserting words in an ordinance which defeat its constitutional life.

Temporary statutes and ordinances are not interchangeable for all survival rules. The ordinance’s constitutional laying, duration and legislative-disapproval conditions are controlling. Automatically importing every statutory-repeal saving would undermine those conditions.

Actual outcome

The ordinances were held a fraud on constitutional power: not laid, repeatedly reissued contrary to D.C. Wadhwa, and lacking the claimed enduring legal effect. They did not confer permanent government-employee status. Nevertheless, the Court moulded relief to prevent recovery of salaries already paid during the ordinance tenure under the High Court’s directions.

This outcome concretely refutes both extremes: the employees did not obtain the asserted permanent status, but salary payments were not mechanically clawed back solely on an abstract “everything disappears” theory.

Review and anti-abuse connection

The President/Governor’s satisfaction is not immune from scrutiny. Courts do not decide whether the material was adequate or politically wise; they can examine absence of relevant satisfaction, oblique purpose or fraud/abuse. Repeated promulgation to evade the legislature is constitutionally impermissible. Accountability is enforced through mandatory laying and the legislature’s decision whether regular law is needed.

Conclusion

When an ordinance lapses or is disapproved, it stops operating as an ongoing source of law. Survival of a specific past consequence must be legally justified under the public-interest/constitutional-necessity test; it is not automatically permanent, and every consequence is not automatically erased. Apply the nature of the consequence, valid promulgation, laying/approval history and the appropriate relief.

Question: December paper p. 3. DU Krishna Kumar Singh, pp. 165–175, especially 173–175; D.C. Wadhwa, pp. 159–164. The complete case title corrects the shortened title printed in the question.

VERIFIED · RELATEDCentenary Q 5(c) · p. 2

Must there be a Council of Ministers after Lok Sabha is dissolved?

“Is it essential to have Council of Ministers under Art.74 (1) even at a time when the House of the People has been dissolved or when its term has expired?”
Developed model answer

Answer and controlling structure

Yes: dissolution does not create an executive vacuum or a personal Presidential government. Article 74(1)’s Council of Ministers with the PM at its head is mandatory. Article 53 executive power must be exercised “in accordance with this Constitution,” which includes responsible-government provisions.

U.N.R. Rao v. Indira Gandhi, AIR 1971 SC 1002

Lok Sabha was dissolved on 27 December 1970. The petitioner sought quo warranto against the continuing PM, arguing that Article 75(3)’s collective responsibility was impossible without a House and that the President could administer through officers under Article 53. The Supreme Court dismissed the challenge.

The Court refused to convert “shall” in Article 74(1) into “may.” The Constituent Assembly chose Parliamentary government, not a model under which dissolution enabled the President to dispense with Ministers and govern until impeachment. Article 75(3) must be harmonised with 74(1) and 75(2). Actual confidence operations cannot occur in a dissolved House, but the Council does not vanish.

Continuity, not unlimited power

The Council continues to aid and advise. Allocation of business under Article 77(3) and the PM’s Article 78 duties retain operation. The popular House’s dissolution is distinct from President/Council abolition; Rajya Sabha also continues under Article 83(1).

Caretaker conventions and election-related limits are important political safeguards, but do not mean all administrative acts after dissolution are void. Conversely, continuity does not authorise unconstitutional policy or expenditure without appropriation, indefinite delay of elections or evasion of future confidence.

Source nuance on term expiry

The actual judgment concerned premature dissolution and expressly said it was not separately deciding the Article 83(2) expiry contingency, noting RPA Section 14’s provision for it. The DU headnote and this examination question formulate the broader continuity principle to include expiry. Explain that principle from Article 74’s mandatory structure rather than falsely claiming the Court litigated identical expiry facts.

Conclusion

The Council is constitutionally essential during the electoral interval. Dissolution interrupts the House’s immediate confidence machinery, not the mandatory responsible-executive institution. Harmonious construction prevents a switch to personal Presidential rule.

DU pp. 66–68, particularly ¶¶6–10 and dismissal ¶12. Verified centenary question p. 2; Q 5’s part marks are not separately printed.

VERIFIED · RELATEDCentenary Q 5(d) · p. 2

May the Governor override advice refusing prosecution sanction?

“Can a Governor of a State overrule the advice of the State Council of Ministers refusing sanction to prosecute an ex-Minister for corruption?”
Developed case-based model answer

Rule: exceptional, not routine

Ordinarily the Governor acts on Council advice under Article 163. In the exceptional disabling/irrationality situation recognised in M.P. Special Police Establishment v. State of M.P., (2004) 8 SCC 788, independent sanction was upheld. It is not a general appellate veto over Cabinet decisions.

Facts

A Lokayukta inquiry concerned alleged unlawful release of 7.5 acres already acquired by the Indore Development Authority. It found grounds against two Ministers, who had resigned by the report stage, for corruption and conspiracy. The Council refused sanction saying there was no material for conspiracy. The Governor considered the records and granted sanction under the then-operative CrPC Section 197.

The High Court regarded advice as binding and rejected extending the CM-related exception to ordinary Ministers. The Supreme Court’s five-judge Bench reversed.

Competing arguments and reasoning

The prosecution side argued that discretion is not confined to textually enumerated situations; necessary exceptions arise where the Council disables itself. The former Ministers argued that Council consideration was collective and valid, no bias should be presumed, and the Governor was not an appellate body. They invoked necessity to argue that only the Council could decide.

The Court preserved the presumption that high authorities ordinarily act bona fide. It did not infer collective bias without material. But the actual refusal ignored relevant inquiry evidence and was ex facie irrational. Whether conspiracy could be proved was for trial; rejecting sanction as if no prima facie material existed disregarded the proper stage and purpose.

Where apparent bias or demonstrated irrationality/non-consideration of relevant factors disables the ordinary advisory decision, the Governor may act independently. Necessity could not compel acceptance of a plainly defective refusal when a constitutional alternative was available. Otherwise high officials could evade prosecution through a protective Council, undermining democracy and rule of law.

Decision and statutory caution

The Governor’s sanction was upheld; the Council’s refusal and High Court decisions were set aside. Trial was to proceed expeditiously. Sanction allows prosecution; it is not a conviction or a judicial finding that the accused committed every offence.

The judgment’s CrPC Section 197 and its treatment of the Prevention of Corruption Act are historical statutory applications. A present problem also requires the current applicable sanction provision, offence, status and transitional law. Do not use this constitutional case as proof that prosecution of every former public servant today needs no sanction.

Conclusion

The answer is a qualified yes on facts demonstrating the exceptional disabling situation. A mere disagreement with Cabinet, unsupported fear of bias, or gubernatorial political preference is insufficient. Identify the defect, the prima facie material and the relevant statutory sanction requirement.

DU pp. 89–98, especially ¶¶19–34. Centenary question p. 2. This is an adjacent DU case, not one of the ten Topic 4 prescribed decisions.

VERIFIED · RELATEDCentenary Q 8(b) · p. 2 · any two parts

Ordinance-making power of the executive

Write on “Ordinance making power of the executive.”
Developed model answer

Source and necessity

Article 123 provides the President’s ordinance power; Article 213 is the Governor’s counterpart. They allow temporary legislation when the constitutionally required recess condition is met and circumstances render immediate action necessary. At Union level the bar is when both Houses are in session. At State level the Assembly must not be in session, or, in a bicameral State, both Houses must not be in session. Do not state that an ordinance always requires both Houses to be absent simultaneously.

The power is legislative in character but exercised in the responsible-executive framework; it does not create an independent permanent legislature. An ordinance has the same force/effect as an Act while constitutionally valid, subject to legislative competence and constitutional rights.

Limits and duration

It must be laid before the legislature. It ceases six weeks after reassembly, or earlier on the specified disapproval resolution; different reassembly dates are calculated from the later date where the Constitution so provides. It may be withdrawn. The Governor’s proviso requires Presidential instructions in the specified situations involving prior Presidential sanction, necessary reservation or a provision which would be invalid without Presidential assent if enacted by State law.

“Six weeks” is not “six months.” The inter-session maximum and ordinance lifespan are different rules, and an ordinance is not ordinary Parliamentary passage or assent to a Bill.

Anti-repromulgation: D.C. Wadhwa

Bihar’s practice of maintaining legal regimes through repeatedly reissued ordinances was held a constitutional subterfuge. A temporary emergency device cannot be routinely used to bypass deliberation, approval and legislative responsibility. The fact the executive can lawfully promulgate once does not supply authority to perpetuate the same measure indefinitely.

Krishna Kumar Singh: control, review and consequences

The seven-judge decision reaffirmed that re-promulgation evading the legislature is a fraud on constitutional power and that laying is a mandatory obligation. Satisfaction is judicially reviewable for lack of relevant basis, oblique purpose or abuse, not for the court’s preferred political assessment of adequacy.

Continuing rights after lapse are not automatic. The public-interest/constitutional-necessity test, including irreversible consequences, determines justified survival or moulded relief. In the actual Sanskrit-school case no permanent government-service status arose, but salaries already paid under court directions were protected from recovery. See the separate lapsed-ordinance model for fuller treatment.

Connection to legislative sessions and conclusion

Articles 85/174’s recess framework cannot be manipulated to turn an exceptional executive power into a substitute for Parliament/Assembly. Ordinances bridge necessary temporary gaps, while laying, time limits, disapproval and judicial review restore representative control. They are emergency legislation subject to the Constitution, not executive supremacy.

Centenary question p. 2. Adjacent DU D.C. Wadhwa, pp. 159–164, and Krishna Kumar Singh, pp. 165–175; Articles 123/213 are connected provisions outside the assigned ranges.

Other uploaded questions: deliberately not misclassified

The papers also ask general federalism/Article 356, territorial cession/new States, Union–State competence, repugnancy/colourable legislation, trade, tribunals, judicial appointments, locus standi and Delhi governance. They belong principally to other syllabus units. They are not fabricated into Topic 4 PYQs merely because they touch the Constitution. The ordinance and executive questions above are included because they directly explain this topic’s accountability architecture.

15 / APPLICATION LAB · NOT PYQs

Turn the rules into answers

Every question in this chapter is an original teaching problem, not an alleged DU examination question. Try an answer before opening the analysis. Use issue → precise rule → authority → application → conclusion.

ORIGINAL PRACTICE

1. The “unpaid” executive chairperson

An MP accepts chairmanship of a State-government council. The terms provide a fixed monthly honorarium, a government car and free accommodation. She signs a letter saying she will draw nothing. A State exemption Act lists the office. Is Parliamentary membership safe?

Worked application

Issue: Article 102(1)(a), not merely whether cash reached her bank account.

Rule and authority: examine an office, under-government relationship, profit capability and Parliamentary exemption. Jaya Bachchan makes entitlement decisive. A genuinely compensatory reimbursement is different from fixed honorarium/valuable attached facilities.

Application: assuming the government nexus is established, refusing to draw benefits does not remove their receivability. The State exemption may help an MLA/MLC under Article 191, but it is not automatically Parliament’s law exempting an MP under Article 102. Inspect the actual Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act, 1959 and the relevant effective exemption, rather than treating one legislature’s exemption as universally binding.

Forum and conclusion: because the office was accepted during MP membership, the Article 103–ECI route is material. The benefit waiver/State list alone does not establish safety. A valid applicable Parliamentary exemption could change the result; Consumer Education governs a properly enacted retrospective cure subject to its no-reinstatement limit.

ORIGINAL PRACTICE

2. Bail is mistaken for eligibility

A non-MLA party leader has a residual-offence conviction with three years’ imprisonment. He obtains bail and suspension of execution, but the conviction-stay application is refused. His party wins a majority and appoints him leader. Can the Governor swear him in for only five months?

Worked application

Rule: RPA 8(3)’s qualifying conviction/sentence presently disqualifies; the facts expressly exclude a conviction stay. Articles 164/173/191 must be harmonised.

Authorities: Kapur is directly analogous. Anand permits a qualified non-member, not a disqualified appointee. Lily leaves no future statutory three-month grace; Lok Prahari distinguishes an actual conviction stay.

Application: jail status is not eligibility. Five rather than six months does not cure the initial incapacity. Majority support cannot override the legal ground. The Governor is not permitted to create a class of ineligible short-term CMs.

Conclusion: the appointment would be invalid and susceptible to quo warranto. If the conviction is later effectively stayed or set aside, assess the changed legal premise separately. Do not retrospectively invent a conviction stay in the original facts.

ORIGINAL PRACTICE

3. Two Houses, two very different deadlocks

A State Council sits on an Assembly-passed ordinary Bill for more than three months. The Assembly repasses it; the Council does not pass it for more than one month. Meanwhile a Union ordinary Bill is rejected by Rajya Sabha. What routes are available?

Worked application

State: Article 197 gives the Council a suspensive veto. After the first trigger the Assembly can repass; after the second trigger the Bill is deemed passed by both in the Assembly’s second-passage form with Council amendments, if any, accepted by the Assembly. No State joint sitting is required or provided. It still must proceed through the applicable assent route.

Union: Article 108 makes rejection a deadlock ground on which the President may notify a joint sitting, subject to its conditions. Other grounds are final amendment disagreement and more than six months’ delay. A true Money Bill is excluded; an ordinary financial Bill is not automatically excluded.

Time detail: the waiting-period computations exclude the specified prorogation/long-adjournment periods. The three-plus-one summary is not a requirement to wait four months after immediate rejection, and does not count time contrary to the Article.

Conclusion: Assembly predominance resolves the State conflict; bicameral deadlock at Union level can be resolved by combined voting. The mechanisms are constitutionally different.

ORIGINAL PRACTICE

4. “It contains a tax, so it is a Money Bill”

A Union Bill creates a wide regulatory licensing regime and also imposes a tax. Another Bill creates an agency requiring expenditure but contains none of Article 110(1)(a)–(f)’s matters. Classify them assuming the regulatory provisions are not merely incidental to the tax.

Worked application

First: Article 110 requires only the listed financial matters and truly incidental provisions. The assumed broad independent regulatory content means it is not a true Money Bill. It is the Article 117(1) financial-Bill category: introduction in Lok Sabha with Presidential recommendation, and ordinary substantive bicameral passage, not Rajya Sabha’s fourteen-day recommendation route.

Second: expenditure alone does not make it a Money Bill. Article 117(3) applies to the spending Bill: it may originate in either House but cannot be passed by a House unless the President recommends consideration to that House. No Article 117(1) restriction is established by the given facts.

Conclusion: distinguish “only enumerated matters,” mixed enumerated matters, and expenditure without those matters. The label “Finance Bill” is not itself the constitutional test. Classification determines origin, recommendation and upper-House power.

ORIGINAL PRACTICE

5. A confidence test, a dissolved House and two clocks

An Assembly’s last sitting was five months ago. It is prematurely dissolved now. Someone argues the ECI has only one month to finish elections, failing which Article 356 must be imposed. Is that inference valid?

Worked application

Issue: whether Article 174(1)’s maximum gap becomes an election deadline after dissolution.

Authority: the Gujarat Election Reference distinguishes a live functional Assembly from a successor. “Its next session” means the same House. A dissolved body cannot be summoned to another session; constitution follows election/RPA machinery.

Application: no outgoing-to-incoming one-month deadline arises from Article 174. Article 324 and the election law govern ECI action. The Court’s scheme-based expectation of elections within six months of dissolution must not be confused with six months from the old last sitting.

Conclusion: reject the automatic Article 356 cure. Require earliest feasible free and fair elections and institutional assistance; do not replace the rejected deadline with unlimited delay authority. If a separate constitutional-breakdown question arises, evaluate Article 356 on its own requirements.

ORIGINAL PRACTICE

6. The court is asked to be a second Privileges Committee

After a fair inquiry an MP is expelled for grave legislative misconduct. He alleges an internal notice-rule departure and asks the court to prefer his interpretation of the video. In another case the House expels without any real opportunity to answer and claims Article 122 prevents all review. Compare.

Worked application

Power: Raja Ram Pal recognises disciplinary expulsion under Article 105(3), distinct from statutory disqualification.

First challenge: mere procedural irregularity is insulated by Article 122; the court is not an evidentiary appeal. A different preferred inference does not establish constitutional invalidity. The challenger must articulate a permitted serious ground.

Second challenge: a gross fair-hearing deprivation may be substantive illegality/unconstitutionality rather than a harmless rule departure. Article 122 is not a blanket wall. Review is available within Raja’s restrained framework; context and actual prejudice matter.

Conclusion: availability of review and success in review are separate. Neither “inside Parliament, no review” nor “a rule was broken, automatic quashing” is correct. Identify the real character of the defect.

ORIGINAL PRACTICE

7. Vote immunity is used to defend a bribe

An MLA allegedly accepts a bribe to vote a certain way in a Rajya Sabha election. She votes differently and says Article 194(2) protects any case connected with that election. Is the immunity defence good?

Worked application

Protected function: do not dismiss the relevant constitutional electoral vote as wholly outside legislative protection simply because it is not a speech during a routine sitting.

Separate wrong: under the seven-judge Sita Soren ruling of 4 March 2024, accepting a bribe fails the functional/necessity test and is not a protected speech or vote. The immunity aspect of P.V. Narasimha Rao was overruled.

Application: the bribe transaction is distinct; casting the promised vote, a different vote or none does not supply bribery immunity. House discipline and criminal proceedings have different consequences and can coexist.

Conclusion: the constitutional immunity defence fails as to bribery. That does not establish guilt: the prosecution still must prove the applicable criminal offence. Do not use an overruled immunity rule as the present answer.

ORIGINAL PRACTICE

8. Majority, quorum and oath are not one calculation

A 200-seat Assembly votes on an Article 169 Council-creation resolution. 120 members vote: 100 yes, 20 no. Separately, an ordinary sitting of a 60-member Assembly has only nine members. An elected member has also voted before Article 188’s oath. Analyse each fact.

Worked application

Creation: Article 169 requires both a majority of total membership and at least two-thirds present and voting. The 100 yes votes exceed two-thirds of 120 (80), but are not more than half of total 200 (101 required). The resolution fails. Passage would still be only the constitutional predicate for a Parliamentary creation law, not automatic establishment.

Quorum: under the default Article 189 rule it is ten or one-tenth, whichever is greater. A 60-member Assembly therefore needs ten, not six. With nine, the presiding officer must adjourn/suspend until quorum exists.

Unauthorised participant: the membership oath differs from the candidature and ministerial oaths. Article 193 imposes the ₹500-per-day penalty for sitting/voting before compliance. Article 189(2) saves institutional proceedings against later discovery of an unentitled participant; it does not excuse that person’s conduct. This saving does not abolish the separate quorum rule.

Conclusion: always identify the denominator, quorum and individual entitlement separately.

Answer-building checklist

  1. Classify the institution, member/status, Bill or sanction precisely.
  2. Choose the controlling Article and its operative clause, not a vaguely connected Article.
  3. Identify the relevant statutory/rule layer and effective judicial order.
  4. Use the case for what it actually decided; separate submissions from holdings.
  5. Apply the legal distinction to the facts, including timing and forum.
  6. State a qualified conclusion and any fact that could change it.

Quick self-test · 12 original checkpoints

Choose one option per question, then check your answers. Explanations remain available even without JavaScript.

01 Which of these is the correct Article 79 composition?
Explanation

The President is part of Parliament, not a member of either House. Article 79.

02 Rajya Sabha’s State representatives are elected by whom?
Explanation

Article 80(4) specifies elected Assembly members and PR by STV, not the entire State legislature.

03 A non-member Minister’s constitutional window is:
Explanation

Articles 75(5)/164(4). Eligibility and confidence remain necessary; serial reappointment cannot defeat the rule.

04 Which order is legally different for conviction disqualification?
Explanation

Kapur and Lok Prahari. Read the actual order, not the label “appeal pending.”

05 Did Lily Thomas decide the separate Article 14 challenge?
Explanation

DU ¶36 expressly leaves Article 14 undecided; Articles 102/191 and vacancy limits control the ratio.

06 A true Money Bill is retained by the upper House for:
Explanation

Articles 109/198. If not returned in fourteen days it is deemed passed in the lower-House form.

07 State ordinary-Bill deadlock is resolved by:
Explanation

No State joint sitting. The first-stage three-month and second-stage one-month/rejection triggers implement the suspensive veto.

08 Charged expenditure is:
Explanation

Articles 113/114 and 203/204. Charging protects an obligation from the grant vote, not from legal appropriation.

09 Articles 122/212 bar review based on:
Explanation

Raja Ram Pal distinguishes irregularity from substantive illegality/unconstitutionality.

10 Profit under Jaya Bachchan depends primarily on:
Explanation

Genuine compensation for actual out-of-pocket expenses is distinct. Government nexus and exemption also require examination.

11 Article 174’s session gap applies after dissolution as an election deadline from the last sitting:
Explanation

Gujarat Reference. Keep the scheme-based expectation from dissolution separate from the rejected session-based deadline.

12 Under Sita Soren2024, a bribe for a legislative vote is:
Explanation

Bribery is a separate offence and fails functional necessity; immunity rejection is not itself proof of guilt.

Choose your answers first.

Exam mistakes to actively avoid

  1. Counting President/Governor as House members because they constitute the legislature.
  2. Reading uncommenced Council-creation text as proof a Council functions today.
  3. Confusing constitutional maximum with actual sanctioned or occupied seats.
  4. Assuming the 2026 census wording means the seat freeze ends automatically on 1 January 2026.
  5. Assuming women’s reservation is operational without Article 334A’s census/delimitation trigger.
  6. Giving non-member Ministers/AG/Advocate-General a vote under 88/177.
  7. Confusing effective majority for presiding-officer removal with Article 169’s dual majority.
  8. Substituting a Speaker’s casting vote for the special first-instance-only removal rule.
  9. Calling every conviction Section 8(3), despite the listed-offence routes.
  10. Copying the uploaded Section 8(4) as valid law after Lily.
  11. Treating ordinary bail or sentence suspension as conviction stay.
  12. Routing defection through 103/192 rather than the Tenth Schedule.
  13. Making a resignation automatically effective without acceptance/genuineness inquiry.
  14. Calling every finance-related Bill a Money Bill or every upper-House action a veto.
  15. Ignoring the word “only” in the Money Bill definition.
  16. Supplying a State joint sitting which the Constitution does not provide.
  17. Calling a grant vote permission to withdraw money without appropriation.
  18. Saying charged expenditure cannot be discussed.
  19. Confusing Article 201’s legislative six months with a Governor/President deadline.
  20. Presenting April 2025 deemed-assent/timeline rules as the later November 2025 opinion.
  21. Assuming every pending Bill lapses, including Rajya-Sabha-only Bills or Bills pending assent.
  22. Claiming privilege either always overrides or always yields to every right.
  23. Recasting Parliamentary constitutional review as a full evidentiary appeal.
  24. Equating a disciplinary expulsion with an independent future electoral bar.
  25. Asserting bribery immunity using the overruled Narasimha Rao position.
  26. Inventing detailed respondent submissions or a final holding absent from the DU/order text.

Five-class learning route

Class 1Architecture, chambers, offices, sessions79–83/168–172; 85–98/174–187; Gujarat/Jha settingClass 2Eligibility, vacancies and ministerial office84/173; 99–104/188–193; RPA; cases 21–24,27–28Class 3Legislative and financial procedure107–120/196–210; Bill routes; grants; assent supplementClass 4Autonomy, rights and constitutional courts105/194; 121–122/211–212; cases 29–30; Sita updateClass 5Case synthesis and timed answer-writingFive direct PYQs; related problems; revision and Article audit

Twenty terms in usable language

Adjournment
Interruption of a sitting without ending the session.
Prorogation
Termination of a session; the House itself survives.
Dissolution
Termination of the lower House, triggering a new representative body.
Sine die
Adjournment without fixing the next sitting date; not itself dissolution.
Quorum
Minimum membership present required for the meeting under the applicable rule.
Present and voting
The voting denominator excluding those present who abstain.
Effective majority
Majority of all then members in the specified removal context; distinguish sanctioned total and votes cast.
Casting vote
Tie-breaking vote of the presiding officer under the ordinary rule.
Office of profit
Government-linked office capable of yielding relevant personal pecuniary gain, unless exempt.
Qualification
Positive condition for membership, such as citizenship and minimum age.
Disqualification
Constitutional/statutory legal bar to being chosen or continuing membership.
Expulsion
Disciplinary termination of current membership, not by itself a lasting electoral bar.
Conviction stay
Specific judicial suspension of the conviction’s present operation; not merely bail.
Quo warranto
Judicial inquiry into the legal authority to hold a public office.
Habeas corpus
Judicial remedy testing legal authority for detention.
Money Bill
Bill confined to the enumerated financial matters and genuine incidental provisions.
Charged expenditure
Protected from submission to grant vote but discussable and appropriated.
Appropriation
Legal authorisation to withdraw from the Consolidated Fund for the authorised purposes.
Privilege
Functionally justified institutional/member protection enabling legislative duties.
Procedural irregularity
Internal procedural defect, distinct from jurisdictional or substantive constitutional illegality.

A final 90-second answer audit

Have you used the correct House and clause? Have you named the legal trigger and forum? Have you separated source facts, party submissions and judicial holding? Have you applied rather than merely listed cases? Have you acknowledged a dated supplement where relied on? If yes, the answer is structurally strong.

Time planning: for a three-hour, five-question paper, reserving 10–15 minutes for planning/review leaves roughly 33–34 minutes per full 20-mark answer, or 16–17 minutes per 10-mark part. These expanded study models should be compressed accordingly.

  1. Government of India Constitution · as on 1 May 2024

    Supplement for the DU-prescribed case absent as a standalone extract. Actual paragraphs 1–10 control, particularly the interim character and floor-test directions. AI/blog claims of a final mala-fides/fraud judgment were not adopted.

    Reported-order text

    Full judgment

    Full judgment supplement to DU p.126. Amendment chronology, Sections 4(1)/(2), party submissions, retrospectivity, election-stage distinction, declaration, Article 14 and committee-practice reasoning. Particularly ¶¶1–20 and 23–40.

    Full judgment

    Full Special Reference opinion supplements the DU Raja account. ¶¶1–30 facts/submissions; ¶¶141–146 majority answers; ¶147 onward Sarkar dissent; ¶155 on judicial interpretation, ¶¶209–221 on the nuanced answers, and ¶227 declining the abstract judicial-immunity question.

    Full majority and dissent

    Official five-judge opinion, Special Reference 1/2025, In Re: Assent, Withholding or Reservation of Bills by the Governor and President of India. ¶¶98–102 verify the options after repassage. ¶165.1–165.14 supply conclusions on discretion, inaction review, timelines and deemed assent.     Official 111-page opinion

Open the four source pages used for the verified question inventory

Currency, completeness and use

Prepared 30 September 2026. The teaching baseline is DU 2022; the Constitution text is the official 1 May 2024 edition; later additions are individually dated and bounded. No claim is made that every amendment, latest office-holder, current seat occupancy, State-specific exemption, institution-specific rule change or judgment through preparation date has been exhaustively checked.

This is a comprehensive academic study guide to the assigned ranges and supplied material, not personalised legal advice or a replacement for authoritative law in litigation. Quotations should be checked against the official PDF where precision is critical. Sources are clickable when online; the complete study content, diagrams, quizzes and reference text work without network access.

79Constitution of Parliament

There shall be a Parliament for the Union which shall consist of the President and two Houses to be known respectively as the Council of States and the House of the People.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 79 · Read the explanation →

80Composition of the Council of States

(1) The Council of States shall consist of— (a) twelve members to be nominated by the President in accordance with the provisions of clause (3); and (b) not more than two hundred and thirty-eight representatives of the States and of the Union territories.

(2) The allocation of seats in the Council of States to be filled by representatives of the States and of the Union territories shall be in accordance with the provisions in that behalf contained in the Fourth Schedule.

(3) The members to be nominated by the President under sub-clause (a) of clause (1) shall consist of persons having special knowledge or practical experience in respect of such matters as the following, namely:— Literature, science, art and social service.

(4) The representatives of each State in the Council of States shall be elected by the elected members of the Legislative Assembly of the State in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote.

(5) The representatives of the Union territories in the Council of States shall be chosen in such manner as Parliament may by law prescribe.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 80 · Read the explanation →

81Composition of the House of the People

(1) Subject to the provisions of article 331, the House of the People shall consist of— (a) not more than five hundred and thirty members chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies in the States; and (b) not more than twenty members to represent the Union territories, chosen in such manner as Parliament may by law provide.

(2) For the purposes of sub-clause (a) of clause (1),— (a) there shall be allotted to each State a number of seats in the House of the People in such manner that the ratio between that number and the population of the State is, so far as practicable, the same for all States; and (b) each State shall be divided into territorial constituencies in such manner that the ratio between the population of each constituency and the number of seats allotted to it is, so far as practicable, the same throughout the State: Provided that the provisions of sub-clause (a) of this clause shall not be applicable for the purpose of allotment of seats in the House of the People to any State so long as the population of that State does not exceed six millions.

(3) In this article, the expression “population” means the population as ascertained at the last preceding census of which the relevant figures have been published: Provided that the reference in this clause to the last preceding census of which the relevant figures have been published shall, until the relevant figures for the first census taken after the year 2026 have been published, be construed,— (i) for the purposes of sub-clause (a) of clause (2) and the proviso to that clause, as a reference to the 1971 census; and (ii) for the purposes of sub-clause (b) of clause (2) as a reference to the 2001 census.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 81 · Read the explanation →

82Readjustment after each census

Upon the completion of each census, the allocation of seats in the House of the People to the States and the division of each State into territorial constituencies shall be readjusted by such authority and in such manner as Parliament may by law determine: Provided that such readjustment shall not affect representation in the House of the People until the dissolution of the then existing House: Provided further that such readjustment shall take effect from such date as the President may, by order, specify and until such readjustment takes effect, any election to the House may be held on the basis of the territorial constituencies existing before such readjustment: Provided also that until the relevant figures for the first census taken after the year 2026 have been published, it shall not be necessary to readjust,— (i) the allocation of seats in the House of the People to the States as readjusted on the basis of the 1971 census; and (ii) the division of each State into territorial constituencies as may be readjusted on the basis of the 2001 census, under this article.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 82 · Read the explanation →

83Duration of Houses of Parliament

(1) The Council of States shall not be subject to dissolution, but as nearly as possible one-third of the members thereof shall retire as soon as may be on the expiration of every second year in accordance with the provisions made in that behalf by Parliament by law.

(2) The House of the People, unless sooner dissolved, shall continue for five years from the date appointed for its first meeting and no longer and the expiration of the said period of five years shall operate as a dissolution of the House: Provided that the said period may, while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, be extended by Parliament by law for a period not exceeding one year at a time and not extending in any case beyond a period of six months after the Proclamation has ceased to operate.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 83 · Read the explanation →

84Qualification for membership of Parliament

A person shall not be qualified to be chosen to fill a seat in Parliament unless he— (a) is a citizen of India, and makes and subscribes before some person authorised in that behalf by the Election Commission an oath or affirmation according to the form set out for the purpose in the Third Schedule; (b) is, in the case of a seat in the Council of States, not less than thirty years of age and, in the case of a seat in the House of the People, not less than twenty-five years of age; and (c) possesses such other qualifications as may be prescribed in that behalf by or under any law made by Parliament.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 84 · Read the explanation →

85Sessions of Parliament, prorogation and dissolution

(1) The President shall from time to time summon each House of Parliament to meet at such time and place as he thinks fit, but six months shall not intervene between its last sitting in one session and the date appointed for its first sitting in the next session.

(2) The President may from time to time— (a) prorogue the Houses or either House; (b) dissolve the House of the People.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 85 · Read the explanation →

86Right of President to address and send messages to Houses

(1) The President may address either House of Parliament or both Houses assembled together, and for that purpose require the attendance of members.

(2) The President may send messages to either House of Parliament, whether with respect to a Bill then pending in Parliament or otherwise, and a House to which any message is so sent shall with all convenient despatch consider any matter required by the message to be taken into consideration.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 86 · Read the explanation →

87Special address by the President

(1) At the commencement of the first session after each general election to the House of the People and at the commencement of the first session of each year the President shall address both Houses of Parliament assembled together and inform Parliament of the causes of its summons.

(2) Provision shall be made by the rules regulating the procedure of either House for the allotment of time for discussion of the matters referred to in such address.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 87 · Read the explanation →

88Rights of Ministers and Attorney-General as respects Houses

Every Minister and the Attorney-General of India shall have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, either House, any joint sitting of the Houses, and any committee of Parliament of which he may be named a member, but shall not by virtue of this article be entitled to vote.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 88 · Read the explanation →

89The Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Council of States

(1) The Vice- President of India shall be ex officio Chairman of the Council of States.

(2) The Council of States shall, as soon as may be, choose a member of the Council to be Deputy Chairman thereof and, so often as the office of Deputy Chairman becomes vacant, the Council shall choose another member to be Deputy Chairman thereof.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 89 · Read the explanation →

90Vacation and resignation of, and removal from, the office of Deputy Chairman

A member holding office as Deputy Chairman of the Council of States— (a) shall vacate his office if he ceases to be a member of the Council; (b) may at any time, by writing under his hand addressed to the Chairman, resign his office; and (c) may be removed from his office by a resolution of the Council passed by a majority of all the then members of the Council: Provided that no resolution for the purpose of clause (c) shall be moved unless at least fourteen days’ notice has been given of the intention to move the resolution.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 90 · Read the explanation →

91Power of the Deputy Chairman or other person to perform the duties of the office of, or to act as, Chairman

(1) While the office of Chairman is vacant, or during any period when the Vice-President is acting as, or discharging the functions of, President, the duties of the office shall be performed by the Deputy Chairman, or, if the office of Deputy Chairman is also vacant, by such member of the Council of States as the President may appoint for the purpose.

(2) During the absence of the Chairman from any sitting of the Council of States the Deputy Chairman, or, if he is also absent, such person as may be determined by the rules of procedure of the Council, or, if no such person is present, such other person as may be determined by the Council, shall act as Chairman.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 91 · Read the explanation →

92The Chairman or the Deputy Chairman not to preside while a resolution for his removal from office is under consideration

(1) At any sitting of the Council of States, while any resolution for the removal of the Vice-President from his office is under consideration, the Chairman, or while any resolution for the removal of the Deputy Chairman from his office is under consideration, the Deputy Chairman, shall not, though he is present, preside, and the provisions of clause (2) of article 91 shall apply in relation to every such sitting as they apply in relation to a sitting from which the Chairman, or, as the case may be, the Deputy Chairman, is absent.

(2) The Chairman shall have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, the Council of States while any resolution for the removal of the Vice-President from his office is under consideration in the Council, but, notwithstanding anything in article 100, shall not be entitled to vote at all on such resolution or on any other matter during such proceedings.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 92 · Read the explanation →

93The Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of the People

The House of the People shall, as soon as may be, choose two members of the House to be respectively Speaker and Deputy Speaker thereof and, so often as the office of Speaker or Deputy Speaker becomes vacant, the House shall choose another member to be Speaker or Deputy Speaker, as the case may be.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 93 · Read the explanation →

94Vacation and resignation of, and removal from, the offices of Speaker and Deputy Speaker

A member holding office as Speaker or Deputy Speaker of the House of the People— (a) shall vacate his office if he ceases to be a member of the House of the People; (b) may at any time, by writing under his hand addressed, if such member is the Speaker, to the Deputy Speaker, and if such member is the Deputy Speaker, to the Speaker, resign his office; and (c) may be removed from his office by a resolution of the House of the People passed by a majority of all the then members of the House: Provided that no resolution for the purpose of clause (c) shall be moved unless at least fourteen days’ notice has been given of the intention to move the resolution: Provided further that, whenever the House of the People is dissolved, the Speaker shall not vacate his office until immediately before the first meeting of the House of the People after the dissolution.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 94 · Read the explanation →

95Power of the Deputy Speaker or other person to perform the duties of the office of, or to act as, Speaker

(1) While the office of Speaker is vacant, the duties of the office shall be performed by the Deputy Speaker or, if the office of Deputy Speaker is also vacant, by such member of the House of the People as the President may appoint for the purpose.

(2) During the absence of the Speaker from any sitting of the House of the People the Deputy Speaker or, if he is also absent, such person as may be determined by the rules of procedure of the House, or, if no such person is present, such other person as may be determined by the House, shall act as Speaker.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 95 · Read the explanation →

96The Speaker or the Deputy Speaker not to preside while a resolution for his removal from office is under consideration

(1) At any sitting of the House of the People, while any resolution for the removal of the Speaker from his office is under consideration, the Speaker, or while any resolution for the removal of the Deputy Speaker from his office is under consideration, the Deputy Speaker, shall not, though he is present, preside, and the provisions of clause (2) of article 95 shall apply in relation to every such sitting as they apply in relation to a sitting from which the Speaker, or, as the case may be, the Deputy Speaker, is absent.

(2) The Speaker shall have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, the House of the People while any resolution for his removal from office is under consideration in the House and shall, notwithstanding anything in article 100, be entitled to vote only in the first instance on such resolution or on any other matter during such proceedings but not in the case of an equality of votes.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 96 · Read the explanation →

97Salaries and allowances of the Chairman and Deputy Chairman and the Speaker and Deputy Speaker

There shall be paid to the Chairman and the Deputy Chairman of the Council of States, and to the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the House of the People, such salaries and allowances as may be respectively fixed by Parliament by law and, until provision in that behalf is so made, such salaries and allowances as are specified in the Second Schedule.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 97 · Read the explanation →

98Secretariat of Parliament

(1) Each House of Parliament shall have a separate secretarial staff: Provided that nothing in this clause shall be construed as preventing the creation of posts common to both Houses of Parliament.

(2) Parliament may by law regulate the recruitment, and the conditions of service of persons appointed, to the secretarial staff of either House of Parliament.

(3) Until provision is made by Parliament under clause (2), the President may, after consultation with the Speaker of the House of the People or the Chairman of the Council of States, as the case may be, make rules regulating the recruitment, and the conditions of service of persons appointed, to the secretarial staff of the House of the People or the Council of States, and any rules so made shall have effect subject to the provisions of any law made under the said clause.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 98 · Read the explanation →

99Oath or affirmation by members

Every member of either House of Parliament shall, before taking his seat, make and subscribe before the President, or some person appointed in that behalf by him, an oath or affirmation according to the form set out for the purpose in the Third Schedule.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 99 · Read the explanation →

100Voting in Houses, power of Houses to act notwithstanding vacancies and quorum

(1) Save as otherwise provided in this Constitution, all questions at any sitting of either House or joint sitting of the Houses shall be determined by a majority of votes of the members present and voting, other than the Speaker or person acting as Chairman or Speaker. The Chairman or Speaker, or person acting as such, shall not vote in the first instance, but shall have and exercise a casting vote in the case of an equality of votes.

(2) Either House of Parliament shall have power to act notwithstanding any vacancy in the membership thereof, and any proceedings in Parliament shall be valid notwithstanding that it is discovered subsequently that some person who was not entitled so to do sat or voted or otherwise took part in the proceedings.

(3) Until Parliament by law otherwise provides, the quorum to constitute a meeting of either House of Parliament shall be one-tenth of the total number of members of the House.

(4) If at any time during a meeting of a House there is no quorum, it shall be the duty of the Chairman or Speaker, or person acting as such, either to adjourn the House or to suspend the meeting until there is a quorum.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 100 · Read the explanation →

101Vacation of seats

(1) No person shall be a member of both Houses of Parliament and provision shall be made by Parliament by law for the vacation by a person who is chosen a member of both Houses of his seat in one House or the other.

(2) No person shall be a member both of Parliament and of a House of the Legislature of a State, and if a person is chosen a member both of Parliament and of a House of the Legislature of a State, then, at the expiration of such period as may be specified in rules made by the President, that person’s seat in Parliament shall become vacant, unless he has previously resigned his seat in the Legislature of the State.

(3) If a member of either House of Parliament— (a) becomes subject to any of the disqualifications mentioned in clause (1) or clause (2) of article 102; or (b) resigns his seat by writing under his hand addressed to the Chairman or the Speaker, as the case may be, and his resignation is accepted by the Chairman or the Speaker, as the case may be, his seat shall thereupon become vacant: Provided that in the case of any resignation referred to in sub-clause (b), if from information received or otherwise and after making such inquiry as he thinks fit, the Chairman or the Speaker, as the case may be, is satisfied that such resignation is not voluntary or genuine, he shall not accept such resignation.

(4) If for a period of sixty days a member of either House of Parliament is without permission of the House absent from all meetings thereof, the House may declare his seat vacant: Provided that in computing the said period of sixty days no account shall be taken of any period during which the House is prorogued or is adjourned for more than four consecutive days.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 101 · Read the explanation →

102Disqualifications for membership

(1) A person shall be disqualified for being chosen as, and for being, a member of either House of Parliament— (a) if he holds any office of profit under the Government of India or the Government of any State, other than an office declared by Parliament by law not to disqualify its holder; (b) if he is of unsound mind and stands so declared by a competent court; (c) if he is an undischarged insolvent; (d) if he is not a citizen of India, or has voluntarily acquired the citizenship of a foreign State, or is under any acknowledgment of allegiance or adherence to a foreign State; (e) if he is so disqualified by or under any law made by Parliament.

Explanation.—For the purposes of this clause a person shall not be deemed to hold an office of profit under the Government of India or the Government of any State by reason only that he is a Minister either for the Union or for such State.

(2) A person shall be disqualified for being a member of either House of Parliament if he is so disqualified under the Tenth Schedule.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 102 · Read the explanation →

103Decision on questions as to disqualifications of members

(1) If any question arises as to whether a member of either House of Parliament has become subject to any of the disqualifications mentioned in clause (1) of article 102, the question shall be referred for the decision of the President and his decision shall be final.

(2) Before giving any decision on any such question, the President shall obtain the opinion of the Election Commission and shall act according to such opinion.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 103 · Read the explanation →

104Penalty for sitting and voting before making oath or affirmation under article 99 or when not qualified or when disqualified

If a person sits or votes as a member of either House of Parliament before he has complied with the requirements of article 99, or when he knows that he is not qualified or that he is disqualified for membership thereof, or that he is prohibited from so doing by the provisions of any law made by Parliament, he shall be liable in respect of each day on which he so sits or votes to a penalty of five hundred rupees to be recovered as a debt due to the Union.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 104 · Read the explanation →

105Powers, privileges, etc., of the Houses of Parliament and of the members and committees thereof

(1) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution and to the rules and standing orders regulating the procedure of Parliament, there shall be freedom of speech in Parliament.

(2) No member of Parliament shall be liable to any proceedings in any court in respect of anything said or any vote given by him in Parliament or any committee thereof, and no person shall be so liable in respect of the publication by or under the authority of either House of Parliament of any report, paper, votes or proceedings.

(3) In other respects, the powers, privileges and immunities of each House of Parliament, and of the members and the committees of each House, shall be such as may from time to time be defined by Parliament by law, and, until so defined, shall be those of that House and of its members and committees immediately before the coming into force of section 15 of the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978.

(4) The provisions of clauses (1), (2) and (3) shall apply in relation to persons who by virtue of this Constitution have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, a House of Parliament or any committee thereof as they apply in relation to members of Parliament.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 105 · Read the explanation →

106Salaries and allowances of members

Members of either House of Parliament shall be entitled to receive such salaries and allowances as may from time to time be determined by Parliament by law and, until provision in that respect is so made, allowances at such rates and upon such conditions as were immediately before the commencement of this Constitution applicable in the case of members of the Constituent Assembly of the Dominion of India.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 106 · Read the explanation →

107Provisions as to introduction and passing of Bills

(1) Subject to the provisions of articles 109 and 117 with respect to Money Bills and other financial Bills, a Bill may originate in either House of Parliament.

(2) Subject to the provisions of articles 108 and 109, a Bill shall not be deemed to have been passed by the Houses of Parliament unless it has been agreed to by both Houses, either without amendment or with such amendments only as are agreed to by both Houses.

(3) A Bill pending in Parliament shall not lapse by reason of the prorogation of the Houses.

(4) A Bill pending in the Council of States which has not been passed by the House of the People shall not lapse on a dissolution of the House of the People.

(5) A Bill which is pending in the House of the People, or which having been passed by the House of the People is pending in the Council of States, shall, subject to the provisions of article 108, lapse on a dissolution of the House of the People.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 107 · Read the explanation →

108Joint sitting of both Houses in certain cases

(1) If after a Bill has been passed by one House and transmitted to the other House— (a) the Bill is rejected by the other House; or (b) the Houses have finally disagreed as to the amendments to be made in the Bill; or (c) more than six months elapse from the date of the reception of the Bill by the other House without the Bill being passed by it, the President may, unless the Bill has elapsed by reason of a dissolution of the House of the People, notify to the Houses by message if they are sitting or by public notification if they are not sitting, his intention to summon them to meet in a joint sitting for the purpose of deliberating and voting on the Bill: Provided that nothing in this clause shall apply to a Money Bill.

(2) In reckoning any such period of six months as is referred to in clause (1), no account shall be taken of any period during which the House referred to in sub-clause (c) of that clause is prorogued or adjourned for more than four consecutive days.

(3) Where the President has under clause (1) notified his intention of summoning the Houses to meet in a joint sitting, neither House shall proceed further with the Bill, but the President may at any time after the date of his notification summon the Houses to meet in a joint sitting for the purpose specified in the notification and, if he does so, the Houses shall meet accordingly.

(4) If at the joint sitting of the two Houses the Bill, with such amendments, if any, as are agreed to in joint sitting, is passed by a majority of the total number of members of both Houses present and voting, it shall be deemed for the purposes of this Constitution to have been passed by both Houses: Provided that at a joint sitting— (a) if the Bill, having been passed by one House, has not been passed by the other House with amendments and returned to the House in which it originated, no amendment shall be proposed to the Bill other than such amendments (if any) as are made necessary by the delay in the passage of the Bill; (b) if the Bill has been so passed and returned, only such amendments as aforesaid shall be proposed to the Bill and such other amendments as are relevant to the matters with respect to which the Houses have not agreed, and the decision of the person presiding as to the amendments which are admissible under this clause shall be final.

(5) A joint sitting may be held under this article and a Bill passed thereat, notwithstanding that a dissolution of the House of the People has intervened since the President notified his intention to summon the Houses to meet therein.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 108 · Read the explanation →

109Special procedure in respect of Money Bills

(1) A Money Bill shall not be introduced in the Council of States.

(2) After a Money Bill has been passed by the House of the People it shall be transmitted to the Council of States for its recommendations and the Council of States shall within a period of fourteen days from the date of its receipt of the Bill return the Bill to the House of the People with its recommendations and the House of the People may thereupon either accept or reject all or any of the recommendations of the Council of States.

(3) If the House of the People accepts any of the recommendations of the Council of States, the Money Bill shall be deemed to have been passed by both Houses with the amendments recommended by the Council of States and accepted by the House of the People.

(4) If the House of the People does not accept any of the recommendations of the Council of States, the Money Bill shall be deemed to have been passed by both Houses in the form in which it was passed by the House of the People without any of the amendments recommended by the Council of States.

(5) If a Money Bill passed by the House of the People and transmitted to the Council of States for its recommendations is not returned to the House of the People within the said period of fourteen days, it shall be deemed to have been passed by both Houses at the expiration of the said period in the form in which it was passed by the House of the People.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 109 · Read the explanation →

110Definition of “Money Bills”

(1) For the purposes of this Chapter, a Bill shall be deemed to be a Money Bill if it contains only provisions dealing with all or any of the following matters, namely:— (a) the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax; (b) the regulation of the borrowing of money or the giving of any guarantee by the Government of India, or the amendment of the law with respect to any financial obligations undertaken or to be undertaken by the Government of India; (c) the custody of the Consolidated Fund or the Contingency Fund of India, the payment of moneys into or the withdrawal of moneys from any such Fund; (d) the appropriation of moneys out of the Consolidated Fund of India; (e) the declaring of any expenditure to be expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India or the increasing of the amount of any such expenditure; (f) the receipt of money on account of the Consolidated Fund of India or the public account of India or the custody or issue of such money or the audit of the accounts of the Union or of a State; or (g) any matter incidental to any of the matters specified in sub-clauses (a) to (f).

(2) A Bill shall not be deemed to be a Money Bill by reason only that it provides for the imposition of fines or other pecuniary penalties, or for the demand or payment of fees for licences or fees for services rendered, or by reason that it provides for the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax by any local authority or body for local purposes.

(3) If any question arises whether a Bill is a Money Bill or not, the decision of the Speaker of the House of the People thereon shall be final.

(4) There shall be endorsed on every Money Bill when it is transmitted to the Council of States under article 109, and when it is presented to the President for assent under article 111, the certificate of the Speaker of the House of the People signed by him that it is a Money Bill.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 110 · Read the explanation →

111Assent to Bills

When a Bill has been passed by the Houses of Parliament, it shall be presented to the President, and the President shall declare either that he assents to the Bill, or that he withholds assent therefrom: Provided that the President may, as soon as possible after the presentation to him of a Bill for assent, return the Bill if it is not a Money Bill to the Houses with a message requesting that they will reconsider the Bill or any specified provisions thereof and, in particular, will consider the desirability of introducing any such amendments as he may recommend in his message, and when a Bill is so returned, the Houses shall reconsider the Bill accordingly, and if the Bill is passed again by the Houses with or without amendment and presented to the President for assent, the President shall not withhold assent therefrom.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 111 · Read the explanation →

112Annual financial statement

(1) The President shall in respect of every financial year cause to be laid before both the Houses of Parliament a statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government of India for that year, in this Part referred to as the "annual financial statement''.

(2) The estimates of expenditure embodied in the annual financial statement shall show separately— (a) the sums required to meet expenditure described by this Constitution as expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India; and (b) the sums required to meet other expenditure proposed to be made from the Consolidated Fund of India, and shall distinguish expenditure on revenue account from other expenditure.

(3) The following expenditure shall be expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India— (a) the emoluments and allowances of the President and other expenditure relating to his office; (b) the salaries and allowances of the Chairman and the Deputy Chairman of the Council of States and the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the House of the People; (c) debt charges for which the Government of India is liable including interest, sinking fund charges and redemption charges, and other expenditure relating to the raising of loans and the service and redemption of debt; (d) (i) the salaries, allowances and pensions payable to or in respect of Judges of the Supreme Court; (ii) the pensions payable to or in respect of Judges of the Federal Court; (iii) the pensions payable to or in respect of Judges of any High Court which exercises jurisdiction in relation to any area included in the territory of India or which at any time before the commencement of this Constitution exercised jurisdiction in relation to any area included in a Governor's Province of the Dominion of India; (e) the salary, allowances and pension payable to or in respect of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India; (f) any sums required to satisfy any judgment, decree or award of any court or arbitral tribunal; (g) any other expenditure declared by this Constitution or by Parliament by law to be so charged.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 112 · Read the explanation →

113Procedure in Parliament with respect to estimates

(1) So much of the estimates as relates to expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India shall not be submitted to the vote of Parliament, but nothing in this clause shall be construed as preventing the discussion in either House of Parliament of any of those estimates.

(2) So much of the said estimates as relates to other expenditure shall be submitted in the form of demands for grants to the House of the People, and the House of the People shall have power to assent, or to refuse to assent, to any demand, or to assent to any demand subject to a reduction of the amount specified therein.

(3) No demand for a grant shall be made except on the recommendation of the President.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 113 · Read the explanation →

114Appropriation Bills

(1) As soon as may be after the grants under article 113 have been made by the House of the People, there shall be introduced a Bill to provide for the appropriation out of the Consolidated Fund of India of all moneys required to meet— (a) the grants so made by the House of the People; and (b) the expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India but not exceeding in any case the amount shown in the statement previously laid before Parliament.

(2) No amendment shall be proposed to any such Bill in either House of Parliament which will have the effect of varying the amount or altering the destination of any grant so made or of varying the amount of any expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, and the decision of the person presiding as to whether an amendment is inadmissible under this clause shall be final.

(3) Subject to the provisions of articles 115 and 116, no money shall be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India except under appropriation made by law passed in accordance with the provisions of this article.

Official Constitution,1 May 2024 edition · Article 114 · Read the explanation →

115Supplementary, additional or excess grants
